descs.en: The boy next door followed her to university and stayed “unofficial” for years. She loves him. She just doesn’t know how to go from friends to forever.

titles.en: The Boy Next Door Never Left

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Eliana Lin and Wang Yu Chen grew up next door to each other in the Walled City, with a knee-high wall between their front steps. On the night she finishes school she can't sleep and goes to sit on her step at two in the morning. He comes out with his blanket and sits down beside her, and somewhere before dawn he realises he's in love with her. In the morning he turns down the better medical school in the north and follows her up the hill. He tells everyone it was the course.

She works it out in a fortnight and climbs onto his roof at Mid-Autumn to tell him to stop hovering. He kisses her before she's finished the sentence. After that they're together, in secret, because that's how she wants it. She's the youngest Lin, born the night her mother died, and her father can barely look at her. At night, on five screens, she cleans the family's name out of places it shouldn't be, for Chen Si, and tells nobody. Yu Chen never asks her to stop. He brings tea.

Nobody cheats, and nothing hangs on a misunderstanding. The hard parts are being seen (holding his hand on the hill in daylight), a father who has never once asked her what she wants, and one word she has been afraid of all her life, because people say forever and then they're in a hospital. He's willing to wait, and he won't pretend he isn't.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Eliana has been in the corner of every Lin book so far: asleep under a ladder, filming everyone's kisses for the spreadsheet, opening Haozhen's phone in under four minutes. I kept wondering who was waiting for her on the kerb when she got home.

Yu Chen looks like the clean one, and mostly he is. But he reads her food orders every night because they're on his card, he picked his medical school because of her, and he lied once, to his face, to the cousin who raised him. I didn't want the book to tell him off for any of that. What I love most about him is that in seven years he never once asks her to be someone else. He makes more tea.

This is the softest book I've written since The Softest Kind of Love. They're adults the whole way through and they get together early. Their first times are shy and clumsy, with a lot of laughing and starting again, because he researches everything and she wrecks the plan. Her father is hard on her, and there's a death in an emergency department and a bad morning at the flower market. Nobody has a baby. They get a porch, a jar in a wall and two desks facing each other.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a 21+ friends-to-lovers romance, gentle and funny for most of its length, but it has some hard moments:

• Love scenes throughout, heated and detailed but not explicit, from He Researched This Part Too on

• A mother who died giving birth, mentioned, and a father's grief and coldness towards the daughter she had (throughout; most of all Nineteen, and Nobody Says It, The Neighbour and the Cold Gaze, The First Lin Child to Say No to His Face and Elowen Takes Her Side)

• The heroine's secret work for a crime syndicate, and a man's hands broken because of something she found, mentioned (He Already Knew)

• A sister abducted, and human trafficking referred to but not shown (The Fence, The Photograph)

• A nineteen-year-old's death after a road accident, with resuscitation in an emergency department (The Night He Lost One)

• Threatening messages and photographs from strangers (The Boy Next Door, He Always Waits)

• A cyber-attack on the family, a crowd stampede, a crushed leg and heavy bleeding (The Breach, Thirty-Six Hours, Someone Else's Blood)

• An attack with a broken bottle at work, a head injury and stitches (The Ring in the Jar)

• A partner who reads her food orders to know when she hasn't eaten, and a lie told to the police for her, shown without judgement (He Already Knew, The Detective Already Knows)

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Yu-er — Eliana's family name. Her sisters use it when they want something. Yu Chen uses it all the time, and it's the only time it comes without a favour attached.
The tall house — the Lin family house in the Walled City: old, narrow, too many stairs, a red door, and three front steps under a small tiled roof.
The porch — those three steps, with the crack in the third one, where everything that matters between them happens at two in the morning. From 2026 it runs the width of both houses.
The old Song house — next door to the Lins. Yu Chen's uncle's house, which he bought from Wei Long; later rebuilt with one long room and two desks facing each other.
The persimmon tree — in the Song garden. Its best branch hangs over the Lin side, so by old neighbourly rule its fruit are Lin persimmons. Ripe every October.
The jar — a plum-jam jar of Nainai's, kept behind a loose brick in the garden wall under the persimmon branch. Notes go in it. You don't read one until the writer has gone inside.
The Eraser — what the Syndicate calls Eliana, because she erases the Lin family's footprints. She hates the name.
The fence — what she built in October 2022, after her sister was taken: a watch on the family's names, faces and addresses that wakes her wherever she is. Two short buzzes mean family.
FENCE — her own security firm, from March 2026, in two rooms above a dumpling shop on Terrace Road. For the first month the sign was a sticky note: FENCE. Legal. Mostly.
The Spreadsheet — Eliana's record of every family secret, kept for years. "You're on a spreadsheet" is a warning.
DRAW (OFFICIAL) — Eliana's caption on the video of the paper twins' birthday party at Fig Tree Lane. Raiden contests it every year.
Red egg — a boiled egg dyed red, a traditional birthday gift. One is left at Eliana's door before dawn every 18 February. She thinks for years she knows who leaves it.
Study room 4B — the quiet room at the end of the library's fourth floor, booked to "Wang Y.C." every weekday morning since March 2022. Nobody has ever found out how.
Graduate-entry medicine — a four-year medical degree for students who already have a first degree. Yu Chen's, at the university on the hill, 2021 to 2025.
OSCE — the practical part of medical finals: timed stations with examiners and actors playing patients.
Mid-Autumn — the harvest festival at the full moon of the eighth lunar month: mooncakes, family dinners and lanterns. Every year Yu Chen puts a white rabbit lantern on his roof.
PLAN — Yu Chen's plans, in capitals, on small squares of paper. PLAN, PLAN B, PLAN C. She wrecks every one.
Nainai — grandmother on the father's side. Yu Chen's lives in the north and has had a letter from him every month for years.
The Lins, the Wangs and the Songs — Yu Chen's father was a Wang from the north, the younger brother of Xing Yue's father. His mother was a Song, Wei Long's aunt, which is how he came to live in the old Song house next door to the Lins.

chapters.title: The Boy Next Door Who Never Left
chapters.desc: The night she finishes school, Eliana can’t sleep and goes to sit on her front step at two in the morning. Yu Chen brings his blanket out and sits with her, and before it gets light he works out that he’s in love with her.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to talk. I’ll just sit here. That’s allowed.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
Yu Chen had three emails, and he’d been reading them on his front step for an hour, like they might change. They didn’t.

The medical school in the north was the better school. It was an hour on the train from Nainai, who ended every letter with The north has better doctors and better weather, underlined twice. Then the university on the hill, on the far side of the city. Then the polytechnic, where he’d sat his last paper two weeks ago, offering him a master’s with the fees paid.

All three wanted an answer by the end of June. He hadn’t told a soul about any of them.

Auntie Dai came out behind him with her shopping trolley.

“Soup’s on the stove.”

“Thank you.”

“Eat it. Don’t look at it. Eat it.”

“I’ll eat it.”

She peered at the phone in his hand.

“What’s that?”

“Emails.”

“From who?”

“Some schools.”

“Which schools?”

“…Schools.”

“You’ve been sitting there since four. The step isn’t going anywhere.”

She clicked her tongue at him and went off down the lane, one trolley wheel squeaking the whole way.

His phone buzzed. The course group chat.

Biomed 2021: LEAVING DRINKS TONIGHT. yu chen you’re coming, no excuses!!

He typed Sorry, can’t. Have a good night. Then he muted it.

Twenty-one. A degree, nearly. A house. His father’s money, which he’d been allowed to touch since January and hadn’t. And he couldn’t pick one email out of three. Brilliant.

The lane had gone orange. Past the tall house, the old man was singing to his birds again, badly. Then she came round the corner.

Alone. School bag on one shoulder. Hood down for once, because of the heat, and her hair escaping its pencil. She was eating a green ice lolly and frowning at her phone like it owed her money. She looked up, saw him, and lifted the lolly.

He lifted a hand.

“Finished?”

“Chemistry.”

She stopped at the bottom of her own three steps. They were an arm’s length from his, with the knee-high wall and its iron rail between them. Green juice was running down her wrist. She licked it off.

“It was fine. I finished early and sat there for forty minutes doing nothing. The man at the front kept checking I was alive.”

“What flavour is that?”

“Green.”

“Green isn’t a flavour.”

“It is now.”

“Well done, anyway.”

She stared at him. Like he’d said it in French.

“…Yeah.”

Then she went up her steps, and the red door shut.

No car in the lane. Lin Jian would be at the fishing-net building. Ah Sim would have left noodles. Was that it? Was that the whole party? He went in and ate the soup. He didn’t answer any of the emails.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning her light was still on. He could see it from his desk if he leaned back far enough to nearly fall off the chair. Top window of the tall house. Blackout curtains that never quite met. One white line down the middle.

In front of him was a sheet of paper with three columns. Under the north he’d written better school and Nainai. Under the polytechnic, money. Under the hill, nothing at all. Why nothing? He knew why. That was the problem.

Then the red door’s bolt went. It stuck, and it carried across both gardens with every window open. You could have heard that bolt from the moon.

He went to the front window. She was on her steps. Third one, against the rail, in a black hoodie with her knees pulled up inside it. The step was stone. It would be cold even in June.

He stood there and told himself to go to bed. Then he pulled the blanket off his bed, the blue checked one that had been his mother’s, filled his flask from the pot on his desk, and went down. He stepped over the low wall by the iron rail. She heard him. She didn’t turn round.

He shook the blanket out, sat down beside her, and put half of it round her shoulders.

“You don’t have to talk. I’ll just sit here. That’s allowed.”

“I wasn’t going to talk.”

“Okay.”

“I’m not sad, either. Before you start.”

“I didn’t start.”

“You’re doing the face.”

“What face?”

“The one you do at Auntie Dai’s knee. Like everybody’s a patient.” She pulled the blanket tighter. “You’re not even a doctor. So you can stop.”

He stopped doing the face. He wasn’t sure he’d been doing it.

She took the flask out of his hand without asking.

“What’s in it?”

“Chrysanthemum. Pear. Some rock sugar.”

She drank from the lid and screwed her face up.

“Ugh. That’s too sweet.”

She drank the rest of the lid. Poured another.

“That’s the only thing I’ve tasted all week.”

She held the lid in both hands to warm them. Her hands were always cold. It was practically a medical condition.

“Everyone’s leaving,” she said. “Did you know? Half my year are going abroad. The other half are going north. A girl was crying in the toilets after the exam because her boyfriend’s going somewhere with SNOW.”

“Snow’s not that bad.”

“She says he’ll meet someone in a ski jacket.”

He laughed. She didn’t.

“You’re not going anywhere,” he said.

“I’m going up the hill. Computer science. If my results are fine, which they will be, because they’re always fine.” She didn’t look at him. “I checked who else from my school is going. It’s me and a boy who eats paper.”

“Eats paper?”

“Corners. Off his notes. All through maths.”

He laughed again before he could stop it. She looked pleased for half a second. Then she remembered she was in a mood.

“I’m going to know nobody. I’ll have to say my name to strangers every single day. For a MONTH.”

“You could write it on your hood.”

“Don’t.”

She turned the lid round in her fingers.

“Nobody in my house said well done, either. Elowen texted. Baba wasn’t back. Ah Sim made noodles, which is well done in Ah Sim, but still…”

She shrugged under the blanket.

“You said it. On your step. You were the only one.”

He opened his mouth to tell her about the hill.

I’ve got a place there too. Easy. Six words. She’d turn and look at him. She’d know the course, because she knew everything, and she’d ask why the hill and not the north. And then what? What was he going to say to that?

He looked at her. His tea in her hands. Her hair coming down. His mother’s blanket round her, and that frown at the lane, like the lane had done something to her personally.

Oh.

He knew what he’d say. It hit him like missing a step in the dark. He was in love with her.

Since when? Tonight? Last week? No idea. He’d only noticed now, on her cold step, because she’d said the only one, and he’d wanted it so badly that his chest hurt. Great. Wonderful. He sat very still, like there was a wasp on his arm.

She noticed. She noticed everything.

“What?”

“Nothing.” He looked at the lane. “Your hair’s coming down.”

She felt for the pencil. Found it hanging. Didn’t fix it.

“Leave it.”

He left it. He put both hands on his knees, where they’d behave.

She stole more of the blanket, which left him one corner. Then she pushed her bare feet under his leg on the step.

He jumped.

“Your feet are like ice!”

“So move.”

“They’re actually blue.”

“They’re not blue.”

“In this light they’re blue.”

“Then don’t look at them.”

He stayed put. He kept his eyes off her feet, too.

After a minute she stopped pretending her feet had got there by accident and leaned her shoulder against his arm. Through her hoodie he could feel how cold she was all over. He tucked his last corner of blanket over her knees. She let him. She didn’t say thank you.

“You’ll go too,” she said. Her eyes were shut. “You’ve finished. People who finish go.”

He kept his mouth shut. He didn’t trust what would come out.

What was true and wouldn’t scare either of them? He was still hunting for it when her head got heavy on his arm. Her breathing changed. The lid tipped in her fingers. He caught it before it fell. She slept right through it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stayed. The cat came back along the wall and gave them a long look. A moped went by on the main road. The stone came up through his jogging bottoms. His arm went numb from the shoulder down, and he let it, because if he moved she’d wake up and go in, and this would be over.

What was he going to do? No idea. Where wasn’t he going? The north. That part was easy.

The sky went grey over the Walled City. A bird started up in the persimmon tree behind his house. The noodle man came and rattled his shutter halfway up. He looked along the lane at the two of them on one step under one blanket, went back to his pots without a word, and banged his ladle on the side of one. Three times.

Yu Chen had no idea what that meant. He suspected it was rude.

At five the bolt stuck in the red door behind him.

Elowen came out in jeans with her car keys, dressed for the flower market. She’d stayed over in her old room for the early start. She stopped on the top step and looked down at her sister, asleep on his shoulder with her mouth open and her glasses crooked.

“How long has she been out here?”

“Since two.”

“On the stone?”

“On the blanket. Mostly.”

Elowen looked at Eliana’s face. Then at his arm. Then at the flask lid in his hand.

“Is your arm dead?”

“Completely.”

Something moved at the corner of her mouth. She didn’t ask him anything else.

“Thank you, Yu Chen.”

She crouched and shook her sister’s knee. Eliana woke up the way she always did. All at once, and furious. She looked at Elowen. At him. At the sky.

“…What time is it?”

“Five. Bed.”

“I wasn’t asleep.”

“You were snoring.”

“I don’t SNORE.”

Eliana got up with the blanket still round her and went in half asleep, one end of it trailing up the steps behind her like a tail. He watched it go through the red door.

He didn’t ask for it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went home over the low wall and meant to go upstairs. Instead he sat down on the kitchen floor with his back against the cupboard under the sink and the empty flask in his lap. His legs had stopped taking orders. He sat there until the grey went white.

Then he got up, opened his laptop on the kitchen table, and accepted the place on the hill.

He wrote to the north. Thank you. No. The polytechnic could wait a few days. Nainai would be furious. He’d write to her on Sunday, like he did every month, and this time he’d tell her why. He’d never written it down anywhere before.

What would he even put? There’s a girl? She’d be on the phone to his uncle inside an hour.

Across the garden, the line of light in her window had gone out.

At seven he boiled the kettle. Chrysanthemum, a pinch of dried pear, a little rock sugar. Five minutes. Into the flask. Then he stood in Auntie Dai’s kitchen holding it, with nobody to give it to.

Auntie Dai let herself in at eight and found him still standing there.

“You’re up early.”

“I didn’t go to bed.”

“Tsk. Who’s that for?”

He looked at the flask.

“Next door.”

chapters.epigraph: “It’s the best medical course in the country. You being here is a coincidence.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
Eliana had a plan for her first day at university. Nobody would look at her. Nobody would say her name. She’d go home at the end of it and nobody would know she’d been there at all.

The plan lasted as far as the kerb.

He was sitting on it. Of course he was. He’d been on that kerb most mornings since June, whether she was going anywhere or not, beside his father’s old green bicycle with his elbows on his knees. When the red door shut behind her he stood up, all of him, which took a while. Across the basket on the front of the bike, folded very neatly, was a white coat.

“What’s that.”

“They gave them out on Friday. There’s a thing at nine where we put them on in front of a professor.”

“You’re not wearing it on the bus.”

“I’m not getting the bus.”

“Did you sleep?”

“Did you?”

“I asked first.”

“…Some.”

“Liar.”

From inside the house, Ah Sim’s voice came up the hall.

“Eliana! Your BUN!”

The red door opened a crack, a paper bag came flying out, and the door shut again. Yu Chen caught the bag one-handed.

“Morning, Ah Sim.”

Ah Sim didn’t answer. She never did, before nine. He gave Eliana the bun.

He never got the bus. He’d cycle up the hill, get there first, and stand at the gate looking like he’d been waiting for an hour. Every time. It was obnoxious.

She came down the steps.

“There are three medical schools in this city. You did your degree at the polytechnic. They’ve got one now. A whole building. I saw it on the news.”

“It’s not as good.”

“There’s also the north.”

He took the monitor bag off her shoulder before she could stop him and hung it on his handlebars.

“It’s the best medical course in the country. You being here is a coincidence.”

She looked at him from under her hood. He looked back. He had a face people trusted. Old women at the market trusted it. Baba’s drivers called him the Song boy and let him carry things. But the tops of his ears had gone pink, and she was the only person alive who knew to check.

“You’re still a liar, Next Door.”

“Your bus is coming.”

She’d been saving this since August, when he’d told her on this exact kerb, like it was nothing. Medicine. On the hill. Like he’d just decided it over breakfast. But nobody applied to one place, and he’d never once said where else he’d tried. She was going to find out. She hadn’t told him that part.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bus went up the hill in a long, slow zigzag. Past the hospital at the bottom with its new glass tower. Past the flats and the shrines and the tea shops. At every corner she could see him below on the road, riding steadily, white coat in the basket, her monitor swinging off his handlebars.

He beat the bus. He always did.

By the time she got off at the top he was standing inside the gates in the coat, bike locked to a rail, her bag at his feet. A crowd of students in matching white coats had gathered round him like he was a bus stop. One of them was a girl with short hair and a lot of rings.

“Yu Chen! One picture! First day! Everyone in!”

Eliana stopped dead by the gatepost.

He smiled at the girl. Pleasant. Careful. It didn’t go anywhere.

“Sorry. I’m meeting someone.”

He stepped out of the picture before they took it. The girl’s face fell.

“Lunch, then? We’re all going to the canteen.”

“I’ve got plans. Thanks, though.”

He picked up the monitor bag and walked across the stones to Eliana. The group behind him might as well have been furniture.

People looked at him like that? Since WHEN? She hated it. She also hated that she hated it. So she filed it away to look at later, pushed her glasses up, and took her bag back.

“Your friends want a picture.”

“I met them on Friday.”

“She wants a picture with YOU.”

“She’ll live.”

“What plans?”

“What?”

“You told her you’ve got plans. What plans?”

“Noodles. Behind the library.” He looked down at her. “Registration’s in the computer science building. It looks like a fish tank. Desk’s on the ground floor. I checked.”

“I know where it is. I’ve got a map.”

He held out a folded sheet of paper.

“Now you’ve got a better one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Registration was a long table with four students in purple T-shirts behind it, a queue, and a lot of noise. When she got to the front, a boy with a lanyard beamed at her.

“Hi! Amazing. Name?”

Eliana opened her mouth. Nothing came out.

This always happened. She could talk to Elowen for an hour. She could talk to Yu Chen all night. She could talk to anyone on earth through a keyboard. But put a stranger’s face in front of her and ask her one question, and her voice ran off and hid.

“Sorry? Name?”

She dug out her student card and slid it across.

“Lin Yu. Amazing! Welcome! Do you want to sign up for anything? Gaming society?”

She shook her head.

“Coding club? You’d love coding club.”

Head.

“Hiking? We go up the back of the hill on Saturdays, it’s—”

She shook her head so hard her glasses slid.

“Okay! Amazing! Here’s a coffee voucher!”

She said thank you so low it might not have happened. Then she went and stood behind a pillar and breathed. Was every day going to be this? Four years of it? She was going to die in a fish tank.

She unfolded his map.

It was the whole campus in black pen, neat as a textbook, every building labelled in his small square writing. The fish tank. The library. The noodle stall behind the library, under a tree. The medical school. The old observatory dome. And all over it, in green pen, circles.

Toilets on the third floor of the arts block. Nobody uses them. Bench behind the observatory. Shade after two. Library, fourth floor, after six. Empty. Side door of the fish tank. Doesn’t lock till eight.

Every single circle was a place where nobody would look at her. Her throat closed up. She was about to cry in the computer science building on her first morning because of a MAP, and she was furious with him about it. She folded it very small and shoved it in her hoodie pocket.

Mid-morning her phone buzzed.

Yu Chen: Coat’s on.

Eliana: photo or it didn’t happen

A photo came through. Him, in the white coat, in a corridor, looking at the camera like it had asked him a personal question. The sleeves were too short. Of course they were.

Eliana: the sleeves!!

Yu Chen: They only had one size of tall.

Eliana: you look like a dentist

Yu Chen: Delete it.

She did not delete it. She saved it to a folder called SPREADSHEET, which was where she kept everything she wasn’t ready to think about.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch she sat on the bench behind the observatory in full sun, laptop on her knees. He turned up without the coat, with two boxes of noodles and his flask.

“How was it?”

“Fine.”

“Did you say your name?”

She didn’t answer.

He sat down beside her and handed her a box and the flask. She knew what was inside without looking. Chrysanthemum, dried pear, a bit of rock sugar. He’d started making it in June, the morning after she’d drunk his whole flask on her steps, and he’d made it every day since. She’d never asked him to. He’d never asked if she wanted it.

“I showed them my card.”

“That’s allowed.”

He’d said that in June too, on her step, with half his blanket round her. She’d thought about it more than she meant to, since. She thought about it now, with her noodles going cold, and her face went hot. Thank god for hoods.

“Stop saying that.”

“Saying what?”

“That’s allowed. Like you’re in charge of what’s allowed.”

“Somebody has to be.”

“It’s NOT you.”

He ate a noodle, completely unbothered. She hated him a bit.

A boy ran past after a frisbee. Someone had thrown it far too hard, and it came spinning out of the sun straight at her face. Before she’d even flinched, Yu Chen’s hand came up and caught it. No looking. No putting the noodles down. He tossed it back.

“Sorry!” the boy yelled.

Two girls on the grass had seen it. One leaned over and whispered. They both looked at him, and then at her, small and hooded beside him. What were they deciding? What she was to him? Good luck. She’d been working on that all summer.

He’d gone back to his noodles with his knee an inch from hers. She caught herself staring at his hand on his leg, the one that had caught the frisbee, with a blue pen mark on the side of the thumb. Why was she looking at his thumb? It was a THUMB.

“What?”

“Nothing. You were showing off.”

“I was saving your glasses.”

“My glasses were fine.”

“Your glasses were about to be a frisbee.”

She ate a noodle. Then another one.

“…Thank you.”

“What was that?”

“Nothing.”

“You said thank you.”

“I said NOTHING.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The library was five floors of glass and concrete, with a staircase up the middle that went round and round like the inside of a shell. He carried her monitor bag up it. She told him she could do it herself. He said yes, and picked it up anyway. In return she carried his flask, which he’d refilled from a hot-water tap on the second floor.

“How do you know where the hot water is? You’ve been here three days.”

“I came up in August.”

“To look at the TAPS?”

“To look at everything.”

“That’s weird.”

“It’s useful.”

“It’s weird AND useful.”

She was reading the fourth floor off his map. She wasn’t reading the stairs. Third flight, her foot missed the edge of a step. She grabbed the rail, and the flask flew out of her hand and straight down the gap in the middle of the staircase. It hit the stairs below with a noise like a church bell. Then it kept hitting them. CLANG. CLANG. All the way to the bottom. Every head in the library came up.

She stood clutching the rail with her face on fire. Could you die of this? Medically? He’d know. She wasn’t going to ask.

He went down and got it. He came back up with the flask in one hand and a dent in it near the bottom, deep, the shape of a step.

“I’m sorry. I’m so sorry. I’ll buy you a new one. I’ll buy you a better one, I’ll—”

He turned it round and looked at the dent. Then he unscrewed the top, poured tea into the lid, and drank it.

“Still works. I like it better.”

“You can’t like it better. It’s broken.”

“It’s got character.”

“It’s got a DENT!”

“That’s the character.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She worked on the fourth floor all afternoon at a long table by the window. He went off to the medical school and came back at four with a textbook the size of a paving slab, and sat at the far end of the same table. They didn’t talk. He never once looked at her. And every hour or so, a cup of tea turned up at her elbow.

Around five she slid a sticky note down the table. stop it. He wrote under it and slid it back. Stop what?

“The TEA,” she hissed.

“Shh. Library.”

“You’re not even looking at me when you do it.”

“You’d see me looking.”

“I’d SEE you not looking!”

“That’s worse?”

“That’s so much worse.”

The boy at the next table looked up. She put her hood further forward and drank the tea.

At six the floor emptied, exactly like the map said. Outside, the sun was going down over the harbour and the library steps had gone orange. She stopped on the top step to put her laptop away. The pencil holding her hair up slid out and clattered down the steps, and half her hair fell over her face.

He picked up the pencil and gave it to her. Then, while she was still holding it, he reached out and tucked a loose bit of hair behind her ear.

His fingers were warm. They brushed the arm of her glasses and the top of her ear and were gone. She froze.

It was nothing. He’d done things like it all summer. Pulled her hood up in the rain. Wiped ink off her chin with his thumb. Nothing. So why couldn’t she MOVE?

He’d felt it. He took his hand back like he’d touched the stove.

“Sorry. Was that all right?”

His ears had gone red. Not pink. Red, all the way down.

The girl with the rings. The green circles. The flask with the dent in it. Every crowd she’d stood in today, feeling him somewhere at the edge of it, not looking at her, and knowing exactly where he was the whole time.

“Don’t ask,” she said. “Just don’t do it where people can see.”

He stared at her.

“Okay.”

“Okay?”

“Okay.”

He put his hands in his pockets and walked down the steps beside her to unlock the bike. She put her hair back up on the way down. Her hands weren’t steady. She made very sure he couldn’t see.

✦ ✦ ✦

The message came in at midnight on the channel only one person used. Qian, Chen Si’s assistant, wrote the way he talked. Polite. Nothing wasted.

Qian: A man in the eastern district is offering a buyer a folder of old shipping records. Your father’s name is on every page. Could you look?

She looked. Just after two, the buyer opened the folder. It was empty except for one file, a photo of a persimmon.

Eliana: done

She sat back, took her glasses off, and pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes until she saw colours. That was the bit she liked. When it was over, and nobody had felt anything. Least of all her.

When she opened her eyes, she pulled the curtain back an inch. In the garden next door, the persimmon tree was black against the wall. On the second floor of the old Song house, his light was on. He had lectures at nine. She knew because she had his timetable. She’d had it since the week he got it, and she was never, ever telling him.

She turned off the screens one by one and lay down on the camp bed under the blue checked blanket. His blanket. The map was still folded small in her pocket. She put her hand over it. Then she texted him.

Eliana: go to sleep

Yu Chen: You first.

His light stayed on. So did her phone, on her chest, until the birds started.

chapters.title: The Flask, the Headphones, the Tea
chapters.desc: Ten days in, Yu Chen has her new timetable memorised and a box of the headphones she destroys every fortnight. Eliana has found out she can’t concentrate when he turns pages, which is new and annoying.
chapters.epigraph: “I bought ten pairs. Don’t argue. You go through them like socks.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
Her light went off after four. Yu Chen saw it because he was awake. He was usually awake at some point between two and four, and when he was, he looked. He didn’t even have to sit up. If he turned his head on the pillow he could see past his own curtain, across the garden, to the top window of the tall house. A line of white between her curtains, thin as thread. Then nothing.

After four. Lectures at nine. She’d be on the bus at eight with her eyes half shut, and asleep on the fourth floor of the library by three. He turned over and slept till six. Very efficient.

At eight the red door opened and she came out like a ghost who’d lost a bet. Hood up. Eyes half shut. One shoe not quite on.

“Don’t look at me.”

“I’m not looking.”

“You’re looking. I slept. I slept LOADS.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were thinking it really loudly.”

He held the flask out. She took it without opening her eyes all the way.

“…Thanks.”

“Your shoe.”

She looked down at her shoe. She looked at him. She put her foot in it properly and stamped off to the bus stop like it was his fault.

✦ ✦ ✦

If anyone had asked, he’d have said he was organised. Nobody asked. Wei Long had moved out two years ago into a flat by police headquarters and only came round on Sundays to eat Auntie Dai’s food and say he was too thin. Auntie Dai asked nothing at all. So there was nobody to explain it to. Which was lucky, because out loud it would have sounded bad.

He had a notebook. Her timetable was in the back, copied off the computer science website the week it went up. Every module. Every room. He knew she had Programming on Mondays and Thursdays in the big hall in the fish tank. He knew she had a maths tutorial on Wednesdays with a man in sandals, and that she hated it, because she’d come out of the first one with her mouth in a straight line and not said a word till the bottom of the hill.

He knew she killed a pair of headphones roughly every two weeks. White, wired, always the same make. She said wireless ones could be listened to by anyone who cared to try, and she’d know, because she was usually the one listening. She wound them round her phone, her fingers, her pencil. She knotted them in her pocket and picked at the knots in lectures until something inside gave up.

In August he’d found the shop that sold them and bought ten pairs. The box was in his bag. He’d been carrying it for three weeks, waiting for the right moment. There was no right moment. He was aware.

And every morning, before Auntie Dai came in, he made her tea. Chrysanthemum. A pinch of dried pear. A bit of rock sugar. Water off the boil. Five minutes, strained, into the flask. He’d read that chrysanthemum was good for tired eyes. Was it true? No idea. She drank it. That was the whole study.

The flask had a dent near the bottom now. He turned it so the dent faced out when he put it in his bag. He liked people seeing it. He didn’t look into why.

✦ ✦ ✦

The mentoring meeting was in a corridor on the third floor of the old hospital block, outside a door marked SURGERY — RESIDENTS. The medical school gave every new student a mentor from the hospital. His was his cousin. Coincidence? He didn’t believe in those any more than Eliana did. Somebody in the north had made a phone call.

Wang Xing Yue came out late, in green scrubs, a cap in one hand and his glasses shoved up on his forehead. Twenty-nine. A surgeon. He walked like the corridor was his. He looked at Yu Chen like he was checking him for bleeding.

“You. Sign this.”

Yu Chen signed it.

“Twice a term. Ten minutes. If you’re failing, sooner. Don’t be failing.”

“I won’t.”

Xing Yue looked at the form.

“Why here?”

“It’s the best course.”

“It’s the third best course. The north is better. Grandmother wanted you in the north.”

“I know.”

“She told my father you’d gone south because of a girl.”

Yu Chen looked at the wall behind his cousin’s head. There was a poster about handwashing. Five steps. He read all five.

“Grandmother says a lot of things.”

“She does.” Xing Yue folded the form in half. “She’s usually right, which is the annoying part.”

A nurse stuck her head out of the door.

“Dr. Wang! Bed four’s asking for you. Loudly.”

Xing Yue went back in without another word. Yu Chen walked down three flights of stairs and out into the sun, and found his hands had gone cold.

Because of a girl. Thanks, Nainai.

✦ ✦ ✦

In anatomy after lunch, the girl with all the rings sat down next to him. She’d been at the gate on the first day. Since then she’d asked for his number, his notes from Tuesday, and whether he wanted to come to a thing the second years were having on Friday. He’d given her the notes, because notes cost nothing. He’d said no to the rest. Politely. Every time. Her name began with J. He was fairly sure.

“You’re always running off. Where do you go?”

“Library.”

“Which floor? I’ll come.”

“I’m bad company. I don’t talk.”

“You’re talking now.”

“Not for much longer. Sorry.”

“Friday, then? The second-year thing?”

“I can’t on Friday.”

“You don’t even know what time it is.”

“I still can’t.”

She laughed like he’d made a joke, and stayed where she was. He didn’t mind. Other people went past him like weather. He was polite to them, and afterwards he couldn’t have told you a single thing they’d said.

He opened his textbook to the bones of the hand. There was a yellow sticky note on the page.

A drawing in black biro. Two people on a step under a tiled roof, side by side, with one big blanket round both of them. The blanket had checks. The smaller one had a pencil sticking out of her hair and was holding a flask that wasn’t hers. That was all. No words.

When had she even touched his bag? He looked at it for as long as he could stand. Then he looked up at the ceiling of the lecture hall, which was concrete with a long crack across it, and stared at the crack until his face was normal again.

“Are you okay?” said the girl beside him. “You’ve gone all red.”

“It’s warm in here.”

“It’s freezing in here.”

“I run hot.”

He did not run hot. He peeled the note off the page, very carefully, by one corner, and put it inside the back cover of his notebook with the timetable. The lecturer said scaphoid. He wrote it down. He had no idea what it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fourth floor emptied after six, like always. She was already there, at the far end of the long table, sitting on her chair with her knees up and her laptop balanced on them. Nobody had ever told her that wasn’t how chairs worked. She didn’t look up.

He sat down at the other end with three metres of table between them and put the flask in the middle where she could reach it.

“You found it.”

“Found what?”

“The note.”

“What note?”

She typed faster.

“There wasn’t a note. I don’t know about any note.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t say okay like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’ve put it somewhere.”

He opened his textbook. He had put it somewhere. Inside the back cover, next to her timetable, which was its own problem.

They worked. The harbour went from blue to grey to black in the window, and the lights came on along the far shore. He looked up now and then. He couldn’t help that.

She had her headphones in and she was frowning at her screen. She frowned when things went well. When things went badly her face went perfectly smooth. Her glasses slid down and she pushed them up with one knuckle without stopping. Then he noticed she hadn’t blinked.

He counted. He couldn’t help that either. At three minutes he got up, walked down the table, poured tea into the lid, and put it by her hand.

“Yu-er. You haven’t blinked in three minutes. Drink this.”

She took one earphone out and looked up at him with dry red eyes.

“You were counting?”

“Drink it.”

“That’s so weird. Who counts blinks?”

“Doctors.”

“You’ve been a doctor for TEN DAYS!”

“Drink it, and then shout at me.”

She opened her mouth to argue. Then she picked up the lid and drank the whole thing, and blinked about six times, hard, like he’d made her, and glared at him over the rim. He went back to his chair.

Ten minutes later he turned a page. Something kicked him under the table.

She hadn’t moved. She was typing, eyes on the screen, totally calm. But her foot, in a grey sock, had come all the way down the table under there and was resting on his shin.

“You turn pages too loud.”

“Sorry.”

“You’ve been turning them too loud since Monday. I can’t think.” She typed something and deleted it. “It’s so annoying.”

He turned the next page as quietly as a page could be turned.

Her foot stayed exactly where it was, warm through his trousers, for the next hour, and nobody said one word about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday night she’d disappeared. She hadn’t gone anywhere. Her light was on at ten. At midnight. At two. Still on when he got up. She came out of the red door looking straight through him like he was part of the kerb, grey in the face, talking fast under her breath to nobody. When he said her name, she jumped a foot.

It had started in June, a week or two after her exams. He didn’t know exactly what she did on those nights. He had a fair idea. He’d never asked. In July, the first morning he’d seen her come out like that, she’d stopped on the top step and said it.

“If you ask, I’ll have to lie to you. I don’t want to lie to you. So don’t ask.”

So he hadn’t. Not then. Not Tuesday. Instead he’d come home at lunchtime and found Auntie Dai in the kitchen.

“Can you make the pork and chive ones? The ones that keep?”

“For you?”

“For next door.”

Auntie Dai looked at him over the chopping board for one flat second.

“How many?”

“However many she’ll eat.”

“So, nine.” She was already getting the flour down. “That girl eats like a bird with a grudge.”

At seven he’d taken a box round to the back gate of the tall house. Ah Sim had opened it. Small, old, with a ladle she seemed to carry everywhere. She’d been taking things from him at that gate all summer. Soup when Eliana had a cold in July. A lamp when her desk light died. A bag of lychees.

“Dumplings,” he said. “Pork and chive.”

Ah Sim looked at the box. Then at him, like he was a slightly suspicious vegetable. She sniffed.

“She hasn’t eaten since Sunday.”

“I know.”

Ah Sim’s eyes narrowed. Wrong answer. She took the box and shut the gate in his face.

On Wednesday the box came back over the wall, empty and washed, with a sticky note on the lid. A dumpling with a smile on it. He kept that one too.

✦ ✦ ✦

Back on the fourth floor, she fell asleep. He watched it happen. Her typing slowed. Stopped. Her head went down in stages until her cheek was on her forearm on the table, glasses crooked, one earphone out, mouth a bit open.

He waited five minutes to be sure. Then he went down the table. He moved her laptop back from the edge and saved what she’d been doing. He didn’t read it. He took off his grey jumper and put it round her shoulders. She made an annoyed noise, pulled it closer in her sleep, and kept going.

He stood there. The top of her head was right there. Her hair was falling out of its knot, the pencil had slid sideways, and she smelled of green-apple shampoo and tea. He could have bent down and put his mouth on her hair. Nobody would see. She’d never know.

He thought about it for exactly as long as it took to notice he was thinking about it. Then he went back to his chair and took out his notebook.

He kept the plans at the front. Revision, mostly. A list of things the house needed. This week’s page said PLAN in capitals, with her deadlines and his underneath. He turned to a clean page.

Not while she’s asleep. Not until she knows.

He looked at that. Then he wrote underneath it, smaller. Friends. Hers.

Because there was the other thing. Ten days on the hill, and she’d spoken to nobody but him. Not at registration. Not in lectures. Not in the noodle queue. She had a map with green circles and a boy at the other end of the table, and nothing else.

And part of him liked it. A lot. He liked being the one who knew where she went when the tall house was too quiet. He liked that if anyone wanted to find her, they’d have to ask him first. He sat with that for a minute. It didn’t go away. It wasn’t going to.

Fine. He’d find her some friends anyway. He’d read something. He put the notebook away.

When the librarian came round to switch the lights off, Eliana woke up with a jump, his jumper half off her shoulders and a red crease down her cheek from her sleeve.

“You let me sleep.”

“You needed it.”

“No no no, I had a thing due!” She dragged the laptop over. “I’ve lost it. I’ve lost the WHOLE—”

She stopped. Scrolled. Looked at him over her glasses.

“I saved it. I didn’t read it.”

She didn’t say thank you. She put the laptop in her bag, stood up, and pulled his jumper on properly over her hoodie. She looked like a pile of washing with a face. Then she walked out ahead of him without giving it back.

“That’s my jumper.”

“Is it?”

“It’s got my name in it.”

“Then it’s well labelled.”

He followed her down the shell of the staircase. At the bottom she stopped and held out her hand behind her without turning round.

He put the box of headphones in it. She looked down. Ten pairs. White. Still in their plastic.

“What’s this?”

“I bought ten pairs. Don’t argue. You go through them like socks.”

“I don’t go through SOCKS—”

“Yu-er.”

“…Fine.”

She tucked the box under her arm inside his jumper and walked off into the warm dark towards the bus stop.

He unlocked the bike and rode down the hill behind the bus the whole way, where he could see the back window and a hood leaning on the glass. Halfway down, his phone buzzed in his pocket. He read it at the bottom, at the lights.

Eliana: this is your fault

chapters.title: Mid-Autumn, on the Roof
chapters.desc: Eliana climbs onto his roof at Mid-Autumn to pick a fight, because she’s worked out he didn’t end up at her university by accident. He doesn’t deny it. He kisses her in the middle of her sentence instead.
chapters.epigraph: “Stop. You’ve been circling me since September. I’m not blind. Say it.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
There were four of them at the long table for Mid-Autumn, and eleven chairs.

Elowen had come in the afternoon with two boxes of mooncakes from the good bakery on Harbour Road and gone again before dark, back to the house on the hill and her husband, who did not come to the Walled City for festivals yet and might never. Raiden had rung to say he was busy. He’d been busy a lot since the summer, and he never said with what. Elara was on a night placement and had sent a photo of herself eating a mooncake in a corridor in scrubs.

So it was Baba at the head, Evangeline at the far end, Eliana halfway down, and Ah Sim going in and out with dishes nobody had asked for.

Baba put his spoon down.

“The orchids. On your sill. They’re doing well?”

Evangeline nodded.

“And the duck. The usual man?”

“The usual man.”

“Good.”

He looked at the greens in front of Eliana. She hadn’t touched them.

“Tell her to eat something green. She lives on noodles.”

Ah Sim looked at Eliana. Eliana looked at the greens.

“I’m right here, Baba.”

He went back to his soup. The clock in the hall ticked. Evangeline slid the dish one inch closer to Eliana’s bowl. That was Evangeline for eat two and you can go.

Eliana ate two. Ah Sim went past with the rice and patted her head without stopping.

“Good girl.”

“Can I be excused?”

Nobody said no. Nobody said anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d been building the case for a week.

She did it the way she did everything. With a spreadsheet. Column A, the date. Column B, where she’d been. Column C, where he’d been. It started as a joke, the night after the library steps, because she couldn’t sleep. By Friday it wasn’t a joke.

On Sunday night Elowen rang while she was reading it for the third time.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“…Food.”

“Eliana.”

“Ah Sim made fish. I ate the fish. Ask her.”

“I will.” A pause. Shop noises behind her, buckets, a hose. “You sound weird.”

“I’m not weird.”

“You sound like you’ve found something.”

Eliana looked at her screen. Row after row after row of him.

“Elowen. Hypothetically.”

“Oh no.”

“If someone you knew turned down a better place. Somewhere else. To go to the same place as you. And then never said. Is that… is that weird?”

There was a long pause. The hose stopped.

“Hypothetically. Does this person make you eat?”

“That’s not the question.”

“It’s my question.”

“…Sometimes.”

“Then I’m not answering yours.” The hose started again. “Eat breakfast. Love you. Bye.”

She hung up. Eliana stared at the phone. Useless. Her whole family was useless.

She went back to the spreadsheet. Two offers for graduate-entry medicine. The north, an hour from his grandmother, the better school. And the hill. He’d accepted the hill early on a Saturday morning in June. She knew which Saturday. She’d woken up in her own bed at noon that day with his blanket round her and no idea how she’d got upstairs. She’d found all of it before her tea went cold.

A master’s at the polytechnic, with money. Turned down three days later. Anatomy group swapped from Tuesday mornings to Thursday afternoons, first week. So he was in the library on Tuesday mornings. Which was her free period.

Fourth floor every evening. The bench at lunch. The kerb. The gate. Ten pairs of headphones, because he knew how often she broke them, and she had never once told him that.

It made her feel sick. Then angry, which was easier. Everybody watched her. Baba’s drivers told him where she was. Elowen rang every night. Ah Sim counted the noodle packets and thought Eliana didn’t know. And Yu Chen was supposed to be the one who didn’t. He just sat with her. That was the whole point of him.

Wasn’t it?

Now, two days later, she stood at her window with a mooncake taste still in her mouth. Across the garden, on the flat roof of the old Song house, next to the water tank, there was a white paper lantern. A rabbit, one ear bent. He put one up every Mid-Autumn.

Somebody was sitting next to it. She put her shoes on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The persimmon tree stood in the corner of the Song garden. Its biggest branch came over onto the Lin side, low enough to grab if you stood on the rim of Mama’s biggest flowerpot.

Up the branch on her hands and knees. Over the wall. Into the fork. Up through the leaves. The persimmons were still green and hard, and every single one of them smacked her in the face personally. From the top it was one long step onto his roof, if you didn’t look down. She didn’t look down.

He was sitting against the water tank with his legs out, the rabbit beside him, a box of mooncakes open on the gravel, his notebook on his knee. He looked up when the leaves shook. He didn’t look surprised. That made it worse.

“You’re not wearing a coat.”

“I don’t need a coat.”

“It’s cold up here at night.” He pushed the box towards her. “There’s lotus seed. I saved you the one with two yolks.”

“I don’t want the one with two yolks.”

“You always want the one with two yolks.”

She did. That wasn’t the point.

The moon was coming up behind her, huge and yellow, bright enough to throw her shadow across the gravel to his feet. She pushed her glasses up her nose.

“Stop.”

He waited.

“You’ve been circling me since September. I’m not blind. Say it.”

He put his notebook down on the gravel. Closed.

“You had two offers. The north was better. You took this one the morning after the steps.”

“Yu-er—”

“Then you turned down MONEY at the polytechnic!”

“I didn’t want the master’s.”

“You moved your anatomy group so you’d be in the library when I’m in the library.”

“The Thursday tutor’s better.”

“You know how often I break my headphones. I never told you that!”

“You didn’t have to.”

“You’re at the gate every morning before the bus. You’re at the bench. You’re on the fourth floor. Every single day, Wang Yu Chen. I made a spreadsheet.”

“I know you did. You made one in July, when the man at the fish stall short-changed Ah Sim. He gave her back two years of money.”

“Don’t make it a joke.”

“I’m not.”

He wasn’t. He sat very still against the water tank and looked up at her. He didn’t look caught. He looked like he did watching patients in his course videos. Like every word mattered, and he was keeping all of them.

“So say it. Say it was the course.”

He stood up. It took a while. There was a lot of him. Standing, he was a head and a half taller than her, and with the lantern behind him she could only see the shape of his face.

“It wasn’t the course. You know it wasn’t the course. I came because you came. I’ve never pretended otherwise to you.”

Oh.

She’d expected a lie. She’d planned the whole thing on the camp bed. He’d say the course. She’d show him the spreadsheet. He’d go red and say okay, okay. She’d tell him to stop hovering. He’d stop. Done.

He’d just SAID it. On his own roof. Like it was obvious, and she was strange for needing it out loud.

That was so much scarier than a lie. So she kept going.

“You can’t do that.”

“I already did.”

“You can’t just arrange your whole life round me! That’s insane. People don’t DO that. What if I’d gone abroad?”

“You didn’t.”

“What if I fail? What if I hate it and leave at Christmas, and you’re stuck halfway up a hill on a course that isn’t even the best one, because of ME?”

“Then I’ll—”

“No! You don’t get to decide that.”

“Eliana.”

“You don’t get to follow me round with tea like I’m going to break if you look away. I’m not going to break. I’m not a child.”

“I know you’re not.”

“I don’t need anyone standing over me watching me eat, I get enough of that at home, I get it from EVERYONE, I thought you were the one person who didn’t, I thought—”

He took her face in his hand.

No asking. Not one word. One big warm hand along her jaw, thumb by her ear, fingers at the back of her neck under her hair. He bent his head and kissed her in the middle of the sentence.

The rest of the sentence went somewhere. She never found out where. His mouth was warm and tasted of lotus seed. His hand was steady. Her glasses got knocked crooked against his cheek. For one whole second she stood there with her arms hanging and her eyes wide open, totally unable to move.

Then she grabbed his collar.

Both hands. She didn’t decide to. Two fistfuls of his shirt, and she yanked him down and kissed him back, hard, up on her toes. Their teeth knocked. He made a startled noise into her mouth. His other arm came round her waist and lifted her, and her toes left the gravel.

“Yu-er,” he said against her lips.

“Shut up.”

He laughed, one breath of it, and kissed her again. Slower. Like he’d been waiting all summer and had no plans to hurry now. His thumb moved once along her jaw and her knees went.

So THIS was what everyone was going on about. Oh no. Oh no, she wanted more. She wanted so much more of it that it actually hurt.

And that was when she froze. Because she did want it. More than anything. And he was the one person she’d never been afraid of losing, because she’d never had him in a way you could lose. He was just next door. He was just there.

Now he was holding her face on a roof. It was real. If it was real, it could end. Everything that could end did.

She let go of his collar. She put both hands flat on his chest and shoved.

He let her. He stepped back at once, his hand gone from her face. He stood in the lantern light with his shirt pulled crooked where she’d grabbed it, breathing hard, staring at her.

“Yu-er.”

“Don’t.”

“I’m not sorry.”

“I didn’t ASK if you were sorry!”

She went back over the edge of the roof into the tree.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came down faster than she’d ever gone. Green persimmons, face, again. A twig down the back of her hoodie. She missed the flowerpot, landed on her knees on the paving, and ripped one of them open through her jeans.

“Ow. OW. Ow.”

Above her, the leaves moved. He was at the edge of the roof. The lantern glowed behind him.

“Are you hurt?”

“No!”

“You said ow.”

“I say ow all the time. It’s a word. It’s a normal word.”

“You said it three times.”

“Go INSIDE, Next Door.”

“I’m not going anywhere.” His voice came over the wall low and steady. “I live next door.”

He meant it to help. She knew he did. Don’t run. I’m here. I’ll be here when you come back. It did help. But she stood in the dark with her knee bleeding and heard the other thing under it. He wasn’t going anywhere. He’d made sure. In June.

She went inside and up the stairs on the edges, past Baba’s door. Evangeline’s door was open a crack, like always. As Eliana went past it, it opened the rest of the way.

Evangeline stood there in her nightdress. She looked at Eliana’s knee. She looked at Eliana’s hair. She reached out and picked a green persimmon leaf out of it, and held it up between two fingers.

“I was getting air.”

Evangeline looked at the leaf. Then at her.

“Lots of air. On the… in the garden.”

Evangeline went back into her room. Eliana heard a drawer. Then Evangeline came out again and put a plaster in her hand, folded Eliana’s fingers over it, and shut the door.

“Thanks, Ev,” she whispered.

She went up the last flight, shut her own door, and stood with her back against it in the dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she went to the window. She stood beside it, out of sight, curtain an inch open, hand over her mouth. Her mouth still felt hot. Her knee stung. She was so angry she could scream, and she was smiling, and she couldn’t stop either one. Which would be left when she took her hand away?

He’d kissed her. He hadn’t even ASKED. Right in the middle of her telling him off, like he’d been sure of her the whole time. And he’d been right to be sure. That was the worst bit.

The rabbit was gone. On the second floor of the old Song house his light was on, curtain open. She turned off her desk lamp. Then the screens, one by one. Then the red light on the extension lead she usually covered with tape. She stood in total dark and watched the gap.

His light stayed on. One minute. She counted. Then it went off.

He’d waited for hers. She lay down on the camp bed in her clothes with the blue checked blanket up to her chin and opened the spreadsheet. Bottom row. Empty.

Column A, the date. Column B, his roof. Column C…

She typed he kissed me. Deleted it. Typed it again. Her phone buzzed on her chest.

Yu Chen: Put something on your knee.

Eliana: that didn’t count

Yu Chen: The knee?

Eliana: THE ROOF

He didn’t answer that.

She lay in the dark with two fingers on her mouth and waited. He still didn’t answer. He didn’t have to.

It counted.

chapters.title: Not Official, She Says
chapters.desc: The morning after the roof, Eliana turns up with a typed list of rules: nobody knows, and it doesn’t get a name. Yu Chen agrees to every one of them and adds one of his own.
chapters.epigraph: “Fine. No name. But I’m not going to lie and say it isn’t the best thing that’s ever happened to me.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
She knocked on his door at seven in the morning with a piece of paper. She’d written it out by hand first, at three, and decided her handwriting looked scared. So she’d typed it. Then she’d printed it with a pillow over the printer so Baba wouldn’t hear. It was folded in four, in her hoodie pocket, and she had her hand clamped on it like it might escape.

He opened the door in a grey T-shirt and tracksuit bottoms, hair sticking up on one side, the dented flask in his hand. The whole hall smelled of chrysanthemum.

“You’re early.”

“Let me in before somebody sees.”

He didn’t say a word about last night. He just stood back.

His kitchen was at the back, looking onto the garden and the persimmon tree and the wall. Over the wall, the back of the tall house. Her own window, high up, curtains shut. She’d never stood in his kitchen and looked at her own window before. You could see it really, really clearly. She didn’t love that.

She slapped the paper on the table and pushed it across. He sat down and read it out loud. Of course he did.

“One. It doesn’t have a name.”

“You don’t have to read it OUT.”

“Two. Nobody knows. Nobody’s in capitals. Not Wei Long. Not my sisters. Not Ah Sim. Not Auntie Dai.”

“Yes. Good. Silently, please.”

“Three. No holding hands on the hill.”

“I can hear you.”

“Four. Nothing where people can see. See three.” He looked up. “You’ve cross-referenced.”

“Keep going.”

“Five. If anyone asks, we’re neighbours. Which we are.”

“That one’s just true.”

“Six. You don’t say sorry about last night. You’re not sorry.”

He read it again, silently this time. She watched him. Her hands were doing something stupid in her pocket.

“Number six.”

“You’re not.”

“No.” He looked up. “I’m not.”

She’d expected a fight. That was the whole point of a list. He’d pick at it, she’d defend every line, she’d win. She’d prepared answers. Her reason for number three took nearly a minute to say.

“Aren’t you going to argue?”

“With which one?”

“Any of them! Number three. Number three is unreasonable.”

“Number three’s fine.”

“Number THREE is FINE?”

He got up, found a pen in the drawer by the cooker, and sat back down. At the bottom of her list, under six, in his square capitals, he wrote:

7. THIS IS REAL. I WON’T SAY IT ISN’T.

He turned the paper round and pushed it back.

“Fine. No name. But I’m not going to lie and say it isn’t the best thing that’s ever happened to me.”

She stared at line seven. She had a pen in her pocket too. She could cross it out. She thought about him on the roof, saying I came because you came in exactly this voice, not ashamed of it at all. She left it.

“If you agree to all of it,” she said, and it came out smaller than she wanted, “then I’ll keep—”

She stopped.

“Then it can keep happening.”

“What can?”

He knew what. He was looking at her across the table with his ears going red, and he wanted her to say it. He wanted it badly. She could tell.

She opened her mouth. A key went in the front door.

“Yu Chen! Do you know what they want for PORK now? Thieves! Every one of them!”

Auntie Dai. Twenty minutes early. Eliana grabbed the list, stuffed it in her pocket, and went out the back door and over the wall by the persimmon branch in about four seconds flat. Behind her, through the kitchen window, she heard it.

“Was that a cat?”

“Probably.”

“Why are there two cups?”

“I was thirsty.”

“Tsk. Thirsty.”

✦ ✦ ✦

So it kept happening. On Thursday it happened on the library stairs. Third flight, where the flask had gone over. She stopped and turned round, two steps above him. For once she was exactly his height. Was this what it was like up there? Everyone’s foreheads?

“Hold still.”

“What—”

She put her hands on his shoulders and kissed him. Fast. Right in the middle of whatever he’d been saying about the tea. Then she let go and ran up the rest of the stairs without looking back.

She sat on the fourth floor with her face burning for twenty minutes. He came up eventually and sat at the far end of the table. He didn’t look at her once all evening. She could tell from the back of his neck what that was costing him. Good.

On Friday it happened in study room 4B. A row of little rooms ran along the side of the fourth floor that you could book for two hours. She’d picked 4B because it was at the end, with a pillar outside, so you couldn’t see in from the stairs.

“I need to practise a presentation,” she’d told him. “Out loud. You can listen.”

“You don’t have a presentation.”

“I might one day.”

He came in with his textbook. She shut the door, grabbed the front of his jumper, pulled him down, and kissed him until the textbook hit the floor.

Afterwards they sat on the carpet behind the pillar with their backs against the glass. She laughed into his shoulder because his hair was sticking up and he looked like he’d been hit by a bus.

“You booked a room.”

“Under your name.”

He started laughing too. She felt it through his whole chest.

On Saturday it was the back lane, and it was him. She was going to the shop at the end for energy drinks, in her slippers, past the side gate of the Song house. The gate opened as she went by and a hand came out and caught her wrist.

“Hey—!”

He pulled her into the gap between the wall and Auntie Dai’s bins, where nobody could see from the lane or either house. He kissed her once. Slowly. His hand still round her wrist, her back against the warm brick. Then he let go.

“Morning.”

He went back in and shut the gate. She stood there in her slippers with her face on fire and completely forgot what she’d come out for.

On Sunday it was his kitchen, while Auntie Dai was at the market. They knocked a bag of rice off the counter and it split. They spent twenty minutes on their knees with a dustpan, laughing so hard she got hiccups.

“Stop—hic—stop it—”

“I’m not doing anything.”

“You’re—hic—LOOKING at me—”

He kissed her in the middle of a hiccup. She hiccupped straight into his mouth. They had to start again.

She hadn’t known you could laugh while you did this. She’d thought it would be serious. It WAS serious. It was also the funniest thing that had ever happened to her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She knew why it had to be secret. She just didn’t say it. Not even to him. Part of it was Baba. Baba had never trusted the policeman’s house. Wei Long’s father had once arrested a man who owed Baba money, and after that Baba never said the word Song without his mouth going flat. The policeman was dead now. Wei Long was a policeman too. And Yu Chen lived in the policeman’s house, and Baba still called him the Song boy.

If Baba knew, he’d look at Yu Chen like that. How was she supposed to watch that happen? She couldn’t.

But that wasn’t the real reason. The real reason was simple. If nobody saw it, nobody could take it away. Things people knew about got talked about. Asked about. Tidied up. Ended. Things nobody knew about just kept going. She’d learned that from her screens. The safest thing in the world was something nobody knew was there.

So she tested him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t mean to, the first time. Tuesday, the big canteen under the arts block. He came in with three people from his course. She was at a corner table. She sent a text.

Eliana: sit with them. don’t look at me.

He sat with them. He didn’t look at her. For forty minutes. He ate his rice and listened to a boy with a beard talk about a dissection. He nodded. He said something that made the whole table laugh. Then the girl with the rings sat down next to him and put her hand on his arm while she talked.

He didn’t move his arm. Eliana stabbed her noodles until they broke into bits.

She’d TOLD him to. That was the stupid part. He was doing it perfectly and she was furious and she had no right to be. She was jealous of a girl who’d touched his sleeve, and she couldn’t even say so. To say so she’d have to say what he was. And he didn’t have a name. Rule one. Her rule.

Eliana: bet you can’t keep a straight face if I look at you

He read it. Then he looked up, straight across the whole canteen, for the first time in forty minutes.

His face was perfectly straight. Polite. Pleasant. The face he gave the girl with the rings. Like he’d never seen Eliana before in his life.

She was so annoyed she looked away first. When she looked back he was picking up his tray. He walked right past her table without a glance and out through the side doors at the back, the ones to the corridor by the lifts. She knew that corridor. It was on his map. Corridor by the lifts. Empty at lunch.

She gave it one more minute so it wouldn’t look like anything. Then she went after him.

He was round the corner by the lifts, where there was nothing but a noticeboard and a fire door. He didn’t say a word. He took her by the waist and walked her backwards until her shoulders touched the wall, and kissed her.

Not slow. Not even a bit. He kissed her like forty minutes of not looking had nearly killed him. Her hands went into his hair and she pulled him down harder.

“Someone could see.”

“I know.”

He kissed her again.

“She had her HAND on your ARM.”

“I know.”

“You let her.”

“You told me not to look at you.” He said it against her mouth. “You didn’t say anything about arms.”

“Rule eight. No arms.”

“Write it down.”

The lift went past behind the wall, humming. Somebody laughed back in the canteen. She hung on to the back of his neck until the lift came back.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday a boy in her programming lab pulled her hood down. She didn’t know his name. He was the one with the big laugh who sat at the back and talked through everything. He’d been watching her for a week, like a quiet girl in a hood was a puzzle he could solve in front of his friends. In the corridor of the fish tank he came up behind her, grabbed the top of her hood, and yanked it back.

“Look at that! Lin Yu has a face. Who knew.”

The corridor went cold. Her hair came down. Her glasses went crooked. Everyone was looking. She stood there hugging her laptop, unable to move or say anything, with her face burning all the way down her neck.

Then Yu Chen was there. She hadn’t seen him come in. Side door. Obviously. He came and stood beside her, not touching her, and looked at the boy.

“Put it back.”

It was his pleasant voice. The one he used on the girl with the rings, the one that meant nothing. The boy laughed.

“Who are you, her dad?”

Yu Chen took one step forward, so the boy had to tip his head back to look at him. The pleasant thing went out of his face all at once. What was left was so flat and cold that the two friends stepped back without meaning to.

“Put her hood back. I’m not going to ask again.”

The boy put it back. Badly. It caught on her glasses.

“S-sorry—”

Then he and his friends were round the corner, fast. Yu Chen turned to her.

“Are you okay?”

And he was himself again. Ordinary. Worried. Ears a bit pink. He straightened her glasses with one finger. Then he remembered where they were and shoved his hand in his pocket.

“I’m fine.”

She was. She was shaking, but she was fine. And she’d seen something, and she put it away to look at later with all the other things. That night, at the top of the tall house, she looked. Not at Yu Chen. At the boy with the big laugh.

By morning, every email he sent from his university account went out under the same name. Every forum post. Every piece of work he uploaded. I Pulled A Girl’s Hood Down. It took the university’s IT people six days to change it back.

She showed Yu Chen on Thursday, on the fourth floor, turning her laptop round. He looked at the screen. She braced. Here it came. The frown. The Yu-er. The little talk about how she really shouldn’t. Elowen would’ve done the little talk. Elara would’ve laughed and THEN done the little talk.

He put his hand over his mouth and laughed so hard into his tea that he had to put the cup down.

“You’re not going to tell me off?”

“Why would I tell you off?”

“Because it’s mean!”

“He pulled your hood down.” He wiped his eyes. “Can you make it bold?”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday he tried to introduce her to someone. She didn’t see it coming. They were at the noodle stall behind the library and a girl came up to the counter. Second year, her own department, short fringe, laptop covered in stickers.

Yu Chen looked up from his bowl.

“Oh, hello.” He turned to Eliana. “This is Eliana, she’s in first year. Your brother was on my course at the polytechnic. I thought you two might—”

“Hi! Are you doing the programming module? It’s a nightmare, right? The—”

Eliana looked at her shoes.

She tried. She did. She could feel the words at the bottom of her throat. Yes. It is. What did you get in the first test? None of them would come up. The girl waited. Eliana pulled her hood forward and looked at the noodles and said nothing at all.

“Well… nice to meet you!”

The girl took her bowl and went.

He put his chopsticks down.

“Sorry. I should’ve asked first.”

She looked up to say it didn’t matter. And she saw it. Only for half a second, before he hid it. When the girl walked away, his shoulders came down. Like someone putting down a heavy bag. He’d been relieved. Then he saw her see it. He looked guilty. He looked away.

“Next Door.”

“Mm.”

“You were glad.”

“…A bit.”

“You WANT me to have friends.”

“Yes.”

“And you were glad.”

“Yes.”

She ate her noodles and thought about it all the way down the hill, forehead on the bus window, the green bike going steadily below. He wanted her to have friends. And some part of him, a part he didn’t like, wanted to be the only one.

It didn’t scare her. That was the weird thing. She thought about the corridor by the lifts. About I’m not going to ask again, and the boy’s face going white. About line seven, in capitals.

That night she unfolded the list and pinned it above her monitors, where she could see it from the camp bed. Seven rules. Six of hers. One of his. In the margin beside his capitals, in her own pen, very small, she added: 8. No arms.

For once she was asleep before two.

chapters.title: The Drawing in His Pharmacology Notes
chapters.desc: Eliana can say anything with a keyboard and nothing out loud, so she hides a drawing in his notes and tells him not to look until he’s in the library. He looks in the library and has to walk out into the rain.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t look at it till you’re in the library. If you look on the bus I’ll know, because you go red on buses.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
Eliana: bus today. it’s pouring. you’ll get pneumonia and then you’ll have to treat yourself

He’d been going to cycle anyway. He had a rain cape somewhere. But she’d never once asked him to take the bus with her. So he left the bike in the hall.

She was already at the stop at the end of the lane, under a black umbrella with one broken spoke. He took it off her without asking and held it. Rain ran off the broken bit in a stream, straight onto his left shoulder. He tipped the whole thing her way so it would keep doing that.

“You’re getting soaked.”

“I’m fine.”

“Your whole ARM is wet.”

“It’s one arm.”

“Hold it straight.”

“It is straight.”

“It’s tipped! It’s completely tipped! I can see it tipping!”

He held it straight for three seconds. Then he tipped it back. She glared at him all the way onto the bus.

It was crowded. She got the window. He folded himself into the seat beside her, knees against the seat in front, his leg pressed along hers from hip to knee. Neither of them moved it. Halfway up the hill she took his pharmacology notes out of her bag.

He’d lent them to her on Wednesday. She’d said she wanted to see how medical people organised things. He hadn’t believed that for a second. She put the folder on his knee and kept her hand on top of it, looking out of the window.

“There’s something in it. Don’t look at it till you’re in the library. If you look on the bus I’ll know, because you go red on buses.”

“I don’t go red on buses.”

“You went red on the number nine in August. A woman asked if I was your little sister. You said no, and then you couldn’t think what I was.”

“I could think.”

“You said uh for a whole stop.”

“It was a short stop.”

“You went red from your collar up. It was like watching a kettle.”

She took her hand off the folder. He held it on his knee with both hands for the rest of the zigzag, with her shoulder against his arm and the windows steaming up. He didn’t look once. His collar went hot anyway. Of course it did.

✦ ✦ ✦

He waited until the fourth floor. Ten in the morning, Friday, pouring. The floor was nearly empty. The only other person was a boy asleep face down on a beanbag in the corner. Yu Chen sat at the long table by the window with the rain running down the glass and opened the folder.

It was in the middle, between how drugs got into the blood and how they got out again. A page torn from a sketchbook, folded once.

Black biro, the way she always did them. Quick and careful at the same time. The porch of the tall house. The little tiled roof. The three steps, with the crack across the third. The red paper charm on the door. The iron rail on the low wall. And on the third step, two people under one checked blanket.

The night in June. That was what he saw first. One long and folded up, knees nearly at his chin. One small, with a hood and a pencil through the knot of her hair. Her head was on his shoulder. Just like when the sky went grey.

Underneath, in her handwriting, which was tiny and sloped backwards: don’t go anywhere

He sat and looked at it. He knew what that cost her. She could write a thousand lines of code without blinking. He was nearly sure she could take apart a stranger’s whole life before breakfast and sleep fine after. But she could not say that sentence to his face. Not if you paid her.

The first thing she’d ever left him in the jar in the wall, in July, was a drawing of a cat in glasses with its ears flat. The day after she’d snapped at him over nothing. Because she couldn’t say sorry either.

He folded the page along its fold and put it inside his shirt, flat against his chest. Then he got up, went down the shell of the stairs, out of the library, and stood under the concrete porch in the rain. He couldn’t have stayed in there. He’d have done something stupid in front of the boy on the beanbag.

It was cold, and the rain was coming in sideways. He stood with his back to the wall and his hand flat on the front of his shirt. Was this what having a heart attack felt like? He was a medical student. He should know. He didn’t.

What did you even say back to that? Thank you? He got his phone out and sent the true thing.

Yu Chen: Yes.

Eliana: !!!!!!!

Eliana: STOP

Eliana: i’m in a lecture. i can’t breathe. the man next to me is looking at me

Eliana: you looked on the bus didn’t you

Yu Chen: No. I’m outside the library. I had to leave.

Eliana: why

He looked at the steps in the rain. The same steps where he’d tucked her hair back five weeks ago and she’d told him not to do it where people could see.

Yu Chen: Because there were people.

There was a long gap.

Eliana: ok

Eliana: ok that’s fine then

✦ ✦ ✦

In the afternoon he had a small-group case on the second floor of the medical school. Eight of them round a table with a tutor and a pretend patient’s notes, working out why a man of sixty had fallen over in a supermarket.

The boy with the beard got there first.

“Low sugar!”

“He’s on blood pressure tablets. Three kinds. Page two. And he stood up fast from the bottom shelf.”

“Oh. Yeah. Or that. That’s what I meant.”

The tutor looked at Yu Chen. Yu Chen looked at the boy with the beard.

“It’s what he meant.”

The tutor gave the point to the boy with the beard. The boy with the beard wanted it more. Yu Chen didn’t care. He had a drawing in his shirt.

Afterwards the girl with the rings caught him at the door.

“Coffee? Just coffee. One coffee.”

“I have to get home.”

“You always have to get home. What’s AT home?”

“Soup.”

She stared at him.

“…Soup.”

“Good soup,” he said, and went home.

Auntie Dai was making soup, actually, with the radio on. He went up to his room and came back down with the shoebox, and sat at the kitchen table with it.

“You’re home early.”

“I’ve got a job to do.”

“What’s in the box?”

“Headphones.”

“Whose?”

“…Mine.”

Auntie Dai looked at the skull on the lid. She looked at him. She turned the radio up and went back to the soup without another word, which was worse.

Eliana didn’t throw headphones away. She broke them, and then she kept them, just in case. In July, clearing her desk for another screen, she’d come over the wall with a shoebox with a skull drawn on the lid.

“Keep it. I can’t throw them out. I can’t look at them either.”

There were nearly twenty pairs. Some she’d cut and mended herself, badly, with tape. Some were knotted in ways that would’ve interested a sailor.

He sat there and untangled every single one.
