It took two hours. He did it properly. The way they’d shown him to tie off stitches on a sponge in the skills lab. No pulling. Find the end. Follow it back. He coiled each pair round three fingers and taped it, and on the tape he wrote how long it was now, because the mended ones had all come out different. Full. Full. Missing 10 cm. Missing 22 cm (left side only). Full. He put them back in the box in order. Longest to shortest.

Then he sat back in the kitchen chair and looked at it. This was probably not a normal thing to do for a girl. It was what he had.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight his phone went.

Eliana: come over

No question mark. He looked at the window. Her window across the garden, the line of light down the middle.

He went out of his front door with the shoebox under his arm, stepped over the low wall by the iron rail, and went up her three steps. He lifted his hand to knock on the red door.

It opened before his knuckles touched it. She’d been standing right behind it. In the dark hall, with her hand on the bolt, probably since she’d sent the text. She was in a big grey hoodie. It took him a second to realise it was his. It had gone missing in August.

“That’s mine.”

“Baba’s at a dinner at the office till eleven. Ah Sim’s gone home. Evangeline’s in her room. Elara’s on nights.”

“That’s my hoodie.”

“I know whose hoodie it is.”

She grabbed his sleeve and pulled him in. They went up the stairs in the dark, her first. On the third flight he put his foot down in the middle of a step and it creaked like a gunshot. She spun round and glared at him and jabbed a finger at the edge of the step, where the wood was nailed tight.

“EDGES,” she hissed.

He moved his foot to the edge. Silent. She went up and down these stairs every night without a sound. She’d never told him how. Now he knew. Her room at the top was dark except for the screens. It always looked to him like the inside of a ship.

“I’ve got a maths test on Monday.” She shut the door. “I need to revise. I thought you could… sit there. Be quiet. Turn pages quietly. I don’t know. I just wanted you to come over.”

He gave her the shoebox. She opened it on the camp bed. Coils of white wire in their tape, in order, his writing on every one. She picked one up. Missing 22 cm (left side only). She turned it over in her fingers.

“You went through my shoebox.”

“You gave it to me. It’s been in my cupboard since July.”

She put the coil back in exactly its place. Shut the lid. Put the box on her desk by her keyboard, square to the edge. When she turned round her eyes were bright behind her glasses, and she looked furious about it.

“You’re so weird.”

“I know.”

“I mean it as a—” She flapped a hand. “I don’t know what I mean it as.”

“That’s fine.”

“Don’t say that’s fine. Say that’s allowed. You always say that’s allowed.”

“That’s allowed.”

“Ugh.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The revision did not go well. She sat cross-legged on the floor against the camp bed with a stack of problem sheets on her knees. He sat beside her. Every time she started a problem she looked at him. Every time she looked at him she lost her place.

“I can’t do this with you sitting there.”

“Do you want me to go?”

“No!”

He thought about it. That summer he’d read a lot about all kinds of things, first dates and shyness and how people learned. He’d have died before admitting it. One article had said small rewards made people work. He’d thought it was rubbish.

“One page. One kiss.”

She stared at him.

“You can’t even check it! You don’t know discrete maths.”

“I’ll check it looks finished.”

Her mouth went flat. Then she pulled the first sheet off the pile, put her head down, and did it so fast that her pencil went through the paper at the bottom. She shoved it at him. It looked finished.

He leaned over and kissed her once, slowly, his hand on the side of her face. She made a noise in her throat. When he sat back, she was already grabbing the next sheet.

He’d meant it to last the evening. By page five she was doing them one-handed, with her other hand fisted in the front of his shirt. By seven she’d stopped pretending to give him time to check. By nine she’d climbed into his lap with the sheet still on her knee and her pencil behind her ear, and she was kissing him in the middle of a sum.

He gave up holding his hands still. He put them under the hem of the grey hoodie, his hoodie, flat on the warm small of her back. She shivered and pushed closer. The pencil fell down between them somewhere. She was laughing into his mouth about it. He was laughing too. He couldn’t stop that, and he couldn’t stop kissing her, and he didn’t try very hard at either.

“What page is it?”

“Nine. Eleven. I don’t know.”

“Is that a sum?”

“It’s NEARLY a sum.”

“You skipped ten.”

“Ten’s horrible. I’m not doing ten.”

He kissed her neck, under her ear, where her hair had come down. She went boneless and grabbed his shoulders.

“Okay.” Breathless. “Okay, okay, I’ll do ten.”

She did not do ten. At eleven a car came up the lane. The gate. The red door. Her father’s heavy feet in the hall. They both froze. Her in his lap on the floor of her room. His hands under her hoodie. Problem sheets everywhere. Lin Jian came up one flight, slowly. Then another. Along the landing two floors down. His door shut.

Eliana let her breath out against his neck.

“You can’t go now. He’ll hear the door.”

“I know.”

“You’ll have to stay till he’s asleep. Properly asleep. He snores. You’ll know.”

“I know.”

He could hear Lin Jian snore from his own bed when the windows were open. Was now a good time to mention that? It was not.

✦ ✦ ✦

After one her phone buzzed on the desk. Not the normal buzz. Two short ones. She’d been half asleep against him on the floor in a heap of test sheets, his arm round her. At the sound she was awake all at once, like someone had shouted her name. She was on her feet before he’d moved. She took the phone out to the top landing and pulled the door almost shut. He wasn’t trying to listen. The house carried everything.

“Yes.”

It was her voice. It wasn’t any voice he’d heard her use. Low and flat and quick. Nothing shy in it anywhere.

“Then he’s lying. No. No, I can see it from here, he’s lying, he moved it on Tuesday. Give me twenty minutes.”

A pause.

“No. I’ll do it. Not him. He’ll leave a mess and I’ll have to clean it up anyway.”

A shorter pause.

“Twenty minutes. Tell Qian I said so.”

She came back in and went straight to the desk without looking at him. Her face in the light of the five screens was smooth and white and shut. Her hands were moving before she’d finished sitting down.

He didn’t ask. He’d never asked. He got up and poured what was left in the flask, lukewarm now, into the lid. He put it by her keyboard on the side away from her mouse, where she wouldn’t knock it. She didn’t look round. But her left hand came off the keys, found the lid, drank, put it back, and went on typing.

He sat down on the floor again and picked up the pair of headphones she’d knotted on the bus that morning, and started on it. It took her just over half an hour. He knew because Lin Jian’s snoring had started two floors down, and he timed her against it.

When she finished she sat back and put both hands over her face.

“…Done.”

Then she took them away and looked at him. Sitting on her floor with her headphones half untangled across his knee. Her face came undone a bit. It only ever did that with him.

“You should go. He’s asleep. Keep to the edges.”

She came and knelt in front of him. She took the headphones off his knee and put them on the shoebox. Then she kissed him for no page at all. Gently. Her cold hands on his face.

“Thank you for the box.”

“You’re welcome.”

“Don’t make it a thing.”

“It’s not a thing.”

“It’s a bit of a thing.”

He went down the stairs in the dark, on the edges, the way she’d shown him. Every one was silent. He let himself out of the red door, stepped over the low wall, and stood on his own porch in the wet, looking up at her window.

Her light was still on at three. And at four. At six he filled the flask in Auntie Dai’s empty kitchen and put it on her third step, right by the crack.

At eight the red door opened. She picked the flask up, hugged it to her chest, and looked at him over the wall with her hood up and her eyes pink.

“You didn’t sleep.”

“Neither did you.”

“I did ten.”

“You didn’t do ten.”

“…I did half of ten.”

“Which half?”

She went back inside and shut the door on him. He heard her laughing in the hall.

chapters.title: He Researched This Part Too
chapters.desc: Their first night together goes nothing like his plan: it’s clumsy and shy, they keep laughing, and they start over twice. Afterwards, in the dark, he says the thing she’s most scared of so that she doesn’t have to.
chapters.epigraph: “I love you. You don’t have to say it back. I just didn’t want to be the only one who knew.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
“Auntie Dai’s going to her sister’s this weekend,” he’d said on the bus on Thursday. Looking out of the window. “And Wei Long’s on a case. He hasn’t been round for two Sundays.”

He said it so carefully. So ordinary. Like he was reading out a bus timetable.

“Oh,” she’d said.

That was all. Then she’d thought about it for two whole days.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday night she was at her desk with all five screens lit and a job running. It had come in at nine. A man had been sending messages to one of the women who worked in Chen Si’s building. I know where you live. That kind. From accounts he thought nobody could find.

It took her nearly two hours to find all of them. A few minutes after that, every one of them was in a neat folder in front of his wife, his boss, and the police. So was everything else he’d ever said online under any name. She pressed the last key and sat back, and her whole body was buzzing.

It always went like that when a job went right. Her hands shook. Her heart went too fast. She felt about nine feet tall, like she could climb anything.

She looked at the camp bed. Ha. No. She looked out of the gap in the curtains. His light was on.

Was she really going to do this? Apparently she was. She took the blue checked blanket off the camp bed, wrapped it round her shoulders over her hoodie, and went downstairs on the edges of the steps.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t knock. There was a key to his back door under the loose brick by the step. She came over the wall by the persimmon branch with the blanket on like a cape, let herself in through Auntie Dai’s dark kitchen, and went up his stairs. His were newer than hers and didn’t creak at all. Cheating.

His door was half open. He was lying on his bed in a T-shirt and old jogging bottoms with a textbook on his chest. He looked up when she came in and nearly dropped it on his face.

“Yu-er. It’s midnight. Is everything—”

“Everything’s fine.”

She stood in the doorway in the blanket. Her fingertips were still buzzing.

He sat up slowly. He looked at the blanket. He looked at her face. She watched him get it. His ears went red from the top down, all at once.

“Oh.”

“Yes.”

“…Oh.”

“You said that.”

“I’m saying it again.”

His desk was by the door, under the window that faced her room. His notebook was open on it, the one with the plans. She’d seen it a hundred times. She looked down at it because she couldn’t look at him, and right at the top of the page, in his capitals, it said:

PLAN (IF)

She picked it up.

“Don’t. Eliana. Don’t read that. Put that DOWN.”

She read it. 1. Ask. 2. Ask again. Make sure. 3. Lamp. Not the big light. 4. Slow. 5. Don’t talk about anatomy. 6. If she laughs it’s fine. 7. If she wants to stop, stop. Immediately. Don’t sulk. 8. Blankets (spare, in cupboard). Water.

There was more. A whole other page. She could see the shape of it through the paper.

She turned round with the notebook. He’d put both hands over his face. The back of his neck was the colour of a postbox.

“You made a plan.”

“I make plans for everything.”

“Number five.”

“I panicked.” Into his hands. “I talk about anatomy when I’m nervous. I talked about the bones of the foot to Auntie Dai for twenty minutes once because she asked if I had a girlfriend.”

“How many bones are there?”

“Twenty-six.”

“In one foot?”

“Each. Don’t. Don’t get me started.”

She burst out laughing. She couldn’t help it. It came up out of her right there in the doorway. She couldn’t stop. He took his hands off his face and looked at her. His mouth went crooked. Then he was laughing too, on the edge of his bed, red to the ears.

“I’m going to burn it.”

“You’re not. I’m keeping it.” She put it down on the desk. “Number one. Go on.”

He stopped laughing.

“Do you want to?” he said. “We don’t have to do anything. You can just stay. You can sleep. I’ll take the floor, I don’t—”

She walked over, put one hand flat on his chest, and pushed.

He went over backwards onto the bed with a noise like a dropped bag. She climbed on after him, blanket and all, and kissed him before he could say two.

So much for the plan.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d thought, the few times she’d let herself think about it, that it would be like films. Smooth. Sure. Somebody knowing what they were doing. Nobody knew what they were doing.

He kissed her back carefully at first, hands on her waist over the blanket, like he was following number four. Then she got her fingers in his hair and pulled. He made a low sound in his throat and stopped being careful at all. He dragged her closer by the hips. The blanket slid off her shoulders onto the floor.

Her glasses got in the way. He took them off her face, gently, and reached over to put them on the bedside table, and missed. They clattered on the floor.

“Leave them.”

“You can’t see.”

“I don’t need to see.”

She pulled at his T-shirt. He put his arms up. She got it over his head. It caught on his ears. She had to stop and laugh again, with him stuck inside it, blind.

“Yu-er…”

“Hold still—”

“I AM holding still—”

“Your ears are too big!”

“My ears are a normal size!”

She got it off. His hair was everywhere and he was grinning.

Then she looked at him, and stopped laughing. She’d seen him without a shirt that summer. On his roof in the heat. Coming in from the garden with the hose. She hadn’t LOOKED. Not like this. He was long and thin and warm all over under her hands. When she put her palm flat in the middle of his chest she could feel his heart going as hard as hers.

“All right?”

“Yes.”

He touched the hem of her hoodie. His hoodie. The grey one she’d stolen. He looked at her, asking. She nodded. He lifted it over her head, slowly, and the T-shirt under it, and then he didn’t do anything at all for a second but look. She felt herself go hot from her face all the way down. She wanted to cross her arms over herself. She wanted him to keep looking.

“You’re so beautiful.” He said it like it hurt. “Sorry. I know you hate that.”

“I don’t hate it.”

She did, usually. Not now. Not from him.

He kissed her neck. Her shoulder, where her bra strap was. He moved the strap aside with one finger and kissed the place it had been. Then he took her hand off his chest, turned it over, and kissed the inside of her wrist, right where the pulse was.

She made a noise. She’d never heard herself make that noise in her life. He stopped dead.

“Was that—”

“Don’t stop.”

“I’m checking.”

“Stop CHECKING. Chen. Please. I’m fine, I’m—”

He laughed against her collarbone, and didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

They knocked the lamp over at some point. She wasn’t sure how. He was pulling the duvet back and she was trying to get out of her jeans without getting up, which did not work. Someone kicked the bedside table. The lamp went over, hit the floor, and went out.

Total dark. A long pause.

“Number three.”

She laughed so hard she had to put her face in the pillow.

He found the lamp by feel and put it back and switched it on. It still worked. The shade was crooked now. He looked down at her laughing in his bed with her hair all over his pillow. His whole face went soft.

“What?”

“Nothing. You’re in my bed.”

“I KNOW I’m in your bed.”

He came back down and kissed her until she’d stopped laughing.

Then it was skin, all the way. His warmth everywhere. His weight coming down onto her slowly, on his elbows, careful even now. He smelled of soap and tea and the cold air from the open window. Somewhere out in the lane a motorbike went past and faded. His mouth was at her throat. Her hands were on his back, feeling the long muscles move.

It was strange. It was clumsy. They bumped noses.

“Sorry—”

“Stop saying sorry.”

“Sorry. I mean—”

“CHEN.”

He stopped above her and said her name in a voice she didn’t know. Low and rough.

“Yu-er. Is this—are you sure?”

She wanted to tell him off for asking. Instead her eyes went wet. She nodded. She pulled him closer.

“Yes. Yes. I’m sure.”

And then she did need a second. It came out of nowhere. A kind of fright. The size of it. Her fingers dug into his shoulders before she’d even decided to say anything. He felt it, and he stopped. Completely. He held himself up on his arms over her and waited. In the light of the crooked lamp he looked at her face and didn’t say a word. He just waited.

He always waited. Had he ever, once, made her hurry? No. Not one time. The fright went.

“Okay.” She pulled him back down. “Okay. I’m okay. Don’t you dare say sorry.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were.”

“…I was.”

He kissed her instead. Slow and deep, until she forgot what she’d been scared of. Then they started again, and this time nobody laughed.

It went on. She lost track of how long. She lost track of everything but him. His breath at her ear. His hand flat on her hip. His voice, saying her name over and over, like he was checking she was still there.

“Yu-er. Yu-er. Look at me.”

“I’m looking.”

“Keep looking.”

“Bossy.”

“Please.”

So she kept looking. She wrapped herself round him and stopped thinking. She hadn’t known she could. Her head had never been quiet in her whole life, not for one minute. It was quiet now. Full of him. She arched up into him and clung to him as hard as she could. He made a sound against her neck like something breaking open. She clung harder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards they lay in the dark. He’d switched the crooked lamp off. The curtain was open a little, and there was a stripe of streetlight across the ceiling. She was on his arm with her face against his chest. He had his other hand in her hair, combing it out with his fingers, slowly, like he was untangling headphones.

Her body felt heavy and warm and not quite hers. Like she’d run a long way. She never wanted to move again.

Across the garden, through the gap in his curtain, she could see her own window. Her screens were still on behind the curtains. The thin white line down the middle.

“You can see my room from here.”

“Yes.”

“Like. Really well.”

“Yes.”

She thought about that. She was too tired to think about it properly. She put it away with all the other things, for later.

He’d gone quiet. She could feel him getting ready to say something. His chest went still under her cheek.

“Yu-er.”

“Mm.”

“I love you.”

Just like that. Into the dark. No build-up. Like I came because you came on the roof.

“You don’t have to say it back. I know you can’t. I know what that word is, for you.” His fingers kept going in her hair. “I’m not asking for it. I just didn’t want to be the only one who knew.”

She lay against his chest and didn’t move.

Her throat had shut. The words were down at the bottom of it, in the same place the words went at registration and at the noodle stall, where nothing would come up. She tried. She opened her mouth against his skin and tried. It was like the dream where you try to scream. Because people said it, and then they went into hospital. People said it, and then they didn’t come home. That was what that word was. It was the thing you said before you lost something.

She couldn’t. Her eyes went hot. She didn’t let him feel it.

Instead she sat up a bit, reached down over the side of the bed in the dark, and felt about on the floor until she found it. The blue checked blanket. The one she’d come over the wall in. The one from her step in June, that he’d put round her and never asked for back.

She pulled it up onto the bed and spread it over both of them, on top of his duvet. She tucked it round his shoulders. Then she lay back down against his chest, underneath it.

He didn’t say anything. But she felt him breathe in, long and slow, and felt the breath shake on the way out. His arm tightened. He put his chin on the top of her head and kept it there.

He’d got it. Of course he’d got it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She slept. She didn’t mean to. She never slept properly, not in the dark. She lay on the camp bed and listened to the tall house creak until the birds started. But his bed was warm. He was warm. The blanket smelled of both their houses. The next thing she knew, the stripe on the ceiling had gone grey.

She half opened her eyes. He was awake. On his back, her on his arm, looking at the ceiling. Smiling. Not at anything. Just smiling in the grey light with his whole face, like an idiot.

His lips were moving very slightly. Counting something.

“What are you counting,” she mumbled.

He jumped.

“Nothing.”

“Liar.”

“…Your breathing.”

“Why?”

“In case.”

“In case WHAT?”

“I don’t know. In case.” He turned his head on the pillow and looked at her. “Go back to sleep.”

“How many?”

“I lost count when you talked.”

“Weirdo.”

She pressed her face into his side. His hand came up straight away and settled on her hair. She went back to sleep with him still awake beside her, starting over from one.

chapters.title: He Already Knew
chapters.desc: After a bad job, Eliana finally tells him what she does at night, and finds out he’s known the outline since the summer: the nights she doesn’t eat, the light still on at four. She’s furious, and then she isn’t. He never once asks her to stop.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going to ask you to stop. I’m going to keep feeding you. That’s all.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
The course dinner was in the back room of a hotpot place at the bottom of the hill. He’d said he’d go. So he went.

Twenty of them at one long table. Two pots of broth going. A lot of beer. The boy with the beard was telling the cadaver story again, the one where the hand moved. It hadn’t moved. The girl with the rings had saved him the seat beside her. He took the one across from it.

“Yu Chen! I saved you a seat!”

“This one’s fine.”

“That one’s by the DOOR.”

“I like doors.”

She laughed like that was a joke. He passed the beef before anyone asked. He nodded in the right places. Nobody noticed he wasn’t really there. He was good at this.

Under the table, he got out his phone. Not his messages. The food app.

It was his account, on his card. She’d set it up on his phone in July, sitting on his kitchen floor, because her own cards kept getting frozen by banks that didn’t like how she spent money at three in the morning. She’d put his card on it and said she’d pay him back. She never had. She ordered from her own phone, from the top of the tall house, and every order came up on his.

He knew what it would say. He looked anyway.

Wednesday. Beef brisket noodles, extra radish. Delivered.

Nothing since.

It was Friday night. Two days. Before that, the same order three times in a week. Before that, energy drinks and nothing else, delivered at three and four in the morning.

Fine. That was fine. He’d go home and see.

“Yu Chen.” The girl with the rings was leaning over the table. “We’re going to a bar after. You’re coming. Don’t say you’ve got a thing.”

“I’ve got a thing. Sorry.”

“You ALWAYS have a thing.”

“I do.”

She said the next part lightly. Her eyes didn’t.

“One day you’ll have to tell us what it is.”

He gave her the pleasant smile. He paid for his share and a bit more. He was out on the street with his bike before the second pot came.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her light was on when he got home. It was on at midnight. Close to one, his phone went on the desk.

Eliana: are you up

He didn’t answer. He went.

Over the low wall by the iron rail. Up her three steps. In with the key under the flowerpot, which she’d given him in October and he’d almost never used. Up the stairs in the dark on the edges, past her father’s door, past Evangeline’s, open a crack like always.

Her door at the top was shut. He knocked once, with one knuckle.

“…Yes.”

She was on the floor.

Back against the wall under the monitors, knees up inside her hoodie, arms round them. All five screens were on, but there was nothing on any of them. Just black. The light came down over her hood and left her face dark. The camp bed was made. She hadn’t been near it.

Two cans on the carpet by her foot. Both empty.

He shut the door and stood there.

“Sit down. You’re making the room small.”

He sat on the floor across from her with his back to the camp bed.

“I need to tell you something.”

“All right.”

“Don’t say all right like a doctor.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t say okay like a doctor either.”

He kept quiet. That seemed safest.

She pulled her sleeves down over her hands.

“What I do. At night. When you see me in the morning and I look like that. I know you see it. I said don’t ask, and you haven’t, and I—”

She stopped.

“I don’t want you to not know any more. I can’t. So I’m going to tell you, and then you can decide if you still want to sit there.”

He waited.

“Since June. Since the week after exams. Chen Si’s people found out what I could do. From something in the spring I’m not talking about.”

“Okay.”

“They offered me work. I look after their computers. Their messages. I watch for people who want to hurt them, and I find them first.”

“Okay.”

“And I clean. That’s the main thing. Anywhere Baba’s name is. Old shipping records. Files people kept. Stuff people want to sell. I find it and it goes away.”

“Okay.”

“They pay me a LOT. I’ve barely spent any of it. Nobody knows. Not Elowen. Nobody.”

She looked up at him then. Braced.

“There. That’s what I am.”

He didn’t know what she saw on his face. He knew what wasn’t there. He wasn’t surprised, and he couldn’t make himself pretend to be. He watched her see that. He watched her face change.

“You knew.”

“Not all of it.”

“How much?”

He thought about lying. It would have been kind. He’d written on her list in September that he wouldn’t.

“Who for. Since the summer, more or less. Not exactly what. I heard you on the phone that night in October. Tell Qian I said so.”

She didn’t move.

“And there’s a car that comes to the end of the lane some nights and doesn’t park. Chen Si’s assistant gets out. You go down. I’ve seen it from my window.”

“Your window.”

“And your light. On nights you work, it doesn’t go off before four. Other nights, about two. I can tell which is which.”

“From your bed.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him. He made himself look back.

“What else?”

He could have stopped there. She might have been angry about that much, and forgiven it by Monday.

He took his phone out of his pocket, opened the app, and held it out across the gap.

She didn’t take it. She leaned forward and read it in his hand. He watched her read Wednesday. Watched her scroll down with one finger, through last week, and the week before, the energy drinks at three, the noodles, the long gaps. He watched it go into her.

“I forgot.” Her voice had gone tiny. “I forgot it was yours.”

“I didn’t.”

Her eyes came up from the phone to his face. Then back down at the list of her own meals.

“You read this. Every night.”

“Before I sleep.”

He put the phone down on the carpet between them, face up.

“You haven’t eaten since Wednesday lunchtime. Unless Ah Sim got something into you. I don’t think she did. She gave me a look at the gate tonight. The fishmonger look.”

She got up.

Fast, all at once, the way she woke up. She stood in the middle of her dark room with her fists balled in her sleeves and her face white. He stayed on the floor. There was nothing to do but stay.

“You’ve been COUNTING me.”

“Yes.”

“The whole time! You sit next to me in the library and you’re counting what I eat, when I sleep, you’re lying in bed looking at my window, you’re—”

She pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes, glasses and all.

“I thought you were the one who didn’t! Everyone else does it. Baba’s drivers tell him where I am. Elowen rings every night.”

“I know.”

“Ah Sim counts the noodle packets, she thinks I don’t know. I thought you just SAT there. I thought that was the whole point of you.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Stop saying you know! And sorry! Stop SAYING things!”

It came out loud. Two floors down, her father’s snoring stopped.

They both froze.

It started again.

She took her hands off her face. Her eyes were wet. She looked furious about that too.

“Say something.” Much lower. “Say why.”

He thought about how to say it true without making a speech. She hated speeches.

“I’ve never told anyone. Not Wei Long. Not Nainai. Nobody knows what you do at night but you and me and whoever pays you.”

“That’s not why.”

“I’ve never used any of it to make you do anything. I’m not going to. I don’t care what you find. I won’t ever ask what you find. That’s yours.”

“That’s still not WHY.”

He looked at the phone on the carpet.

“I wanted to know when you hadn’t eaten. So I could bring something. That’s all I’ve ever done with it.”

She stood there.

“I’m not going to ask you to stop. I’m going to keep feeding you. That’s all.”

The screens hummed.

She sat back down on the carpet where she’d been. She didn’t look at him. She pulled her knees up and put her chin on them.

“Something happened tonight.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“There was a man,” she said. “A clerk. In a freight office in the eastern district.”

“Okay.”

“He was selling copies of old records. The kind with Baba’s name on. To someone who wanted them for a court case. Qian asked me to find out who.”

“And you found him.”

Her chin dug into her knees.

“In an afternoon. Last week. I sent Qian the name. That’s the job. That’s always the job. I find the name, I send it, I never ask what happens next. It’s not my part.”

He waited.

“Tonight Qian wrote to say thank you. The matter was resolved.”

“…And you looked.”

“I never look. I LOOKED.” She held her hands out in front of her and stared at them. “He’s in City Hospital. The one at the bottom of the hill. He went in on Wednesday night. Both his hands. They broke both his hands. Because I found him. That’s what resolved means.”

Yu Chen didn’t say anything.

“You’re going to be in there,” she said. “On the wards. One night somebody’s going to come in like that. You’ll stand at the end of the bed being nice to him, and it’ll be because of me.”

“Maybe.”

“What if it’s you who sets the fingers? And you come home and tell me about it. And I have to sit there.”

“Then I’ll set the fingers. And come home. And you can sit there.”

She stared at him.

“I’m not going to tell you it’s fine,” he said. “I don’t know if it’s fine. You didn’t break his hands. You’re allowed to feel sick about it. You don’t have to decide anything tonight.”

Her eyes were red behind her glasses. Her mouth was shaking at one corner. And she was angry, still. He could see it. At him. At Qian. At the clerk’s hands. At herself for looking.

She came across the carpet on her knees, grabbed his face in both cold hands, and kissed him.

Not gently. Like she was still shouting at him. Hard, with her glasses banging his cheekbone and her fingers digging into his jaw. He made a sound against her mouth. She shoved him back against the frame of the camp bed and kept kissing him, harder, like that could shut it all up. The room. The screens. The hospital at the bottom of the hill.

He let her. He kissed her back. He put his hands on her waist under the hoodie to keep her there.

“I’m still angry,” she said into his mouth.

“I know.” He stopped. “Sorry.”

She bit his lip for that. Not hard. He laughed. She pulled back an inch and looked at him in the light from the screens, hair coming down, glasses crooked, face wet. Her mouth wobbled. She put her forehead down on his and stayed there, breathing.

When she kissed him again, it was different. Slower. Her hands slid down off his face to his shoulders. She kissed the corner of his mouth, then the middle, like she was checking he was still the same person. He didn’t hurry her. Then she made a cracked little sound against his lips, and the kiss went wet and salty, because she was crying. No noise. The way she always did.

He kept kissing her, slowly, anywhere he could reach. Her temple. The side of her nose, under the glasses. The wet place on her cheek.

“Don’t stop.”

He didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Around two he went downstairs on the edges and found Ah Sim’s kitchen in the dark.

He didn’t turn the light on. There was congee in a pot on the back of the stove, cold, with a plate over it. He heated it on the lowest flame so it wouldn’t catch. He found a bowl, and the jar of pickled radish she liked. Then he made tea in Ah Sim’s pot on the windowsill, with chrysanthemum from the tin beside it.

There’d been a tin of chrysanthemum beside that pot since the summer. Ah Sim didn’t drink it. Had she bought it for Eliana? Because of him? He’d never asked. He wasn’t going to start now.

He carried it all up on a tray.

She was where he’d left her, with the blue checked blanket round her shoulders. He put the tray down in front of her, picked up the bowl, and blew on the first spoonful before he handed it over.

“I’m not hungry.”

“I know. Eat it anyway.”

“I’m not a baby.”

“Babies don’t get radish.”

She ate it. The whole bowl, slowly. Then about half the radish out of the jar with her fingers. Then the tea. He sat beside her against the wall under the screens and watched every spoonful and didn’t say a word. When she’d finished, she put the bowl down and tipped sideways into him, all at once, and put her head on his shoulder.

“You’re still weird.”

“Yes.”

“The app is weird. The window’s weird. If anyone else did it, I’d—”

She didn’t finish.

“I know. I could stop.”

She was quiet for a while.

“Don’t.” She said it to his shoulder. “I mean. Don’t stop.”

Her hand found his on the carpet and gripped it.

“Baba never looked. Not once. Not even to see if I’d eaten. And you’ve been lying in bed looking at my window every night since June, and I…” She stopped. “It should feel bad. It’s supposed to. I keep waiting for it to.”

He turned his hand over under hers.

“Two rules,” she said. “Mine, this time. You don’t ask what I find.”

“Okay.”

“And you don’t go near my computers. Ever. Not even to move a cup.”

“Done.”

“You said that too fast.”

“I’ve been doing both since July. I’m only agreeing to keep doing them.”

She laughed, wet, into his shoulder. Then she pulled the blanket off her own shoulders and put it over both of them, and settled against him under it on the floor of her room, with the tea going cold on the tray and five black screens humming over their heads.

Sometime before four she fell asleep, all at once, like she had on the step in June. Her hand stayed in his.

At half past five the screens went off by themselves, one by one. He hadn’t known they did that.

At six he slid out from under her, careful, and tucked the blanket back round her, and put a cushion from the camp bed under her head. He picked up the tray. And he left his phone on the carpet by her hand, face up, with the app open.

She should have it for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

She brought it back at eight, over the wall.

He was on his back step with the flask. She came along the persimmon branch in socks and his grey hoodie, dropped down by Auntie Dai’s bins, and held the phone out.

He took it. There was a new order on it, from twenty minutes ago.

Pork and chive dumplings, two portions. Soy milk, hot. On its way.

“One’s yours,” she said. “Don’t make a thing of it.”

“I’m not making a thing of it.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m eating.”

“You haven’t even GOT them yet.”

The doorbell went round the front. She looked at him. He looked at her. They both went for the side gate at the same time, and she got there first, because she cheated.

chapters.title: The Second Winter
chapters.desc: The heating in the tall house breaks, and Eliana is sent to Zhao’s for the weekend after her father turns down Yu Chen’s offer of a warm room next door. They get through the weekend by text, and on Sunday night they meet at the garden wall.
chapters.epigraph: “He said no to my house. He didn’t say anything about the wall.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
The boiler in the tall house died on Thursday night with a BANG that woke the whole lane. By Friday afternoon you could see your breath in the kitchen. The boiler man lay on his back in the cupboard under the stairs for an hour with a torch in his mouth. Then he crawled out and told Baba in the hall.

“Part’s got to come from the other side of the harbour. Monday.”

“Monday.”

“Earliest. Could be Tuesday.”

Baba looked at him.

“Monday.”

It was the voice he used for men who owed him money.

“…Monday,” said the boiler man.

Eliana was on the stairs in two hoodies and a scarf. She heard Baba go into his study and shut the door, and pick up the phone. There was a long pause.

“Elowen.”

She crept up three more stairs to hear better. He was worse on the phone with Elowen than with anyone. Elowen had married a man he was frightened of, and now she was a bit frightening herself.

“The heating’s broken.”

A pause.

“Elara’s on nights. She’ll sleep at the hospital. Evangeline says she’ll be fine with the electric heater.”

Pause.

“I have a coat. I’m not asking about me.”

Longer pause.

“There’s the question of Eliana.”

Then he stopped. She could hear him breathing.

“Would your husband mind. Two nights.”

She sat down on the stair. She knew what that had cost him. She also knew he hadn’t asked HER. He’d asked Elowen. Elowen would ask Zhao. And at some point somebody would tell Eliana where she was sleeping. Great. Love that for her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The boy next door was at the gate when the boiler man left. She saw him from the front window. Grey coat, bicycle, standing on the pavement like he’d just happened to be passing his own house. He had not just happened. On Fridays he had cases until four. Auntie Dai had told him. Auntie Dai told Ah Sim everything over the back gate, and nothing in the lane stayed secret longer than an hour. Except the two of them.

Baba came out on the porch to see the boiler man off. He saw Yu Chen. He stopped.

“Mr. Lin.”

Polite. He was always polite. His ears were going pink in the cold.

“Auntie Dai mentioned the heating. My house is warm. There’s a spare room at the back she can make up. For Eliana, or anyone. It’s only next door.”

Behind the curtain, Eliana put her hand over her mouth. Baba looked at him for a few seconds. Then he turned his head and spoke to Uncle Mok, who was at the bottom of the steps with the car keys. Like Yu Chen wasn’t there at all.

“My daughter will stay with her sister. Not in the policeman’s old house.”

He went back in. The red door shut. Through the glass, she watched Yu Chen stand there. His hand on the handlebar went tight. Then it let go. If she hadn’t been staring right at his hand she’d never have known.

He nodded to Uncle Mok. Politely. He wheeled his bike the few steps to his own gate and went in.

She stood behind the curtain with her face burning. She’d known it would be no. She hadn’t known Baba would say the policeman’s old house in that voice. About a house where somebody had come out at two in the morning to sit on her step while her own father slept two floors up. And he hadn’t even LOOKED at him.

She went upstairs and packed one small bag of clothes and one enormous bag of everything else. Then she took the blue checked blanket off the camp bed and stood there holding it. She couldn’t take it to Elowen’s. Elowen would ask.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in his kitchen, standing at the counter with the kettle, not doing anything with it. She climbed onto Mama’s biggest flowerpot and hissed over the wall.

“Next Door!”

He came out of the back door at once. Like he’d been waiting. He’d been waiting. She held the blanket out over the top of the wall.

“Keep it. Elowen will ask.”

He took it and held it against his chest.

“You’ll be cold.”

“Zhao’s house has heating in the FLOORS. Elowen told me. You can lie on the floor in socks and it’s warm.” She looked at him. “I’m sorry. About Baba.”

“You don’t have to be.”

“He didn’t even look at you.”

“No.” A pause. “I’m used to it.”

That was worse. That was so much worse. She stood on the flowerpot with her hands on the freezing top of the wall. She wanted to climb over it and put her arms round him. She couldn’t. Baba’s study window looked right onto this garden, and Uncle Mok was coming at five.

He looked at her hands on the bricks. Then he reached up, took them both, and held them between his. He breathed on them. Once. Twice. Warm.

“Your hands are always cold.”

“It’s January!”

“They’re cold in June.”

“…Text me.”

“You first.”

“I’ll be bored. I’ll text you all night.”

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana: there’s a camera in the hall pointing at where the door USED to be. he moved the door. nobody noticed for four years

Eliana: i told him. he looked at me like i’d given him a puppy. then he just GAVE me the wifi password

Eliana: 38 minutes. five holes. one of them is the garage. i could open his garage from the road

Eliana: he’s sitting on the floor next to me. he’s been on the floor for two hours. he says hm

Yu Chen: What does hm mean?

Eliana: everything. it’s the best word anyone has ever invented

Eliana: elowen made fish. he said i had to eat it. i ate it

Yu Chen: All of it?

Eliana: most of it. stop counting

It was past midnight. She was on the rug in Zhao’s living room with three laptops round her and the floor warm under her, exactly as promised. Elowen had gone up at eleven. Zhao was on the floor beside her with a printed diagram of his own house covered in her red ink, reading it the way other people read love letters.

Eliana: what did you have for dinner

Yu Chen: Noodles.

Eliana: what kind

Yu Chen: Your kind.

Eliana: you’re a MEDICAL STUDENT. you know what’s in them

Yu Chen: Auntie Dai’s off till Monday. I can’t cook.

Eliana: i’m telling auntie dai

Yu Chen: She’ll make me eat fish.

She laughed into her sleeve. Zhao looked up from the diagram. He looked at her for four seconds. Then he went back to it.

“Who’s that?”

She nearly dropped her phone.

“Nobody! Ah Sim. It’s Ah Sim. She texts in full sentences.”

“Hm.”

Zhao turned a page of the diagram.

“Ah Sim,” he said. “Hm.”

He didn’t say anything else about it, then or ever. She decided she loved him.

Eliana: is your light on

Yu Chen: Yes.

Eliana: turn it off and go to sleep. i can’t see it from here anyway

He didn’t answer that. She knew he hadn’t turned it off. Much later, when the laptops had gone dark, she lay on the warm floor with her hood over her face and tried to be glad. She was glad. Zhao’s house was a good house. It had locks she liked and a man in it who liked her, and her sister was happy here. But there was no window across a garden. No thin line of somebody else’s light. It was like trying to sleep in a hotel.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday night he sent her one message, and she didn’t answer it for an hour.

Yu Chen: Your father came out into the garden tonight. He stood by your mother’s pots.

She was at Zhao’s kitchen table with a bowl of congee Elowen had put in front of her. She turned the phone face down. Then face up again. Then she took it out to the back door, where the cold was, and rang him.

He picked up before it rang.

“Hi.”

“What did he do?”

“Nothing. He had his coat on. He stood there.”

“And?”

“Then he looked up at your window. It was dark, because you weren’t there. He kept looking at it.”

“For how long?”

“A while. Then he went in.”

She leaned her forehead on the cold glass of Zhao’s back door.

“He was probably checking the gutters.”

“Maybe.”

“He doesn’t look at me, Chen. He looks past me. Always.”

“I know. I’m only telling you what I saw.”

“Why?”

“Because you’d want to know. Even if you didn’t want to.”

Behind her, Elowen’s voice came from the stove.

“Eliana. Congee. Now.”

“I have to go.”

“Eat it all.”

“Stop COUNTING.”

“I’m not counting. I’m asking.”

She hung up and went back in and ate the congee, because Elowen was watching. She thought about Baba in his coat by Mama’s empty pots, looking up at the top of the house. She tried very hard not to.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning Baba’s car came. Zhao carried her enormous bag out to the top of the steps and put it down, and looked at her.

“The guardhouse box. I had it moved this morning. Split in two. One on each side of the house.”

“Good.”

“And the garage.”

“I saw. New code. Eight digits.” She paused. “It’s my birthday backwards, isn’t it.”

Zhao looked faintly embarrassed.

“I needed a number I’d remember.”

She hadn’t planned it. She stepped forward and hugged him, as far as her arms went, which wasn’t far. Her face against his chest. One second. Then she let go, grabbed her bag, and went down the steps without looking back. At the car, she turned round.

“Brother-in-law.”

He waited.

“The lemon tree blind spot. Don’t fix that one.”

“Why not?”

She looked past him into the hall, where Elowen was standing by the long window, watering the lemon tree.

“Because that’s where you two always stand, when you think nobody’s looking.”

She got in and texted him before they’d even reached the gate.

Eliana: the garage code is my birthday backwards. he’s an idiot. i love him

Eliana: i mean zhao. obviously zhao

Yu Chen: I assumed.

Eliana: there’s a blind spot in the hall by the lemon tree. i told him not to fix it. it’s where they stand when they think nobody’s looking

The car went down the hill. Her phone buzzed again.

Yu Chen: Is there one in your house?

She stared at that for the whole of the harbour road. She didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The heating was still off. The part was still coming Monday. Possibly Tuesday. They ate supper in their coats, Baba and Evangeline and her, at the long table, Ah Sim’s soup steaming in front of them like three little fires. “Was the heater warm enough?”

Evangeline nodded.

“Has the boiler man rung?”

“No.”

“He’ll ring.”

“He won’t.”

“Then you’ll ring him.”

“Then I’ll ring him.”

He didn’t ask Eliana anything. Halfway through the soup he looked down the table at her. His eyes stopped somewhere just beside her left ear. Then they went back to his bowl.

Her room was freezing. Her breath came out white in the light of the screens. The camp bed was bare. Around eleven she went down to the garden.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was something on top of the wall. Under the persimmon branch, where the wall sat in shadow from both houses. A long rolled shape, like a sleeping cat. She climbed onto Mama’s flowerpot and put her hand on it. It was warm. The blue checked blanket, rolled tight round a hot-water bottle. Filled not long ago. The heat came right through the wool into her frozen hands.

And next to it, the loose brick had been pulled out of the top of the wall, and the plum-jam jar was sitting in the gap with its lid on and a folded note inside.

She unscrewed it and read the note by the light from his kitchen window. HOT-WATER BOTTLE. FILLED AT TEN. I’M UP. I’LL REFILL IT. Square capitals. That was all.

She stood on the flowerpot hugging the warm blanket in both arms. Then she wrapped it round her shoulders, climbed up onto the wall by the branch, and sat there with her legs hanging down on his side.

His back door opened before she’d even settled. He came out in his grey hoodie with his hands in his pockets and stopped under her, under the branch. He’d been at the kitchen window. Obviously.

“Baba said no.”

“He said no to my house.” He looked up at her. “He didn’t say anything about the wall.”

She laughed. She hadn’t expected to laugh tonight. It came out white.

“That’s a technicality.”

“I’m a medical student. It’s all technicalities.”

“This bit.” She put her hand flat on the bricks. “Right here. Under the branch. Baba’s cameras can’t see it.”

He waited.

“You asked if there was one. In my house. There is. It’s this.” She pulled the blanket tighter. “I did his cameras. The whole house. The gate, the lane, the garden. Raiden was meant to do it and he gave it to me. Baba never knew it was me. He thinks some company did it.”

“You did all of them?”

“Every one. So they could see everything.” She looked down at the black top of the persimmon tree. “Then I moved one. A bit. So it couldn’t see here.”

“Why?”

It was a real question. He was the only person who asked her those.

“I needed one place at home where nobody was watching. Even if it was outside. Even if it was a wall.”

He stepped up onto the edge of Auntie Dai’s raised bed, where the winter cabbages were. That put his face nearly level with hers. He put his hands on the wall on either side of her knees.

“I’m watching. I’m sorry. I’m always going to be.”

“I know.” She looked at him. “That’s allowed.”

She took hold of the two strings of his hoodie, one in each hand, and pulled.

He came the last few inches without any fuss at all. She kissed him there on top of the wall with the blanket round her and the hot-water bottle squashed into her stomach. His face was cold. His mouth was warm. She hung on to the strings so he couldn’t go anywhere. He didn’t try. He made a low sound. His hands left the bricks and went round her, under the blanket. He pulled her right to the edge of the wall. Then over it.

“Chen—!”

She went down into his arms, blanket, bottle and all. He caught her. He didn’t put her down. He turned and leaned her back against the wall on his side, in the dark under the branch, where nobody’s camera could see. Her feet were off the ground. Her arms were round his neck. He kissed her again, slowly, until she’d stopped shivering and started for a different reason.

“You’re freezing,” he said against her mouth.

“You said you’d refill it.”

“I will.”

He stayed put. She didn’t want him to go anyway. She pulled him closer by the back of the neck and kissed him until her face was hot and the hot-water bottle had slid down between them and plopped onto the cabbages. Nobody went after it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later they sat on his back step under the blanket, the refilled bottle on her knees, his flask between them.

“He looked at my window. Last night. You said.”

“Yes.”

“I don’t know what to do with that.”

“You don’t have to do anything with it.”

“Then why tell me?”

“Because he did it.”

“That’s not a reason.”

“I thought you’d want to know.” He was quiet a moment. “I don’t understand him. I’d like to, one day.”

She looked at the side of his face. I’d like to. About a man who’d talked to his driver like Yu Chen was a lamppost.

“February’s the worst.”

He waited.

“In our house. Because of my birthday.” She held the flask lid in both hands. “Everyone knows she died the day I was born. That’s not the bad part. The bad part’s that we go up to the grave at dawn, all of us, and stand there, and then everyone goes to work. Nobody says it.”

“Happy birthday.”

“Nobody. Baba’s never said it. Not once.” She swallowed. “And every year I think, this year he will. Isn’t that stupid? I’m nearly nineteen. I still think it.”

Nothing clever. Nothing at all. He just put his arm round her under the blanket and pulled her into his side, and in the end she put her head on his shoulder.

“It’s next month,” he said.

“I know when it is.”

“I know you know.” He put his mouth against her hair. “I’m just telling you I know too.”

Across the wall, her own window was dark. Two floors below it, Baba’s light was still on, the only light in the whole tall house, yellow behind his curtain in the cold.

“He’s still up,” she said.

“So are we.”

“Is he waiting for something?”

Yu Chen looked at the yellow window for a while.

“Probably the boiler man,” he said.

chapters.title: Nineteen, and Nobody Says It
chapters.desc: On her birthday her father takes the family to the grave at dawn and won’t look at her, and there’s a red egg at her door like every year. That night Yu Chen gives her a whole sky to herself.
chapters.epigraph: “They wouldn’t let me bring a cake in. I asked. So you’ve got the ceiling instead.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
The egg was outside her door before five, like every year. She nearly stood on it. It was on the top landing on a saucer, in the dark. One hen’s egg, boiled hard and dyed red, still a little warm when she picked it up. Nobody else’s door had one. Nobody ever mentioned it. She took it downstairs in her hoodie pocket.

Ah Sim was in the kitchen in her coat with the kettle on and the light off, the way she liked it in the mornings. Eliana stopped in the doorway with her hand round the egg.

“Thank you.”

Ah Sim looked at her for a second. Then she turned back to the kettle.

“Eat it. And wear a proper coat. It’s cold on the hill.”

“I’ve got a coat.”

“A PROPER coat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was cold on the hill. The cemetery sat on the slope above the reservoir road in rows that went up and up like seats in a theatre. Their mother was near the top, where you could see the water. They went up in three cars in the dark. Baba and Evangeline and Elara with Uncle Mok. Elowen and Zhao at the back. Eliana in Raiden’s old car, in the back seat, with her knees jammed against the seat in front because the front seat was full of rolled-up drawings.

“Move them.”

“They’re fine.”

“They’re touching my KNEES.”

“They’re very good drawings. Your knees should be honoured.” Raiden looked at her in the mirror. “You look like a ghost.”

“It’s five in the morning.”

“You look like a ghost who’s been up since three.”

“…Two.”

He held a paper bag back over his shoulder without looking. A pork bun, still hot.

“Eat that before Elowen sees you haven’t.”

His phone buzzed on the dashboard. He flipped it face down so fast he nearly hit the wiper switch.

“Who’s that?”

“Nobody.”

“Nobody texts at five in the morning.”

“Nobody’s an early riser.”

She ate the bun and watched the back of his head all the way up the reservoir road.

Zhao didn’t come up to the grave. He never did. He stood by the cars at the gate with his hands in his pockets and watched the road.

The sky was going grey when they got to the top. Elowen had brought white chrysanthemums from the shop. She knelt and put them in the stone pot and pulled out last year’s dry stems. Baba lit the incense, three sticks, his big hands cupped round the lighter against the wind. Elara cried, because Elara cried at everything, even adverts.

“Sorry. Sorry. I’m fine.”

Elowen passed her a tissue without looking round.

“I know you are.”

“I’m just tired. Nights.”

“I know.”

Evangeline stood at the end in pale blue with her face like something carved.

Raiden stood with his hands in his good coat. Every few minutes, without looking down, he felt for his phone.

His phone lit up in his pocket. He tilted it. Eliana was standing right behind him, and she was very good at reading upside down. Tyres. That was the whole message. Nobody, then. Nobody needed tyres at dawn.

She knew who it was from. She’d known since New Year.

He’d left the New Year’s Eve dinner before the dumplings, with a black line of oil under his thumbnail that he kept trying to hide.

“Friend’s car broke down.”

“What friend?” Elowen had asked.

“A friend. With a car. That broke down.”

On the Sunday after, because she couldn’t sleep and it was easier than thinking, Eliana had looked. It hadn’t taken long. A garage near the Docks, under an old painted sign for a rope and canvas company that had shut before she was born. Bought in December. In the name of a woman called Cao Jia. Paid for by Raiden.

There were three photos of Cao Jia on the internet. In all of them she was on a motorbike, or under one.

And one line in the old-town registry, from the last day of September. Lin Raiden. Cao Jia. Married. She read it twice and said nothing.

Eliana had put it on the spreadsheet and told nobody. Why was he hiding her? She thought she probably knew. She didn’t like it. She watched him feel for his phone again, by their mother’s grave, and kept her face completely still.

Baba stood in front of the stone. He bowed three times with the incense. He said nothing out loud. He never did. Then he stepped back, and the others went up one by one. Eliana went last, like always. She bowed, and put her hand flat on the cold stone for a second, where the name was cut.

When she turned round, Baba was looking at her. Not at her. Next to her. At the stone over her shoulder, or the water past it. His eyes came close and didn’t land. Then he turned and started down the hill, and the others followed him in a line.

Elowen waited. She didn’t say anything either. She took Eliana’s cold hand in her warm one and squeezed it, hard, all the way down the steps to the cars.

That was as close as anyone got. It always was. At the gate, Zhao looked at her for four seconds. That was what he did instead of hello. Then he opened the back door of Raiden’s car for her and shut it after her, carefully, like she might crack.

✦ ✦ ✦

They dropped her at the end of the lane. Everyone else went to work. Yu Chen was on the kerb. She’d known he would be. She’d told him in January, on his back step, that nobody ever said it. She’d been sorry ever since. Now he knew, and now he’d do something about it. That was what he was like. You told him a thing was broken and he went and found the part.

She got out of the car and stood on the pavement with the egg in her pocket. He stood up.

“Happy birthday, Yu-er.”

Plainly. In his normal voice. In the lane, where anyone could hear. The noodle man was putting his shutter up, and he stopped halfway and stared.

She’d wanted it. She’d thought about it every year. Now somebody had said it, out loud, on the right day, and it went into her like cold water.

“Don’t.”

“Okay.”

“I mean it. Don’t do anything. Don’t make a thing.” Her voice was going up. She couldn’t stop it. “I just came back from the GRAVE. I’ve got a lecture at nine. Lecture. Library. Home. Bed. It’s going to be a Friday. That’s all it is. Please.”

He looked at her. She watched him want to argue. She watched him decide not to. That made her want to cry more than if he had.

“Okay.”

He stepped forward and took the zip of her coat, which was open, and pulled it all the way up to her chin. Then he tucked her scarf in at the top.

“Ah Sim said a proper coat.”

“How do you KNOW that?”

“She told Auntie Dai yesterday. Auntie Dai told me.” He held out the flask. “It’s still a Friday. You still need tea.”

She took it. She went to the bus stop without saying thank you. At the bottom of the hill she looked out of the back window. He was on his bike behind the bus, like always. She pressed her forehead to the glass and hated herself for the entire zigzag.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say it again all day. He was at the observatory bench at lunch with noodles. He was on the fourth floor at six. He didn’t mention it once. He read at the far end of the table without a sound and put tea by her elbow every hour.

By evening she felt worse than she had at dawn. She’d told him not to. He hadn’t. The day was nearly gone. Nobody had said it but him, and she’d told him to stop.

Brilliant. Great job, Eliana. Nineteen and a genius.

Then he closed his book.

“I had a plan.”

She looked up.

He got out his notebook, opened it, turned it round, and slid it down the table to her. At the top of the page, in capitals: PLAN (18 FEB).

1. Restaurant, Harbour Road. 2. Museum. After closing. 3. Say something. (Written. Back page.)

The first line had a neat line through it.

“You cancelled the restaurant.”

“I knew you’d hate it. People singing at other tables. I should’ve known in January.”

“When did you cancel it?”

“About two o’clock.”

“You were sitting RIGHT THERE at two o’clock.”

“I went to the toilets on the third floor of the arts block. Nobody uses them.”

She stared at him.

“What’s at the museum?”

“You said not to make a thing.”

“What’s at the museum, Wang Yu Chen?”

He looked at the notebook between them.

“I’d still like to take you. If you’ll come. We can not talk about why.”

She looked at number three. Say something. (Written. Back page.) She put her hand flat on the notebook so he couldn’t take it back.

“I’m not reading the back page.”

“Good. I was going to burn it.”

“I’ll come. If we get noodles on the way. And you don’t read the back page out loud either. Ever.”

“Deal.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The science museum was down by the harbour, a big white building like a stack of boxes, and it had been shut for two hours. Round the back by the loading bay there was a side door, and a man in a lanyard waiting at it with a set of keys and a cigarette.

“Mr. Wang!”

He put the cigarette out.

“Thank you for staying late. I’m sorry it’s so late.”

It was the voice he used for the girl with the rings, and professors, and the boiler man. Pleasant. Correct. Nothing in it. He shook the man’s hand. The man said it was no trouble at all, which from his face meant Yu Chen had paid him for the trouble.

Then the man looked past him at Eliana, and beamed.

“And happy—”

Yu Chen moved half a step, so he was between them.

“She’d rather not.”

Pleasant. Still pleasant. But the man looked at his face and shut his mouth and led them in without another word.

Eliana walked behind Yu Chen down a long dark corridor past the dinosaur bones, with her hood up and her hand hooked into the back pocket of his coat, where he couldn’t see. Holding on.

The planetarium was a round room under a dome. Rows of soft seats that tipped back. A console in the middle with a lot of little lights. The man showed Yu Chen two buttons and a dial, then went up a narrow stair to a booth at the back and shut the door. Nobody else. Rows and rows of empty seats in the dark.

“How much did this cost?”

“You said not to talk about it.”

“I said not to talk about WHY. That’s how much.”

“An hour. After closing. I rang on Monday and asked what it would cost to have it to ourselves for an hour. They told me. I said yes.” He looked round the dome. “They wouldn’t let me bring a cake in. I asked. So you’ve got the ceiling instead.”

She didn’t sit in the seats. She walked down the slope to the middle of the room, past the console, and lay down flat on her back on the carpet in her coat, with her hood up, and looked up at the blank grey dome.

After a second he came and lay down beside her. He was so long his feet went under the first row of seats.

“The seats are better.”

“I don’t want the seats.”

He reached up over his head, found the console’s lowest panel by feel, and pressed something.

The dark went darker. Then the sky came on.

✦ ✦ ✦

What was she expecting? Dots? She’d seen stars. Obviously. From his roof. From the bus. Out of her window at three in the morning when she couldn’t sleep. You didn’t get many in the city. The harbour lights washed them out.

Not like this.

They came on all at once. Thousands. More than she’d known there were, from one edge of the dome to the other and right down to the floor all round. There wasn’t an edge any more. Just sky, and the two of them lying at the bottom of it. Some bright. Some barely there. Some coloured. A long pale smear across the middle of everything, like spilt milk. She knew what it was. She’d never once seen it.

“Is that real?”

“It’s a projector.”

“I KNOW it’s a projector.”

“Then why did you ask?”

“Because it doesn’t LOOK like a projector.”

He reached up again and turned the dial a little. The whole sky started to move. Slowly. Turning round them, the way it actually did every night over the tall house, whether anyone looked or not.

“There.” He pointed. “Low down. Left of the bright one.”

She looked. A small star, not bright, on its own. And next to it, in thin white letters, where there were no other words anywhere in the whole sky, someone had put a label.

LIN YU

“It doesn’t mean anything.” He was talking too fast. “It’s not official. You can’t really buy stars. People sell certificates but they’re nonsense. I asked the man to put a label on. That’s all. It’s just for tonight. I picked a small one. I thought you’d hate a big one.”

She looked at the little star with her name next to it. This morning she’d stood on a hill in the cold and nobody had looked at her. Then everyone had gone to work. She’d told herself that was fair. That was what the day was for.

And now there was a star with her name on it, turning slowly over her head in the dark. Because somebody had rung up on Monday and asked how much.

She started to cry. She didn’t mean to. It came up from somewhere low down and she couldn’t stop it. Lying on her back on the carpet with the tears running sideways into her hood and her ears. No noise. There never was. But her whole chest was shaking with it, and she put both hands over her face.

He didn’t say a word. No what’s wrong. No it’s okay. He rolled onto his side on the carpet. He took her hands away from her face, one at a time, and held them. Then he put his hand under her jaw, turned her face up to him, bent over her, and kissed her.

Gently at first. On her wet mouth, with the stars going round behind his head.

She made a sound. Half a sob. She grabbed the front of his coat with both hands and hung on. He kissed her again, harder. She was still crying. She kissed him back anyway, mouth open, face wet, glasses shoved up crooked, and pulled him down by his coat until he was half over her on the carpet. She could feel his heart through all their layers. The sky went round and round above them both.

She wouldn’t say why. He didn’t ask. He kissed her eyes shut, one and then the other. He kissed the tears off the side of her face. Then her mouth again, slow, until she’d stopped shaking and her hands had let go of his coat and gone round his neck instead.

A voice came down out of the dark from a speaker somewhere. Very polite.

“Five minutes, Mr. Wang.”

Eliana burst out laughing. Wet and cracked, into Yu Chen’s neck. She couldn’t stop that either. He lay on the carpet under the turning stars with her laughing all over him, and she felt him smile against her hair.

“Did he see?”

“He’s in a booth.”

“With a WINDOW?”

“…Possibly with a window.”

“Oh my god.”

“He’s been paid. He didn’t see anything.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They got the last bus home. He’d left the bike at the top of the hill and said he’d get it in the morning.

At the end of the lane, under the noodle stall’s dark shutter, she stopped and took the egg out of her pocket. It was cold now. She’d carried it all day.

“Ah Sim leaves it. Every year. Outside my door, before we go up to the grave. She’s never said a word about it.”

He looked at the egg in her hand.

“Every year?”

“Every year.”

She cracked it on the edge of the shutter and peeled it, careful, and the shell came off in red bits into her palm. Inside it was white and perfect. She broke it in half and held one half out to him.

He took it. He looked at it. Then he looked past her, up the lane, at the tall house, at the dark kitchen window on the ground floor. He opened his mouth. He shut it again.

“What?”

“Nothing.” He ate his half. “Happy birthday.”

This time she let him.

“Say it again.”

“Happy birthday, Yu-er.”

“…Okay. That’s two. That’s enough.” She wiped her eyes on her sleeve. “Don’t push it.”

chapters.title: She Breaks a System for Fun
chapters.desc: Someone has been inside the wall Eliana built for Chen Si, fixed the one mistake she didn’t know she’d made, and sent him a bill for it. Eliana has never been beaten before. She takes it badly, so Yu Chen turns it into a dare.
chapters.epigraph: “She fixed my mistake and sent a bill. A bill. One day I’m going to beat her.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
Eliana Lin was having a great night. For about four minutes.

She’d built the wall over the winter. That was what she called it. It wasn’t a wall. It was a hundred small, careful things stacked round the way Chen Si’s people kept their secrets. Six weeks of work. Qian had told her Mr. Chen was pleased. From Qian, that was basically fireworks.

Once a month she walked round it in the dark. Checking. Like Ah Sim going round the tall house at night, rattling windows that were already shut.

Friday, three in the morning, can of something green in one hand. Rattle, rattle. Fine. Fine. Fine.

Not fine.

There was a weak place. A tiny wrong thing near the bottom, where two of the careful things met. She’d missed it in December. She’d have missed it again tonight if she hadn’t been bored.

Oh, that’s bad, she thought, and for one second she was delighted. A hole! She loved holes.

Then she looked closer.

Someone had already found it. Found it, fixed it, and left. And the fix wasn’t hers. It was neater than hers. Smaller. It did the same job with half the fuss, and there was nothing else anywhere. No mess. No footprints. Just one line, tucked into the one place only the person who’d built the wall would ever think to look.

Fixed. Invoice to client.

She read it four times.

Then she put the can down very carefully on the edge of the desk, the way you’d put down something that might go off.

Who ARE you?

Somebody out there in the sleeping city was awake right now. They’d been in her wall. And they’d been nice about it.

That was the worst part. Was it a joke? A warning? A hello? She didn’t sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at the gate at eight with the flask. He looked at her face once.

“How long have you been up?”

“I slept.”

“When?”

“…Around.”

“Around what?”

“Around the general idea of sleeping.” She took the flask. “Don’t. I’m fine. Something happened at work and it’s FINE.”

He didn’t push. He walked her to the bus stop. The bus came. She sat by the window, and he went off down the lane on the green bike to get ahead of it, like always.

Her phone went at the third stop.

Qian: Mr. Chen received the attached overnight and would value your view.

The attached was a report. Two pages. Plain, short, and right the whole way through. It didn’t show off once, which was so much worse. At the bottom there was a total that made her eyebrows go up into her hood. And a name.

He Si-Mei.

Qian: Mr. Chen has taken Ms. He on. He asks that the two of you share anything you find. He also asks me to say that he does not hold this against you.

Doesn’t hold it against her. DOESN’T HOLD IT AGAINST HER.

She put her forehead on the bus window and stayed like that up the whole zigzag.

✦ ✦ ✦

The tutorial at eleven was eight of them round a table and a postgraduate in a cardigan who liked to go round the room.

“Lin Yu. Question three. Talk us through it?”

She’d done question three. She’d done all of them, and the next sheet, at five in the morning, because it was that or look at the line in the wall again. She knew question three better than the cardigan did.

She opened her mouth. Nothing.

Seven faces turned. Her neck went hot. Then her ears. The cardigan waited with the kind smile, the one that made it worse. Somebody’s chair creaked.

Brilliant. Somebody in this city could walk through her best work in the dark without a sound, and she couldn’t say four sentences to a man in knitwear.

She looked down and typed instead. Straight into the shared document on the big screen at the front. The whole answer, four lines, fast. Then a fifth line, in red, because there was a mistake in the question.

The cardigan read it. His smile went.

“Oh. Right. Yes. That’s—yes.”

He moved on. Nobody looked at her again. She pulled her sleeves down over her hands and thought, at least I’m still better than HIM, and felt like a terrible person.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was already on the bench behind the observatory with two boxes of noodles. He held one out. She sat down and put it on her knee and didn’t open it.

“She sent a BILL.”

“Who did?”

“He Si-Mei. I don’t know who she is. Nobody does. I looked. There’s nothing.”

“Nothing?”

“Do you know how hard it is to leave NOTHING? Everybody leaves something. I leave something.” She stabbed the lid of the box with her chopsticks, through the plastic. “She got into my wall. The winter one. The one I was proud of. She found a mistake I didn’t know I’d MADE. She fixed it. And then she sent Chen Si an invoice. For fixing my work.”

“Is it a big invoice?”

“Huge.”

“Was she right?”

She stared at the harbour for a while.

“…Yes.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t say okay. She was completely right. It’s a better fix than I’d have done. I keep looking at it. I can’t stop.”

He opened his own noodles. She watched him do it. He didn’t understand most of what she did, and he’d said so, more than once, plainly. She liked that he never pretended. But he always got the shape of a thing. Even when the inside was all numbers.

“You used to want this.”

“Want WHAT?”

“Someone else who can see the holes. You told me. In October, on my roof. You said it was lonely, being the only one.”

She had said that. She’d forgotten. He hadn’t.

“Yes, well. That was before she sent a bill.”

“So now there’s one.”

“Now there’s one, and all I want is for her to be worse than me.” She pulled her hood forward. “She’s probably lovely. She probably feeds stray cats. I hope her cats bite her.”

“You don’t hope that.”

“I hope they nibble.”

He laughed through his nose. Then he looked at her over his chopsticks.

“You’ve never had one before. Somebody as good as you.”

She stopped stabbing the box.

Nobody else would’ve said it like that. Elowen would’ve said it didn’t matter, and to go to bed. Baba didn’t know she did any of this. Yu Chen just said the true thing. Her whole life, there’d been one room where she was never small. Now somebody was standing in it, a little higher up, and she didn’t know where to put her feet.

“No,” she said. “I haven’t.”

Three girls came along the path. The one with the rings saw him and waved and called something. He lifted a hand. Gave her the pleasant smile, the one that didn’t go anywhere. They walked on.

“You never actually talk to them.”

“I’m polite to them.”

“That’s not talking.”

“No.” He didn’t make it heavy. “I don’t have a lot left over for people in general.”

“Why not?”

He looked at her.

“Eat your noodles, Yu-er.”

So that was a whole answer, apparently. She opened the box. She was starving, it turned out. She ate half of it in about a minute, hunched over the box. When she looked up he was watching her mouth.

“What?”

He reached over and wiped the corner of her mouth with his thumb. Chilli oil. Then he licked his thumb, without even thinking about it, and went back to his own box.

She sat there with her chopsticks in the air and her face going up in flames.

“You can’t just DO that.”

“Do what?”

“On the BENCH. People walk past the bench.”

“Nobody was walking past.”

“The girl with the rings could’ve come back!”

“She’s gone to the arts block.” He ate a noodle. “Rule four is about things people can see. Nobody saw.”

“I saw.”

“You’re allowed to see.”

She ate the rest with her hood all the way down over her eyes. It didn’t help at all.

“How does it feel?” he asked, when she’d finished. “Her being there.”

She thought about it. The line in the wall. The neat little fix.

“Awful.” A second. “Amazing.” Another one. “Awful.”

“Both, then.”

“I’m going to beat her. One day. I don’t know when. I’m going to get so good she has to send ME a bill.”

“Of course you are.”

He said it like the weather. Like she’d told him it would get dark tonight. He wasn’t teasing. He just believed it. Something that had been rattling in her chest since three in the morning went still.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fourth floor emptied at six. She couldn’t settle.

She opened her own work and kept drifting back to the wall. She read the same page six times. At the far end of the long table, Yu Chen turned pages of his paving slab of a book without a sound. Then he shut it.

“You’re sulking.”

“I’m thinking.”

“You’ve read that page six times. You do this face.” He did the face. It was a very bad impression. It was also, annoyingly, right.

“I do NOT do that face.”

“I can’t fix the bill. I don’t understand the bill.” He poured tea into the flask lid and pushed it down the table to her, all the way, until it stopped by her laptop. “So here’s something you can win tonight.”

She looked up.

“The booking site for these rooms. You’ve been using it under my name all year.”

“…Maybe.”

“So you can obviously get into it. But you do it a day at a time, and you always leave it late.” He nodded down the row of little study rooms along the wall. “4B. Every weekday morning, from now to the end of term. In my name. If you can do it before that tea’s finished—”

“That’s a chore. That’s not a prize.”

“I wasn’t finished. If you can, I’ll take you anywhere you want. Tonight. Right now. My card. And you’re not allowed to complain about the money.”

She looked at the tea steaming in the lid. She looked at him, sitting there with his hands round his cup, trying to turn the worst day of her year into a game. He couldn’t do anything about the bill. So he’d found something he could do.

Idiot. She pulled the laptop towards her.

It was a terrible little website. It had been built by somebody’s nephew in about 2009. She didn’t touch anyone else’s booking, only his. Before the tea had stopped steaming, every weekday morning in 4B said Wang Y.C., from Monday until the last day of term.

“Done.”

He looked at the lid. Still full. He looked at his watch.

“Four minutes.”

“It’s a really bad website.”

“Four minutes, Yu-er.”

“It’s not a big deal.” She shut the laptop and stood up and pulled her hood down, so he couldn’t see that she was pleased. She was so pleased. “Drink your tea. We’re going to the roof.”

“Anywhere in the world. And you pick the roof.”

“I like the roof!”

✦ ✦ ✦

The library roof wasn’t a roof you were meant to go on. There was a door on the fifth floor that said NO ENTRY. It opened if you leaned on it the right way, with your hip. Behind it, concrete steps went up to a flat space with air-conditioning units humming all over it, and a low wall, and the whole hill going down below. The city below that. The harbour at the bottom with its chain of orange lights.

It was cold and clear. You could even see a few real stars over the reservoir, thin, but there. Not like the planetarium. She thought about the planetarium anyway, and her ears went hot again. Great. Her ears were having a very busy day.

She leaned on the wall with his flask and looked out.

“She’s out there somewhere. Up right now. Fixing someone else’s mistakes and sending them a bill.” She drank. “I can’t decide if I hate her or want her to be my friend.”

“Both. You do that.”

She turned round.

“I do NOT do th—”

He kissed her before she got to the end of it.

He’d come up close while she was talking. She hadn’t heard him on the gravel. He took her chin in his hand, tipped her face up, and kissed her right in the middle of her word. The flask lid fell out of her fingers and rolled away across the gravel. She let it go. His hand was warm from his cup. His mouth was warm. The wind came up off the harbour, and she forgot to feel it.

“You’re meant to be taking me somewhere,” she said into his mouth.

“This is somewhere.”

“That’s cheating.”

“You picked the roof.”

She could’ve argued. She could’ve made him fly her somewhere stupid, just to watch him go red working out the flights. But his hands were warm and the wind was cold, and she’d won something tonight, even if it wasn’t the thing she wanted.

She grabbed the front of his coat and pulled him back down.
