He walked her backwards until her shoulders hit the side of one of the big units. It was humming and warm. He kissed her harder. She got her hands inside his coat, then inside his jumper, flat on his stomach. He made a noise into her mouth at how cold they were.

“Your HANDS—”

“You said they’re always cold.”

“I didn’t say put them THERE—”

He didn’t pull away, though. He laughed, and kissed her jaw, and under her ear, the place that made her knees stop working. She hung on to him. She pressed the whole length of herself against him and heard herself say his name out loud. On a roof. One flight of stairs above a door that said NO ENTRY.

“Someone’ll come up,” he said against her neck. Not stopping.

“Nobody comes up. That’s what the sign’s for.”

“That’s not what signs are for.”

“Shh.”

He slid his warm hands under the back of her hoodie, flat on her bare skin. She shivered for a reason that had nothing to do with the wind, and stopped arguing about anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was the one who stopped, in the end, because her teeth were going.

“You’re frozen.” He was already taking his coat off.

“I’m fine.”

“Your teeth are chattering at me.”

“They’re—fine, they’re excited—”

He put the coat round her. It came down to her knees. He did up one button in the middle, very seriously, like a nurse. Then he stood back in his jumper in the wind and looked at her.

“What?”

“Nothing. You look like a tent.”

“YOU look like you’re going to get pneumonia.”

“I’m a medical student. I’d know.”

She found the flask lid by the wall and screwed it back on. Down below, the whole city had its lights on. Somewhere in it, a woman she’d never met was awake in front of a screen, doing exactly what Eliana did. Eliana could feel her out there. Like a light on in a window across a garden.

“Next time,” she said, “I’m going to find HER mistake.”

“What if she doesn’t make one?”

“Everyone makes one.” She pushed her glasses up. “Then I’m going to fix it. And I’m going to send her a bill. And it’s going to be bigger than hers.”

“How much bigger?”

“One coin bigger. So she knows I counted.”

He laughed so hard he had to sit down on the steps. She stood over him in his coat with the flask, extremely pleased with herself, until he pulled her down by the hem of it and kissed her again, and the door at the bottom that said NO ENTRY banged in the wind, and they both jumped about a foot.

chapters.title: Yu Chen Asks Raiden for Advice
chapters.desc: At Raiden and Evangeline’s birthday lunch, Yu Chen asks Raiden how to get on Lin Jian’s good side. The advice is useless, Eliana overhears it, and by the end both men are sworn to silence by a girl with a spreadsheet.
chapters.epigraph: “You want to date my sister. I want to go on living. I think we can help each other.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
He was invited to the birthday lunch as the boy who carried tables.

That was the whole job title. Eliana had said it at the Lin table one Sunday, without looking up from her rice. “The Song boy next door could bring the folding tables up from the cellar. He’s tall. He does what he’s told.” Her father hadn’t said anything. From Lin Jian, that was a yes.

So on Saturday, Yu Chen carried tables.

It was Raiden and Evangeline’s birthday. The ninth of April. They shared it, though they weren’t twins by blood. Raiden explained this to him twice before noon. Yu Chen already knew. Eliana had drawn him the whole family on the back of a lecture handout in October. Lines, dates, little arrows. Then she’d said “forget I told you” and folded it into his pocket. He’d kept it. Obviously.

He hadn’t come for the tables.

Over the winter he’d decided something. One day he was going to stand in front of Lin Jian and say a true sentence about his daughter. And he wasn’t going to get thrown out of the lane for it. To do that he needed to know how the man worked. You didn’t cut into something you hadn’t read about first.

He’d read everything available. That was Eliana. She told him things sideways and then told him to forget them. It wasn’t enough. He needed someone on the inside.

Raiden Lin was on the inside. And Raiden Lin, famously, couldn’t keep anything in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got him by the cellar steps, stacking the last of the chairs.

“Can I ask you something?”

Raiden put a chair down, sat on it backwards, and rested his chin on his arms on the back of it. Plaster on his thumb. Paint on his wrist. A bit of grey string at his collar that he kept touching and tucking back in.

“Anything! I’m the easy one. Everyone says. Elowen’s sharp, Evangeline’s silent, Elara cries, Eliana bites. I’m the one you ask.” He tipped his head. “You want to ask about Eliana.”

Yu Chen didn’t answer. Which was an answer.

“I KNEW it. I’ve known since the flask. Nobody carries a flask up that hill every day for a girl he’s not—” Raiden put a hand on his heart. “That’s so sweet. Does she know?”

“She knows.”

“Does—” A stage whisper. It carried across the whole garden. “Does Baba know?”

“No.”

“Oh, good. Good. Keep it that way. He’ll—”

Raiden drew his plastered thumb across his own throat.

“Figuratively. Mostly. He doesn’t like policemen. You live in the policeman’s house. It’s a whole thing.” He brightened. “But you want advice. On how to get round him. Yes? You’re a planner. You’ve written something down. I can see it on your face.”

Yu Chen had written something down. In the back of the notebook. PLAN (LIN JIAN). Three points. All of them, it would turn out, wrong.

“I want to understand him. Before I ever say anything. I don’t want to get it wrong.”

Raiden looked at him with real fondness. Glass-door fondness. The kind you save for someone about to walk into one.

“Sit down. This’ll take a while, and most of it’s useless, and you’re going to use it anyway. I watched you stack those chairs. You lined them up by height.”

Yu Chen sat on a chair.

“First thing. You can’t approach him. Nobody does. You stand next to the thing he loves until he notices you’re always there. That’s how Zhao did it. Zhao stood next to Elowen for about three years without saying anything, and one day Baba decided he liked him.”

“I don’t have three years.”

“Everyone has three years.” He said it like a fortune cookie. “Second thing. Bring something. Not for him. For the house. A fruit. A tool. Something that says, I’m useful and I won’t steal the spoons. You carried the tables. Good. Keep carrying things.” He leaned in. “Third thing. And this is the one nobody’s going to tell you—”

“Raiden.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana was at the top of the cellar steps with a tray of cold dishes. Yu Chen had learned to be afraid of that exact face.

“What are you doing?”

“Giving advice.” Raiden looked between them. “To the Song boy. About tables. Table-carrying. Technique.”

“You were talking about Baba. I heard you from the kitchen. You did the throat thing. I SAW your hand.”

“I was being helpful!”

“You were being you.”

She came down two steps, put the tray on a chair, and folded her arms. Yu Chen watched her face change. Cold and clear and very calm. Her two-in-the-morning face. The one strangers never got to see.

“Here’s what’s going to happen. Raiden, you don’t tell anyone anything. Not that he asked. Not that I—” Her ears went red. She pushed on. “Not ANYTHING. And in return, I don’t tell anybody you bought a garage near the Docks in December. In the name of Cao Jia. Who builds motorbikes.”

Raiden’s mouth fell open.

“How do you—”

“Who you married in September, at a registry office, on a Thursday, and who you are hiding from this entire family.”

Married.

Yu Chen looked at Raiden. Raiden’s hand had gone straight to the grey string at his collar. He held on to it. Tight. Wallet-on-a-crowded-bus tight.

“Yu-er—”

“And whose number’s in your phone under Tyres.”

“I—that’s—who TOLD you—”

Somewhere in the house, Ah Sim was banging a pot.

“I’ve known since New Year. You’ve been on the spreadsheet since February. So has she. So you keep your mouth shut about mine, and I’ll keep mine shut about yours, and nobody’s throat gets—” she looked at his thumb “—figuratively anything.”

Raiden had gone faint.

“You have a spreadsheet.”

“Everyone’s on the spreadsheet.”

“Am I a column or a row?”

“You’re a row. She’s a row. There’s a tab.” She picked up the tray. “Lunch is in ten minutes. Wash the paint off. You both look guilty. It’s obvious.”

She went back up. At the top she stopped, without turning round.

“The third thing. The one nobody tells him. What was it?”

Raiden looked at Yu Chen. Then at his sister’s back.

“Baba’s not angry at the boy next door.” For once he wasn’t loud. “He’s angry at himself. He has been for nineteen years. He points it at whatever’s nearest. Lately the nearest thing’s you.” He swallowed. “Whoever loves you is going to have to stand in the way of that. That’s the third thing.”

She stood very still with the tray.

Then she went in without a word.

They sat on their chairs by the cellar steps. Two boys outside the head teacher’s office.

“Married?”

“Shh! Not out LOUD!” Raiden looked at the kitchen window, then back. He tucked the string in. “September. It was… it was a Thursday, she’s right, she’s always right, it’s horrible. Nobody knows. Not Elowen. Not anyone. Jinx has a rule.” He rubbed his face. “How does she KNOW? How does she know things?”

“I don’t ask.”

“You don’t ask.” Raiden stared at him. “Oh, you’re perfect. You’re perfect for her. That’s terrifying.” He held out his plastered hand. “You want to date my sister. I want to go on living. I think we can help each other.”

Yu Chen shook it.

Raiden sighed with enormous pride.

“She’s going to make a frightening wife.”

Yu Chen didn’t correct the word. He didn’t want to.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch he sat at the bottom of the table, below Uncle Mok. That was where the table boy sat.

Nine of them. Ah Sim in and out. Lin Jian at the head, grey and enormous, hands flat either side of his bowl. Elowen on his right, in green. Zhao beside her. Zhao looked at Yu Chen once, for four seconds, and then seemed to lose interest. Yu Chen didn’t believe that for a second. Raiden opposite, scrubbed pink, telling a long story about a crane. Elara, straight from the hospital, nodding off between dishes. Evangeline by the window, silent, eating almost nothing. Eliana halfway down with her laptop shut beside her bowl. Not looking at him. So, looking at him the whole time.

He passed dishes before anyone asked. He said very little. He watched.

They all talked round her. That was the first thing he saw.

“Ah Sim. Has she been eating properly?”

“Noodles. Every night. Noodles.”

“She needs to get out more. Look at her. She’s gone the colour of a mushroom.”

“A nice mushroom…”

“Elara, you’re asleep.”

“I’m resting my eyes.”

Over her head. Pleasantly. Like she was a little kid in the room. Eliana ate her rice and didn’t look up.

His chopsticks stopped.

Then Lin Jian spoke. He didn’t say much. He never did. He looked down the table, somewhere past his youngest daughter’s left ear, and said it to Elowen.

“Tell her she’s not to be on that computer so late. The neighbours can see her light at four in the morning. It looks like something.”

The neighbours. Yu Chen kept his face very still. He could have told Lin Jian the exact minute it went off. Last night it had been ten past four. The night before, nearly five.

The table carried on. Elowen started something smoothing. Raiden laughed about the crane.

“I can hear you, Baba.”

Eliana said it to her bowl. Lin Jian didn’t answer. He reached for the fish.

Yu Chen put his chopsticks down.

He didn’t decide to. It went the way it had gone in the corridor of the fish tank, with the boy who’d yanked her hood. The nice face slid off the front of him. What was under it was cold. Steady. Much older. It didn’t care who was at the head of the table.

“She said she can hear you.”

He didn’t raise his voice. He said it the length of the table, from the seat below Uncle Mok.

The whole table shut up. Even Raiden.

Lin Jian looked up. He looked down the table at the table boy. Properly. For the first time all day. Was he going to be thrown out? Into the lane, chair and all? Probably.

“She’s right there. You’re talking about her light. You could ask her about it. She’d tell you. She tells me.”

Nobody moved. Zhao had stopped eating. Raiden was studying his plate like it had a map on it. Elowen’s hand had come off the table. Eliana had gone white.

Yu Chen held Lin Jian’s eyes. The most frightening man in the Walled City. Fine. He’d talked about her like she was furniture. Yu Chen found he didn’t care about anything else in the room at all.

Then he put the face back on. Deliberately. Like a lid on a pot.

“Sorry. That wasn’t my place.” He picked his chopsticks up. “The fish is very good, Ah Sim.”

Ah Sim was in the doorway.

“It’s carp.”

Well. That settled that.

Raiden said something about the crane again, much too loud. Elowen answered it. The table started up. Lin Jian went back to his bowl.

But two dishes later Yu Chen glanced up, and Lin Jian was looking at him again. From under those heavy brows. It wasn’t anger. What was it? He couldn’t name it. It looked almost like a man recognising something.

Across the table, Eliana was staring at him with her mouth open. So was Raiden. Zhao had turned his whole head, like Yu Chen had only just come in.

Under the table, something kicked his ankle. Hard. Eliana. Then it stayed there, her socked foot pressed against his, all through the soup.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took the empty rice tub into the pantry, because the top shelf was high and it saved Ah Sim the stool. The door opened behind him and shut.

“You are an IDIOT.”

“I know.”

“You said she said she can hear you. To Lin Jian. To his FACE. At his TABLE.” One finger in his chest. She was walking him backwards. “Nobody does that! Zhao doesn’t do that! And Zhao once—” The finger waved. “You don’t SAY things to Baba. You stand next to the thing he loves until—”

“Raiden already gave me that one.”

“Raiden’s an idiot TOO.”

Her ears were red. Her eyes were bright. He’d learned to tell her two kinds of furious apart, the cold one and this one. This wasn’t the cold one.

“You scared me. You went like you went with the hood boy. Cold. And it’s—”

“Does it frighten you?”

She stopped.

“No.” He watched it surprise her. “That’s the problem. It should. It doesn’t.”

He kissed her.

He didn’t ask. He took her by the waist and turned them both round, so it was her back against the rice sacks and not his. Then he kissed her. In the dark, with dried fish and star anise all round them, and a whole family on the other side of the door. She made a squeak against his mouth. Then she grabbed two fistfuls of his shirt and went up on her toes and kissed him back. He lifted her the last little bit. A bag of rice slid sideways behind her and thumped onto the floor.

“They’ll HEAR—”

“Then be quiet.”

That made her laugh. Laughing wasn’t quiet. He had to kiss it out of her, and that didn’t work either, she just laughed into his mouth instead.

The door opened.

Ah Sim stood there with the empty soup pot. She looked at them. The boy next door with his arms round the youngest Lin. Eliana with her hand still twisted in his shirt. The rice bag on the floor.

She took her time about it.

“The rice goes on the high shelf.”

“Yes, Ah Sim.”

She put the pot in the sink. She took a jar of pickled radish off the low shelf. She went out and pulled the door nearly shut behind her, not quite. Then, in the kitchen, to nobody:

“Tell them the cake’s coming.”

Eliana put her face in his chest and shook.

“She’s not going to say anything,” she managed. “She never does. She’s the most frightening woman Raiden’s ever met, and she leaves me noodles.” She looked up. The laugh went out of her face. “You stood up for me. At the table. Nobody does that. Elowen smooths it. Everyone smooths it. You just… said it.”

“He was talking about you like you weren’t there.”

“I know.” She grabbed his collar and yanked it straight, both sides, much harder than it needed. “Don’t do it again.”

“I’ll do it again.”

She looked at him. She didn’t argue. He watched her decide not to, and put it away somewhere for later. A strand of hair had come out of her pencil. He tucked it back behind her ear. She went pink all over again.

Then she went up on her toes and kissed him once more, hard and fast, for no reason. She ducked out to tell everyone about the cake.

He picked up the rice bag. He put it on the high shelf. Then he stood in the dark a moment with his hand flat on the shelf and his heart going.

He’d come to understand the family. Instead he’d told the head of it, at his own table, that he was wrong.

He didn’t regret it. That was the part that would’ve frightened anyone who thought he was soft.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden caught him at the gate at dusk, with his coat on and his car keys in his hand.

“Fourth thing.”

“You said there were three.”

“There’s always a fourth thing.”

Raiden looked back at the tall house. The study light was on.

“He looked at you. After. Did you see? He looked at you like you were a drawing he hadn’t finished.” He shook his head. “I’ve been trying to get that look for twenty-four years. You got it with one sentence and some carp.”

“Is that good?”

“I have no idea!” Raiden beamed. His phone buzzed in his pocket. He looked at it and his whole face changed. Went soft and stupid. Yu Chen didn’t need to see the screen. He knew what it said at the top.

“Tyres?”

“Shut up.” Raiden put it away. “You didn’t see anything. I didn’t see the pantry. Ah Sim told me nothing. Ah Sim only looked at me. It was very loud.”

He went off down the lane, touching his collar.

Yu Chen went home over the wall. At his desk, he got the notebook out and turned to the back. PLAN (LIN JIAN). Three points.

He crossed out all three.

Underneath, in capitals, he wrote one new line: STAND IN THE WAY.

Across the garden, her light came on. Then his phone.

Eliana: you’re still an idiot

Eliana: thank you

Eliana: don’t do it again

Eliana: (do it again)

chapters.title: A Hackathon, Allegedly
chapters.desc: He takes her to his family’s house by the sea for a weekend, and everyone at home thinks it’s a coding retreat. Wei Long, who raised him, rings twice with terrible advice. Nobody does any coding.
chapters.epigraph: “Bring fruit. Don’t talk about her father. Actually, don’t talk at all — you talk too much when you’re nervous.” — Song Wei Long
chapters.content:
The cover story was a hackathon.

“A what?” Baba had said. To Elowen. Not to her.

“A coding weekend,” Eliana had said, to the table. “With people from my course. At a friend’s place by the sea. Four of us. It’s for a competition.”

She’d practised it on the camp bed for two nights. Baba looked at the fish.

“If your sister says so.”

Elowen said so. After looking at Eliana for slightly too long.

So on Friday Eliana packed one bag of clothes and two laptops, and told nobody that the four of them were two of them. Or that the friend’s place belonged to the friend.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found that bit out on the last bend of the coast road.

He’d hired a car for the weekend because he didn’t own one. He drove it like it might be taken off him at any moment, both hands on the wheel, ten under the limit. Two hours south. Then the road came round a cliff, and he slowed down, and there it was.

A white house on the cliff. Long and low, with a whole wall of glass facing the sea. A flat roof. Steps cut down the rock to a little strip of sand that nobody else could get to. No other house anywhere. Just sea, out to a flat line. And birds.

“Whose is THAT?”

He pulled in. His ears had gone red.

“Mine. Well. My father’s. It’s in the trust. I come about twice a year and open the windows.”

“You OWN a CLIFF?”

“Just the top bit.”

She knew he had money. He’d bought the Song house off Wei Long. Auntie Dai came every day. There was a trust, and a lawyer called Mr. Quan. But money in the Walled City was something you kept in a drawer. It wasn’t a cliff.

“Auntie Dai’s cousin keeps it aired. There’s food in.” He turned the engine off and looked at the steering wheel. “Sorry. I should’ve said. I didn’t want you to say no.”

“Why would I say no?”

“Because it’s a lot. And you don’t like a lot.”

That was true. She didn’t have an answer. So she got out of the car and looked at the sea instead. It was so big and so blue that she forgot to be cross for at least a minute.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long rang at six, while Yu Chen was carrying the bags in.

She knew who it was before he said anything. His face went a notch more careful. Only Wei Long did that to him. He stood by the glass with the phone at his ear.

“Yes. No. It’s fine. Yes. No, it’s—Wei Long. It’s fine.”

He held the phone away from his ear and looked at it. From across the room she could hear a flat voice still going.

“He wants to talk to you.”

“WHAT? No! Why?”

“I don’t know. He’s never wanted to talk to anyone.”

He held it out like it was hot. She took it.

“…Hello?”

“You’re the Lin girl.” Dry. Flat. Not warm, not unkind. Like reading out a number plate. “He’s never taken anyone to that house. He took me once. To open the windows. I raised him from fifteen. So you can see this is serious.”

Strangers turned her to stone. This one didn’t. He wasn’t trying to be liked. It was weirdly restful.

“Okay.”

“I’m not going to ask what your intentions are. I know his. He writes them to his grandmother every month.” A pause. “One question. Then you can give him back.”

“Okay.”

“Are you going to be careful with him? He’s careful with everyone. Nobody’s ever been careful with him back. That’s the whole question. You don’t have to say it out loud. He’s standing right there doing the face.”

She looked at Yu Chen. He was standing by the glass doing the face.

“Yes.”

“Good. Give him back.”

She gave him back. He listened to another minute with his ears going redder and redder.

“I do NOT talk too much when I’m— No. Goodbye, Wei Long. Goodbye.”

He hung up and looked at her.

“What did he say to you?”

“He asked if I liked the house.”

He looked at her for a long time. He didn’t believe her at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t code.

She’d brought two laptops out of habit. They sat zipped in their bags all weekend. She’d told Qian she’d be away. Qian had written back Understood and nothing else. For two whole days nobody needed anything found or cleaned or watched.

The quiet in her head was so strange that for hours she kept checking her phone to see what was wrong. Nothing was.

Elowen: How’s the hackathon?

Eliana: very hard. lots of coding

Elowen: Send me a picture of the coding.

She sent a picture of her laptop bag on the table. Zipped. Beside it, through the glass, the whole sea.

Elowen: Yu-er. That’s the sea.

Eliana: it’s an outdoor hackathon

Elowen: Who’s the other three?

Eliana: people

Elowen: Hm.

She’d been at Zhao’s too long. Eliana turned her phone face down and went swimming.

✦ ✦ ✦

The water in the cove was cold and clear. She swam out past the rocks and lay on her back and looked at the sky. He sat on the sand in shorts with his feet in the water and watched her the whole time, like a lifeguard who’d been paid in advance.

When she came out he wrapped her in a towel the size of a tent and dried her hair with another one, roughly, like you’d dry a dog. It stood up all over her head.

“You’ve ruined it.”

“It was wet.”

“It was STYLED.”

“It was in a pencil.”

She ducked out from under the towel and looked at him. He had sand on his eyebrow. She didn’t tell him.

Then she slept. That was the strangest part. In the afternoon, on a chair in the sun by the glass, mouth open, two whole hours. She woke up with a line down her cheek from the cushion. He was beside her reading. For once he wasn’t watching her. He was just there.

“You let me sleep again.”

“You keep doing it. I think it’s the sea. We should bottle it.”

On the table beside her there was a plate. Apple. Cut into rabbits. Every piece had two little ears where he’d notched the skin. There were nine of them, sitting in a row.

“What’s this?”

“Fruit.”

“They’re RABBITS.”

“Auntie Dai taught me. She says nobody says no to a rabbit.” He didn’t look up from his book. “They’re easier to eat if they’ve got ears. That’s science.”

“That’s NOT science.”

She ate all nine. She held the last one out to him on her fork, ears first. He ate it off the fork without looking up, and turned his page, and his whole neck went pink.

✦ ✦ ✦

He tried to buy her a rig.

He did it badly. That was how she knew it was real. Saturday dinner, over the food the cousin had left.

“I’ve been thinking. You’re always saying your machine at home is slow. I could easily—”

“No.”

“I didn’t finish.”

“You don’t have to finish. The answer’s no.”

“It would make your work easier.”

“That’s not the point.”

She put her chopsticks down. She felt herself go cold, the first time all weekend. She couldn’t stop it.

“I buy my own tools. All of them. With my own money, which I earn, doing the thing you don’t ask about. You can buy me tea. You can buy ten thousand pairs of headphones. You can buy a PLANETARIUM, apparently, I’m still not over that. But not the tools. The tools are mine.”

He looked at her.

“Okay.”

“That’s it? Okay?”

“You drew a line. It’s your line.” He reached for the rice. “I’ll buy the tea.”

No sulk anywhere in it. She sat there braced for a fight that wasn’t coming. The cold went out of her. What did you even do with someone like that? You drew a line round yourself. He just picked up his chair, moved it to the other side, and kept sitting with you.

“You’re not allowed to be this reasonable. It’s annoying.”

“I know.”

“Buy the tea.”

“I’m going to buy SO much tea.”

She fed him a piece of fish off her own chopsticks to shut him up. He ate it. He looked extremely pleased with himself. It didn’t work at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long rang again on Saturday night. Yu Chen took it on the roof.

She’d gone up to see the stars. Real ones, thick across the whole sky. Better than the ceiling. She wouldn’t tell him that. He came up after her and his phone went, and he answered it a little way off along the roof, with his back to her.

She wasn’t trying to listen. The roof was just very quiet.

“Fruit. Yes. You said. —I don’t talk too much, that’s— Fine. I won’t talk at all.”

A pause.

“What? —Why are you telling me that?”

A longer pause. His back had gone very straight.

“I’m on holiday, Wei Long. —No. I haven’t heard anyone say that. —Okay. —Yes. I’ll keep my eyes open.”

Then something she didn’t catch. Then, much louder than he meant it:

“The Eraser? That’s a stupid name.”

She went cold to the ends of her fingers.

She knew that name. She hated it. It was what Chen Si’s people called her when they thought she couldn’t hear. And Wei Long was saying it. To Yu Chen. On a roof two hours from home.

What did Wei Long know? How much? Did he know it was her?

Yu Chen came back. He put the phone in his pocket and sat down next to her on the warm concrete.

“What did he want?”

“To tell me to bring fruit when I meet your father.” He looked at the sea. “And not to talk about your father. And not to talk at all, because I talk too much when I’m nervous.”

“Do you?”

“No.”

“You do, a bit.”

“Only about bones.”

He’d heard the name. She knew he had. He’d said it out loud. Now he kept his mouth shut about it, and asked nothing, and just sat there with his shoulder against hers and looked at the sea, like the call had been about fruit.

She put her head on his shoulder. She felt him go still with surprise, then settle.

“He worries,” he said, after a while. “About everything. All the time. It’s the only way he knows how to—” He stopped. “He thinks the world’s full of dangerous people.”

“It is full of dangerous people.”

“I know.” He turned his head. “I’m not scared of any of them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The last night, it was her.

They went down the rock steps in the dark with a torch and the blue blanket. He’d brought it from home. Of course he had. They spread it on the cold sand above the tide line and lay there listening to the sea. You could barely see it. Just a pale line coming and going.

He’d been building up to something all evening. She could tell. He went quiet in a particular way, and he’d been doing it since dinner. He kept touching his jacket pocket. There was a folded square of paper in it. She’d seen the corner.

She lay on the blanket and waited. Her heart was going harder than she let him know.

He didn’t do it.

She felt him decide. Felt the breath go out of him. His hand pressed the pocket flat.

“I had a thing I was going to say. I’m not going to say it. Not tonight.”

“Why not?”

“It’s too soon. And I know what that sort of thing is, for you.” He was looking up at the sky. “I’d rather say it in ten years than say it too early and watch you run up a tree.”

“I’d go DOWN a tree. I always go down.”

“Down a tree, then.”

She knew what he meant. She knew the word for the thing he hadn’t said. It started with a sound she couldn’t make. The hospital word. The one people said before they didn’t come home.

And he’d carried it all the way down a cliff, and then decided, lying next to her on his mother’s blanket, not to make her hear it.

“You can be scared of it,” he said. “The whole thing. For as long as you like. You can be scared of it forever and still have tonight. Tonight doesn’t need the other thing. Tonight’s just the beach.”

She rolled over onto him and kissed him.

First. Which she hardly ever did. Not like this, with her whole body, starting it cold. She felt him go still under her in surprise. Then his arms came up round her and hauled her the rest of the way on top of him. The sea went in and out behind them. The sand was cold under the blanket. His heart was going under her hand. She put everything into it that she couldn’t put into the word. This she could do. She’d always been able to do this.

“Eliana—”

“Don’t say the thing.” She kissed him again. “Not tonight.”

So he didn’t. He rolled her over onto the blanket instead, slowly, with one hand under her head so her hair wouldn’t get in the sand. Too late. Her hair was already full of sand.

It was cold. She didn’t care. She got her hands up under his jumper and he hissed.

“Your HANDS.”

“You knew about my hands.”

“I forget. Every time. It’s like a sneeze.”

He undid her shirt one button at a time. Kissed every place he uncovered. Her collarbone. The middle of her chest. The soft bit under her ribs that made her laugh and grab his hair.

“Ticklish.”

“I’m NOT.”

He did it again. She shrieked. A bird somewhere in the rocks complained about it. Every time the wind came off the sea, he pulled the edge of the blanket back up over her. Like it was his whole job.

“Nobody can see,” she said. It was the first time in her life she’d said that as a reason to keep going.

“Nobody at all.” Against her stomach.

After that she stopped keeping track. Sand in the blanket. Sand in her hair. Sand somewhere down the back of his collar, which he was going to find in the morning and complain about. His weight, warm against the cold. His breath at her ear. The sea going in and out behind them, louder than either of them, so for once she didn’t have to be quiet.

She wasn’t. She heard herself, out loud, under the open sky. She felt him smile against her throat.

“Don’t LAUGH at me—”

“I’m not laughing. I’m happy. It looks the same.”

She pulled him down by the shoulders until he stopped smiling, and he said her name into her neck. Low and rough. Like somebody had dragged it out of him.

Afterwards they lay tangled in the blanket while the tide crept up the sand towards their feet. She wasn’t scared of anything. Not one thing. A cliff, a dark sea, no other house for a mile, and the blanket off her own front step.

“The tide’s coming in,” he said, eventually.

“Let it.”

“It’s going to get the blanket.”

“…Fine. Save the blanket.”

He carried it, and her, most of the way up the steps. She let him.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she found the letter.

She wasn’t snooping. She was looking for coffee. There was a letter in the drawer instead. His square capitals. An address in the north. A stamp already on it, waiting to be posted. Dated last week.

She knew she shouldn’t. She read the first line anyway. She was who she was.

Dear Nainai. I’m taking Eliana to the house by the sea this weekend, so I’ll write properly when I’m back.

Then, through the fold:

You keep asking when you’ll meet her. Soon, I think. She’s not ready. So don’t send anything, and don’t tell Xing Yue’s father, and don’t put her name in a letter to anyone. But soon.

She put it back. She shut the drawer.

You keep asking. His grandmother had been asking. For how long? She did the sum she didn’t want to do. Her name in his letters. Month after month. Further back than this weekend. Further back than the planetarium. Back and back. To last summer?

He came in with wet hair.

“Coffee’s in the blue tin, on the—” He saw her face. “What?”

“Nothing! I couldn’t find the coffee.”

He got it out of the blue tin. She watched his back while he did it. A grandmother in the north asking when she’d meet the girl. How long did you have to keep writing someone’s name for your grandmother to start asking?

She wasn’t frightened. That was what frightened her.

Later, packing, she found the folded square of paper in his jacket pocket. She opened it. Of course she did.

PLAN (BEACH). 1. Say it. 2. Don’t say it if she’s tired. 3. If she runs, DON’T follow her up the cliff steps. It’s dark. Let her go. Wait at the top.

Number two had a line under it. Twice.

She folded it back up and put it in her own pocket.

“Have you seen a bit of paper?” he asked at the car. “From my jacket.”

“No.”

“It’s just. It was a list.”

“I haven’t seen any lists…”

He looked at her for a long time. She got in the car, did up her seatbelt, and looked at the sea. She didn’t open either laptop the whole way home.

chapters.title: The Fence
chapters.desc: Evangeline disappears from the flower market and comes back changed, and Eliana, who can find anyone, couldn’t find her in time. Afterwards she builds something to watch for the Lin name, and won’t tell even Yu Chen what it’s for.
chapters.epigraph: “I was three days too slow. It won’t happen again. That’s all I can tell you.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
Evangeline went to the orchid stalls at the flower market before six on Tuesday, the way she did on market mornings, and didn’t come back.

Elowen rang at nine. Her voice was wrong. Eliana had heard it go like that once before, years ago, and never wanted to hear it again.

“She’s not home. Her phone’s dead. The orchid man says she didn’t buy anything. Nobody’s seen her since before six. Baba’s at the market with everyone he’s got.”

“I’ll look.”

“Yu-er—”

“I’ll LOOK.”

She sat down at the five screens with her hood up and her cold hands going, and she looked.

She looked for three days.

✦ ✦ ✦

Finding people was most of what she did. Give her a name and an afternoon. She could tell you where a man slept, and what he was scared of. She’d found a clerk in the eastern district in a few hours once. She still thought about his hands.

She could find anyone.

She could not find her own sister.

There were no cameras at that end of the market. Or there were, and they pointed the wrong way. She knew because she’d looked before, for other jobs. There was no phone to follow. It was dead.

And there was no face.

That was the thing that stopped her cold, at two in the morning on the first night. There were no photographs of Evangeline. Anywhere. Not one. Baba had kept her out of every room with a camera in it since before Eliana was born. There was no picture of her sister anywhere in the world to put in front of a screen and say, find her.

How do you look for someone with no face?

You make one.

Raiden came on the second night. He sat on her floor with a pencil and a pad and didn’t say anything for an hour. Raiden. Not saying anything. For an HOUR.

He got the line of the jaw wrong. Rubbed it out.

“Her chin’s sharper.”

“I know her chin.”

“Then do her chin!”

“I’m DOING her chin, Yu-er—”

Wrong again. Rubbed it out. On the fourth go he got it right. Then he put the pencil down and put his head in his hands, and Eliana had to look away from him, back at the screens.

“Is it her?” He didn’t lift his head.

“It’s her.”

“Okay.” His voice cracked. “Okay. Good. Use it.”

She used it. She watched for that face everywhere she watched. All the places where things got sold that couldn’t be bought in shops.

Nothing.

Elowen rang every few hours.

“Anything?”

“No.”

“Are you eating?”

“Yes.”

“Is that true?”

“…Some of it’s true.”

“Yu-er. Please. I can’t have two of you—” Elowen stopped. Breathed. “Ring me if anything.”

“I will.”

Nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d stopped counting hours on the first night. He’d started again on the second. He couldn’t help it.

Fifty-one.

The light at the top of the tall house hadn’t gone off once. He knew because he hadn’t slept either. Not properly. He’d lie down and look across the garden and get up again.

Nothing on the food app. Nothing since Monday. So he went in.

Over the wall. Key under the flowerpot. Up the stairs on the edges, past Lin Jian’s door, past Evangeline’s. Evangeline’s was shut, for the first time since he’d started coming up these stairs. He looked at it every time.

He put tea by her elbow. She didn’t look round. He took the cold cup away. He put a box of dumplings on the corner of the desk.

“Eat one.”

“Later.”

“One.”

“I’m WORKING, Chen.”

“I know. One.”

She ate one without looking at it. Two hours later he came back and three were gone. Three out of eight. Fine. Three was something.

On the second night he put a hot-water bottle against her feet under the desk. She didn’t notice. Her feet curled round it anyway, on their own.

On the third night he stood behind her chair and watched her not blink for a very long time.

“Yu-er.”

Nothing.

“You haven’t blinked in three minutes.”

“…Busy.”

“Blink.”

She blinked. Once. Furious about it. He’d take it.

He went down to the kitchen and refilled the flask before the last one was empty. Ah Sim was at the table in the dark with her coat on. Like she’d been there since Tuesday. Maybe she had. She looked at him over the teapot.

“She eating?”

“Three dumplings.”

Ah Sim nodded. Like he’d told her the weather. Then she pushed a plate of sliced pear across the table at him.

“Take that up.”

He took it up.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday night she fell asleep at the desk. She never did that. She woke at three in the morning on Friday with her cheek on the keyboard and Elowen ringing.

“They’ve got her.” Elowen was crying. Elowen didn’t cry. “She’s at Harbourside General. She’s alive. She walked in. She’s alive, Yu-er. She’s alive.”

Eliana sat there with the phone. She couldn’t make her mouth do anything.

“Yu-er? Are you there?”

“…Yes.”

“Did you hear me?”

“Yes. Yes. I heard you.”

She put the phone down on the desk. Then she put her face in her hands and made a noise she’d never made in her life. A sort of hiccup that didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

Baba didn’t sleep those three days either. She knew because she watched the house without meaning to. His study light stayed on. Uncle Mok’s car came and went at all hours. On the second night she heard him on the stairs. A big man going up and down slowly in the dark, checking doors that were already locked.

He didn’t come up to the top. He never did. But once she opened her own door a crack, and he was standing on the landing two floors down, looking up. At the dark above him. Where she was.

She shut the door before he could see her see him. Then she opened it again.

“Baba?”

He was already going back down.

“Go to bed.”

“I’m working.”

“Then work.”

That was all. His door shut two floors down.

Why had he looked up? To check her light? To check she was still there? She hadn’t asked him that. You didn’t ask Baba things like that.

Nobody could tell her how. That was the part she couldn’t put down. Evangeline had walked into the emergency department at Harbourside at three in the morning with four other women. All of them out of a container at West Basin. She wouldn’t say who’d let them out.

“A man,” she said. “Tall.”

That was all anyone got. A man. Tall. Who’d driven them and gone. Eliana went over it for weeks. No record of a truck. No camera that caught it. She looked at every camera for miles. Nothing. Whoever had found her sister had done it without leaving a single mark anywhere she could see. That was supposed to be impossible. Everybody left marks. She left marks. He Si-Mei left marks, tiny ones. He hadn’t. And he’d done in one night what she couldn’t do in three days.

Who WAS he?

She never found out. Evangeline looked at her once across the counter at Elowen’s shop, a few weeks later, while Eliana was doing it again on her phone. Just looked. Eliana put the phone away. She stopped looking, because her sister asked her to without saying a word. She never got over it. Somebody out there was better at this than she was. A stranger. And she couldn’t even say thank you.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the hospital with Elowen at eight on Friday morning.

In the corridor Elowen stopped her with a hand on her arm.

“She’s very quiet.”

“She’s always quiet.”

“Not like this.” Elowen’s eyes were swollen. “Don’t ask her anything. Not today. Promise me.”

“I won’t. I wasn’t going to.”

“I know. I’m saying it for me.”

Evangeline was on a trolley in a borrowed gown, with a girl from the container holding her hand and not letting go. She looked at Eliana. Eliana couldn’t say anything. Evangeline didn’t need her to.

“You looked.”

Evangeline. The first thing she’d said to anyone in the family. It wasn’t a question.

“I didn’t FIND you.”

“You looked.”

Eliana went home at noon and slept four hours straight. Then she woke up and started building.

✦ ✦ ✦

It didn’t have a name yet. It was just a thing she sat down and made. Because she’d sat for three days watching the places where people got sold, and seen nothing, and she was never, ever going to be that slow again.

It watched. Not for Chen Si’s enemies. For her own family. The Lin name, wherever it came up. The address of the tall house. Her sisters’ faces. When she got to Evangeline’s she had to use Raiden’s drawing again, because there was still no photograph. She sat and looked at his pencil line of her sister’s jaw on the screen for a long time before she fed it in.

Three screens for it. Two for ordinary work. If it ever caught anything, it would wake her. Whatever she was doing. Wherever she was.

It took a week, on and off. Between lectures she didn’t go to and a job for Qian she did half asleep.

Qian: Mr. Chen asks whether you require anything. Anything at all.

Eliana: no

Qian: He asks me to say that the offer does not expire.

Eliana: thank him

She didn’t need anything Chen Si had. She needed last Tuesday back.

Yu Chen came every evening of that week.

He didn’t ask what she was building. He’d said he wouldn’t. He didn’t, even now. Even seeing her grey and shaking and not eating, sitting at the screens till four. He brought food. He made tea. He kept her alive while she worked, and he asked nothing.

On the Tuesday he reached past her to move a cold cup back from the edge of the desk.

“DON’T.”

They both froze. His hand stopped an inch from the cup.

It was her rule. Not even to move a cup. He took his hand back.

“Sorry.”

He went and stood by the door. She sat there with her face burning, hating herself, and couldn’t say it. Ten minutes later she moved the cup herself. Then she held her empty hand out behind her, without turning round.

After a second he came and put a hot cup into it. She held on to it. And to his fingers, for a bit.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday it was done.

She was still at the desk at midnight when he came up. Three screens, quiet now. Watching. She’d stopped typing hours ago. She was shaking a little. The way you shake when you’ve been cold too long, and someone finally puts you by a fire.

“It’s done.” She didn’t turn round.

He didn’t ask what was done.

“Will you tell me what it is?”

It was the first time he’d asked anything close to it. He asked it so carefully. Leaving her all the room in the world to say no.

“No. I can’t. It’s…” She stopped. “I was three days too slow. Everyone was. Baba had every man he’s got. I had every screen I’ve got. None of us found her. Some stranger did it in a night.” She swallowed. “This is so that never happens again. That’s all I can tell you. Please don’t ask me the rest.”

“I won’t.”

She turned round in the chair.

He was standing in the middle of her dark room. Too tall for it. A box of dumplings going cold in his hand. His face was doing the worried thing, the one he did over Auntie Dai’s knee. She let him. She had nothing left to tell anybody anything with.

“I can’t tonight. I can’t do… anything. I’m sorry. I just want—”

“I know.” He put the dumplings down. “Come here.”

She got out of the chair and crossed the room and he caught her. All of her at once. She put her face in the middle of his chest. He put one hand flat on her back and one on the top of her head, and held her there.

He kept his mouth shut. There wasn’t anything to fix.

She didn’t cry at first. Then she did. Without a sound, in her hood, into his shirt. He felt it. He let her. When her knees went, he went down with her, onto the floor, his back against the camp bed, her in his lap, the blue blanket pulled over both of them.

“I could find anyone,” she said, much later, into his chest. “That’s the whole thing. That’s what I’m FOR. And I couldn’t find her.”

“You built the thing that means you will. Next time.”

“There shouldn’t have to BE a next time.”

“No.” His hand moved in her hair. “But you built it. In a week. Grey and not sleeping.” He leaned his forehead down against hers. Then pulled back and frowned. “You’re warm.”

“I’m fine.”

“You’re warm, Yu-er.”

“I’m on your LAP. Under a BLANKET.” She shoved his forehead away with one finger. “Doctor.”

“Not yet.”

She lay against him with the three screens watching over both their heads.

“Your cousin’s out there looking for someone called the Eraser.”

His hand stopped. Then it started again.

“I know. I heard him say it.”

“On the roof. You said the name. Out loud.” She didn’t look up. “And then you came and sat down next to me and talked about FRUIT.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He thought about it, the way he thought about all her real questions. Properly. Taking his time.

“Because it was your name. Not mine to say.”

His arm tightened round her.

“And because I don’t care what he calls it. I care that you’re on your own in the dark with it. That’s the bit that scares me. Not what you do. How far you’ll go. On your own. Not telling anybody. Then you come out grey in the morning and get the bus.”

“So?”

“So I’m not going to stop you going. I’m just not letting you go on your own.” A pause. “I’ll hold the torch.”

“You can’t even work a torch.”

“I’ll hold it badly. You can point.”

She laughed. Wet, cracked, into his shirt. She hadn’t thought she’d do that tonight.

✦ ✦ ✦

She fell asleep against him on the floor sometime before three. The dumplings went cold. The three screens stayed quiet.

He stayed awake. She knew because every time she half woke up, his hand was still moving in her hair. Slow. Steady. And once his lips on the top of her head, very lightly. Like he was checking she was still there.

In the morning it had a name.

She’d half dreamed it, slumped against him. A fence. The kind you put round something you were never going to let anyone take again.

She typed it at the top of the three screens, where only she would ever see it. Then she went downstairs.

He’d already made the tea. He was standing at Ah Sim’s stove in yesterday’s shirt with his hair flat on one side.

“Did you sleep?”

“Some.”

“Liar.”

“Some,” he said again, and held the flask out, and didn’t ask her a single thing.

chapters.title: The Detective Already Knows
chapters.desc: Wei Long has worked out that the person the Syndicate calls “the Eraser” is the girl next door, the one the boy he raised is seeing. He comes to the garden wall off the record, to decide what to do about her, and to ask Yu Chen about a lie.
chapters.epigraph: “I asked you to your face. You looked at me and you lied. I raised you better than that. Or exactly that well.” — Song Wei Long
chapters.content:
Wei Long came on a Saturday. That was the first wrong thing.

Wei Long came on Sundays. He’d come to Sunday lunch every week since he moved out, four years ago, and ate two bowls of whatever Auntie Dai made, and told Yu Chen he was too thin. Sundays were the arrangement. A Saturday meant he had something to say that he didn’t want to say over soup.

He was on the step in his plain dark coat. In July. Hands in his pockets.

“Is Auntie Dai still here?”

“She left at six.”

“Good. Garden. I don’t want to do this in the house.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went out to the back wall, under the persimmon tree. The branch hung over onto the Lin side, full of hard green fruit. It was nearly dark. Up at the top of the tall house, her window had its thin line of light.

Wei Long looked at it. Then he looked at Yu Chen.

“Sit down.”

Wei Long sat on the edge of Auntie Dai’s raised bed, heavily. Yu Chen stayed standing.

“There’s a person the Syndicate uses. We’ve known about them a few years. No name. No face. No age. They don’t exist on paper. They clean the Lin family out of records. Old shipping files. Court papers. Anything with the old man’s name on it.”

“You told me. Last summer. On the phone.”

“I told you to keep your eyes open.” Wei Long’s face didn’t move. “We call them the Eraser.”

“It’s still a stupid name.”

“It’s not mine. Listen. Last October, after her sister came out of that container, we were watching the places where women get sold. Somebody else was already in them. Faster than us. Anything that mentioned the name Lin went wrong. Or vanished.”

Yu Chen said nothing.

“I looked at that. And at some older things. Same hand in all of them. Same—” Wei Long moved his fingers, looking for a word a policeman would use. “Signature. Neat. No mess. Once there was a photo of a persimmon left in an empty folder. A joke. Whoever it was thought they were funny.”

He looked up at the branch over their heads.

“Lin persimmons.”

The birds on the far side of the wall were going quiet. The old man over there was whistling them in. A long low note. The clack of a cage door.

“The Eraser lives in the Walled City.” Wei Long said it like a shopping list. “The Eraser is a Lin. Twenty. Doing computer science on the hill. Seeing the boy I raised.” A pause. “I’ve known for a while. I wanted to be sure before I said it to you. I’m sure.”

“Okay.”

“That’s the first thing.”

He took his hands out of his pockets.

“In November. The night after I took her sister’s statement. I came here. To this garden. You made me tea.”

Yu Chen remembered the tea. He remembered the cup.

“I asked you, to your face, whether the girl next door was the Eraser. I said I was asking as family. Not as police. And you looked at me.” Wei Long’s voice stayed exactly flat. “And you said no.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen looked at the man who’d raised him.

He thought about lying again. For about a second. Could he? To that face? No. The first lie had been the one thing he’d ever decided mattered more than being honest with Wei Long. You couldn’t protect that with a second lie. You could only own it.

“Yes. I lied to you.”

Wei Long waited.

“You asked if she was the Eraser. I said no. I knew it was a lie when I said it.” He kept his eyes on Wei Long’s. “I’d say it again tomorrow.”

The pleasant face had gone. He felt it go. Same as at the Lin table. Same as with the boy who’d yanked her hood. What was left was slow and cold, and he was talking to the one man he loved besides her, and it didn’t move an inch.

“You said you were asking as family. So I answered you as family. I kept her out of it.” A beat. “You taught me that. You kept me out of things for eight years.”

“I kept you out of trouble. Not out of the law.”

“She hasn’t done anything to anyone who didn’t do it first.”

“That’s not how the law works.”

“I know how the law works. I live in the policeman’s house.”

“Then—”

“She finds names. She cleans up after an old man. She built a thing to watch for her sister’s face, because nobody ever let there be a picture of her sister to look for.”

“Yu Chen.”

“That’s what she does at night. I bring her tea and I don’t ask. You can call it what you want. I’m not going to help you put her name in a file.”

Wei Long didn’t blink. He was very good at not blinking.

“You understand what you’re saying to me. You’re telling a police officer that you knowingly lied to protect someone working for the Syndicate.”

“Yes.”

“And you’d do it again.”

“Yes.”

“You’re the clean one.” Wei Long said it like he was reading Yu Chen’s file back to him. “Your whole life. Top of everything. Never once in trouble.”

“So?”

“The old women at the market trust you with their change. I used to think that was because you were good.” His eyes went up to the window. Back down. “Now I think you keep the whole front of your life polished so nobody ever looks past you at her.”

Yu Chen didn’t deny it. Why would he?

“That’s exactly what it is.”

The whistling on the far side of the wall had stopped. Up at the top of the tall house, the line of light moved. She’d got up. Crossed the room. Sat down again.

Wei Long watched it too.

“I’m not here to arrest anybody.” He sounded tired now. “I couldn’t, on what I’ve got. And I wouldn’t like myself if I did. I came to decide what kind of uncle I’m going to be.”

“Cousin.”

“I worry like an uncle. So I’m an uncle.” He stood up off the raised bed. “Either I pretend I don’t know. Which police don’t get to do.”

“Or?”

“Or I give her a number. Mine.”

“A NUMBER?”

“And I tell her one day this might stop being about keeping her family out of the papers. It might start being about something worse.” He brushed soil off his coat. “When that day comes, there’s a door she can walk through that isn’t her father’s and isn’t the Syndicate’s. I hope she uses it. In a few years. When she’s ready. That’s the other thing. It’s all I’ve got.”

“And me?”

“I’m not making you choose.” He said it fast, like he’d practised it in the car. “I thought about it on the way. You’d choose her.”

“…Yes.”

“Then I’d have lost you. I didn’t raise you to lose you over a lie I’d have told myself.” His jaw worked. “But don’t lie to me again. Not even for her. Say nothing. You can always say nothing. You can’t look at me and lie.”

“Okay.”

“That’s a promise.”

“It’s a promise.”

Wei Long nodded once. Then he did something he almost never did. He put his hand on the back of Yu Chen’s neck. Hard. Brief. Then he took it away.

He was at the side gate before he turned round.

“Whatever she built last October, it’s watching the same places we watch. And it’s better than anything the city’s got.”

He opened the gate.

“That spring just gone. When the arms man went missing for three days. Zhao. Somebody pulled up every camera within five kilometres of the shipyard inside an hour. I always wondered who.”

The gate creaked.

“I don’t wonder now.”

“She’ll want to know the number’s really yours.”

“Tell her it is.” The corner of his mouth moved. On Wei Long that was practically a laugh. “She’ll check anyway.”

The gate clicked.

Up at the top of the tall house, the thin line of light went still. Like whoever was up there had heard the gate too.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t go up her stairs. He hissed her name from under the branch.

The window banged open. Then she wasn’t at the window. She was coming down the persimmon tree in her socks, faster than he’d ever seen her, dropping onto the Lin side and straight back up and over the wall into the Song garden. Into him. Her hands were already in the front of his shirt.

“I heard the gate! That was Wei Long. On a SATURDAY. What did he—”

“He knows.”

She went rigid.

“About the Eraser. That it’s you.”

“He—”

“He’s not doing anything.” His hands came up round her arms. “He’s not arresting anybody. He can’t, and he won’t. He wants to give you a number. His own. For one day. If you ever need a door that isn’t your father’s. That’s all.”

She was shaking. Right through his shirt.

“How long has he… how does he…”

“Since November.” He made himself say all of it. He’d just promised a man in a garden never to lie again. That had to start somewhere. “He asked me. To my face. Whether you were the Eraser. And I said no.”

She stared up at him.

“I lied to him. First time in my life. He worked it out anyway. He came to tell me he knows I lied.” He held her by the shoulders. “I’d do it again. I want you to know that. I lied to the man who raised me, for you. I’d do it again tomorrow. I’m not sorry.”

He watched it go into her. The clean boy. The one the market trusted with their change. Telling her he’d looked his own family in the eye and lied. For a second she looked frightened. Of the size of it. Of what he’d do.

Then the other thing came. The thing from the pantry. Nothing shy in it at all.

She hauled him down by his shirt and kissed him.

Hard. Shaking. Half out of fright. Her cold fists jammed against his chest. Up on her toes in the dark garden. He caught her and kissed her back. Then he took it off her. He turned them half a step, so her back was against the wall under the branch, in the one place none of her father’s cameras could see. He kissed her slow and deep and didn’t say a word. She stopped shaking for the first reason. Started for the second.

“You lied to the POLICE.” Against his mouth. Breathless. “For me.”

“Yes.”

“You’re not even sorry.”

“No.”

He kissed her again. She grabbed the back of his neck and hung on. The green persimmons hung over them. The jar was in the wall by her shoulder. Her whole dark house was behind her.

He took her face in both hands. Just to look. Her glasses were crooked and her mouth was red. She didn’t fix either.

“Auntie Dai’s gone,” he said.

“I know.”

She took his hand and pulled him across his own garden to his own back door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d meant to be careful. He’d been careful for two years about everything that had her in it. He’d been careful for an hour in the garden with Wei Long.

Halfway up the stairs she turned round on the step above him. It put her mouth level with his. She kissed him there, on the stairs, and he forgot what careful was for.

“Lamp?”

“No lamp.”

There was light enough from her window across the garden. She pulled his shirt over his head and dropped it on the landing. Then she put both cold hands flat on his chest, over his heart, and left them there.

“What are you doing?”

“Checking.”

“For what?”

“What someone who’d lie for me feels like. Inside.” She frowned at her hands. “It’s going really fast.”

“I wonder why.”

He picked her up. She laughed, and kicked, and lost a sock. He put her down on the bed and took her hoodie off over her head, and her glasses with it. He put the glasses on the desk where they couldn’t fall. He’d learned.

Then he kissed every bit of her he could reach. Slowly. He wanted her to know he meant each one. Her wrists. The inside of her elbow. The place under her ear. The mark on her shoulder where her strap had been.

“Hurry up.”

“No.”

“CHEN.”

“You’ll live.”

She kept pulling at him. He kept not hurrying. In the end she said his name again, in the other voice. The one that meant she’d stopped arguing. So he stopped making her wait.

Nothing about it was shy any more. She knew where to put her hands. He knew what made her arch, and catch her breath, and grab the headboard. So he did it again. And again.

“Stop—no, don’t stop, don’t you DARE—”

“Make up your mind.”

She bit his shoulder to shut him up. It didn’t shut him up. He laughed into her hair. Then he wasn’t laughing. She had her face in his neck and was saying things into it he’d never heard her say. Not even here.

He’d lied to Wei Long’s face for her. He’d do it again. Lying here with her wrapped round him, he knew exactly what the lie had been for. All of it. The clean front, the polite smile, the top marks. One place in the whole world where nobody was looking at her but him.

He held on to her like someone might come over the wall and take her.

She held on just as hard.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on his chest with one leg over his, and her hair all over his mouth, drawing on his collarbone with one finger.

“Your cousin’s going to hate me.”

“He doesn’t hate people. He writes them down.” He moved her hair off his face. “He’s giving you his own number. That’s not hate.”

“I’m still going to check it’s his!”

“He said you would.”

She laughed against his skin. She went to sleep there, with her hand over his heart. Right where she’d put it at the start.

He stayed awake for a while. Across the garden, her light was still on in the empty room. Nobody up there now. He watched it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long came to Sunday lunch the next day like nothing had happened. He ate two bowls of Auntie Dai’s soup. He told Yu Chen he was too thin.

Auntie Dai banged the lid back on the pot and looked at Yu Chen.

“You look tired.”

Wei Long didn’t look up.

“He’s been studying.”

“On a SATURDAY NIGHT?”

“Very hard.”

He ate his soup.

Afterwards he went out to the garden on his own. Yu Chen watched through the kitchen window. Wei Long stood under the branch and looked up. After a minute a head came over the top of the wall. Hood up. Glasses on. Wary as a cat.

He held a folded piece of paper up to her. She didn’t take it straight away. He said something short. Yu Chen couldn’t hear it through the glass.

She took the paper. She read it. She got out her phone. Wei Long stood there with his hands in his pockets and waited. Bus-stop patient. She looked at the phone. She looked at him. She nodded once, the exact way Wei Long nodded. Then she went back down her side of the wall.

Wei Long came in and put his bowl in the sink.

“She checked it in front of me. On her phone. Under a minute.”

“I told you she would.”

“You did.” His mouth moved again. Twice in two days. A record. “She said thank you. Then she said if I ever put her in a file, she’ll know before the ink’s dry.”

“She will.”

“I know.” Wei Long picked up his coat. “That’s the bit I like.”

chapters.title: He Held the Ladder
chapters.desc: For Elowen’s flower-shop wedding, Eliana strings a sky of lights and won’t say why. The night before, a lanky boy holds her ladder for hours and slips out before anyone finds her asleep. At the wedding Raiden says “my wife” out loud, and nobody introduces the boy next door to anyone.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll hold it. You do the stars. Don’t look down — you never look down.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
Everyone wanted to know why nine forty-one. Eliana wasn’t telling.

Tuesday. Aurelia, with her clipboard.

“Why not nine?”

“Spreadsheet.”

Wednesday. Elowen.

“Why not TEN?”

“Spreadsheet.”

Thursday. Raiden, following her round the shop.

“Is it a birthday? Is it a code? Is it the time Zhao first said a whole sentence?”

“SPREADSHEET.”

She’d got it out of the little red book. She hadn’t meant to. It was the registry book Elowen kept in the drawer under the till, where the time was printed beside the date three and a half years back: a Tuesday, nine forty-one. Elowen thought nobody remembered the time. Zhao remembered the time. Now Eliana had it too.

So the lights would come on at nine forty-one. Thousands of them. And nobody was getting a reason.

✦ ✦ ✦

She rigged them on Friday night, after the shop shut.

It took hours. Wire across the whole ceiling. Every run tested, taped, and taken back to a box under the counter. Her, a tall ladder, her hoodie, and the laptop open on the floor. The shop was dark except for the street.

Yu Chen came at nine.

She’d texted come hold a ladder. Nothing else. He’d come anyway, with a medical textbook under his arm, because he had a test on Monday and he could read at the bottom of a ladder as well as anywhere.

“Where do you want me?”

“There. Hold it. Don’t let go.”

“I’ve never let go.”

“Then keep doing that.”

He held the ladder. For three hours. One hand on each side, his book open on the fold-out step, reading the same page over and over by the light of her laptop.

“Left,” she’d say.

He’d move it left.

“You’ve been up there two hours,” he’d say. “Come down and drink something.”

She wouldn’t.

Once, at the last run over the door, she leaned out too far. The ladder shifted under her. His hands closed on the rails so hard she heard them squeak.

“Don’t look down.”

“I’m not looking down.”

“You never look down. Don’t start now.”

“I’m FINE.”

“I know you’re fine. I’m holding it anyway.”

Near midnight she nicked her finger on the end of a wire. It wasn’t anything. A bead of blood. She stuck it in her mouth and kept going.

“Show me.”

“It’s nothing.”

“Come down two steps and show me.”

She came down two steps. He took her hand, looked at it under his phone torch, and got a plaster out of his wallet. Who kept plasters in their WALLET? He did. He wrapped it round her fingertip, very neat, very tight, and pressed it flat with his thumb.

“Now go back up.”

“You’re so bossy on ladders.”

“Only on ladders.”

By one o’clock the whole ceiling was a sky. Dark. Waiting. She switched it on once to test it, every light at once. She stood at the top of the ladder in the gold with her mouth open, exactly the way everyone would tomorrow. Then she turned it off, set the time, came halfway down, and sat on a rung to check the box on her laptop.

That was the last thing she remembered.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke up on the floor of the shop on Saturday morning with her laptop on her chest. A ladder over her. Somebody’s jacket over her shoulders. His. Grey, warm, smelling of him. He’d gone. Of course he’d gone. He’d tucked it round her sometime in the night and taken himself home over the wall. Before anyone could come in and find the youngest Lin asleep on the shop floor with the boy from next door beside her. Because people would talk. Because he knew her rules better than she did.

Elowen came in the back at six with the flowers.

“Yu-er? Why are you on the FLOOR?”

“Spreadsheet.”

She pulled the jacket round her, quick, so Elowen wouldn’t see whose it was.

Elowen looked at her for a second longer than she needed to. Then she put the buckets down.

“There’s tea on the counter. In his flask.” Over her shoulder. Not turning round. “He left it. For when you woke up.”

Eliana looked at the counter. The dented flask was there. Lid on. Lined up exactly square to the edge. She hadn’t even seen him bring it. She said nothing. Elowen, thank God, said nothing either.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came to the wedding because she told him to.

She’d said it on Thursday. “Come. Stand near me. Bring a book so you’ve got something to do with your hands. Don’t talk to Baba. Don’t let anybody work out what you are.”

“What am I?”

“Don’t START.”

So he came, in the one jacket he owned that wasn’t grey, with a medical textbook under his arm. Because she’d said bring something for your hands and he’d taken it literally. People looked at him. A tall quiet boy nobody knew, standing beside the youngest sister. He gave them the pleasant nothing smile. They went back to their tea.

Nobody introduced him. That was the deal, and it held all night. He was the boy from next door who’d apparently come because Eliana told him to. That was all anyone was getting.

She stood next to him by the cooler with her laptop against her chest, watching the shop fill up.

Baba, in his funeral suit. Aurelia, in gold, in charge of absolutely everything. Chen Si, in grey, by the counter. Evangeline at the back, alone, in pale blue, watching the door. Zhao under the arch Raiden had built, in black, with one of Elara’s sugar flowers in his lapel.

Then Raiden came in, in a silver waistcoat he’d designed himself. And he wasn’t alone.

She was tall and broad-shouldered, in a dark red dress and an old black leather jacket. Grease under her nails. Raiden had his arm round her waist. He stopped in the doorway and clapped his hands.

“Everyone!”

Thirty heads turned.

“Jinx, my wife, she built Xiao Pan’s bike, don’t touch her tools.”

Nobody made a sound.

Wife. Out loud. In the shop. Eliana watched it land on every face, one by one.

Aurelia’s pen stopped. Elowen’s face did nothing at all, which was how you knew. And Baba, a few feet from Eliana by the cooler, went completely still. He was looking at the woman’s left hand. There was a ring on it. A thick plain one, like a washer. There was one on Raiden’s hand too.

Baba looked at that hand for a long time. Then he walked out. Straight past them, out of the door, onto the step, and stood there with his back to the room.

“Is he all right?” Yu Chen, barely moving his lips.

“No.”

“Should someone—”

“Not you. Not EVER you. Stay there.”

“Oh no,” Raiden breathed. “Baba—”

“Leave him.” Elowen, from the arch. Ice.

Raiden looked across the shop. Straight at Eliana.

She gave him nothing. Not a blink. She’d had that registry record in her spreadsheet since February of last year. The last day of September 2021, old town, ten in the morning. She’d never said a word. She wasn’t starting now.

Raiden’s mouth twitched. Then somebody was shaking his hand, and he was off round the room. “This is my wife. This is my WIFE. Have you met my wife?”

Yu Chen bent his head beside her.

“You knew.”

“You were in the cellar. You KNOW I knew.”

“Married, though. September. I thought you were—” He stopped. “Rounding up.”

“I never round up.”

Jinx ended up backed into the corner by the fridge where the roses lived, with people being brought to her one at a time. Eliana waited until there was a gap. Then she went over.

“I’m Eliana, I’m the youngest, I’ve known about you since February 2022, you’re on a spreadsheet.”

She walked off before Jinx could do anything with her face. Behind her, she felt Yu Chen not quite laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the shop, a tall man in glasses came in off the street, a bit out of breath, like he’d walked fast from somewhere, and went straight to Elara and the cake.

Eliana clocked him at once. She clocked everybody. Dark suit. Glasses. Serious. He stood very close beside Elara without touching her and said something about the cake, and Elara went red to the ears. Nobody had introduced him either.

Eliana knew his name. She’d known it since August. Wang Xing Yue. City Hospital. Old-town registry, a Friday morning, six weeks ago. Two witnesses she’d never heard of. And her sister’s name next to his on the line. Elara didn’t know she knew. Nobody knew she knew. She’d put it in the quiet tab and shut it.

Beside her, Yu Chen went very still.

She looked up. He was staring across the shop at the man in glasses. And the man in glasses had seen him, over the buckets of white roses. They were looking at each other with the exact same blank face.

They didn’t nod. That was the thing. Two strangers catch each other’s eye, one of them nods. Everybody does it. These two didn’t. One second, across the whole shop. Then they both looked away at the same moment. Like they’d agreed. Not a muscle moved on either face.

“You know him.”

“My cousin.” Very low. “Xing Yue. He’s Elara’s…” He stopped. “I knew he had someone. I didn’t know it was one of yours.”

She kept her face perfectly still. Should she tell him? It was his cousin. He’d want to know. It wasn’t hers to tell. It was Elara’s.

“Are you going to say hello to him?”

“No.”

“He’s your COUSIN.”

“He’s not saying hello to me either.”

“Why didn’t you nod?”

“Because if we nod, someone asks how we know each other. Then they ask who I am. Then who he is. Then it’s two Wang cousins and two Lin sisters in one room, and your father starts counting.” He looked down at her. “Easier to be strangers. He thought of it the same second I did. He always does.”

“He’s very quick.”

“He’s very annoying.”

Later she saw the man in glasses lean down and say something in Elara’s ear. Elara stared at him with her mouth open. He’s my cousin. Yu Chen. Probably. She added it to the quiet tab.

Would Baba ask his name tonight? Maybe. Eliana wasn’t planning to be there for it.

Just before nine, Baba came back in off the step. Face set. Standing by the arch like nothing had happened.

“He came back in,” Yu Chen murmured.

“He always comes back in. He just takes a while.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine o’clock, thirty people stood in a flower shop, and Baba walked Elowen down the aisle.

Four metres. Twenty seconds. Eliana watched from the back, by the cooler, with the laptop in her arms. Halfway down, Baba stopped and asked Zhao about the lemon tree. Zhao’s face opened up. “Nine lemons,” he said. And she watched her father cry. Her father. In front of everyone. Wet-faced in his funeral suit. Then Elowen. Then everybody.

Chen Si said his four sentences. Elowen said the thing about keeping. Zhao said the thing about the door. Eliana didn’t hear all of it. She was watching the clock in the corner of her screen. The way she’d watched it in the planetarium. The way she watched every clock.

At nine forty-one she pressed one key, and shut the laptop. Every light came on at once. Gold and warm. The whole ceiling a sky. The shop made a noise, a big soft oh, and Zhao took Elowen’s face in both hands and kissed her under it, in front of everyone. Aurelia started counting out loud. Raiden whistled. Baba found something very interesting to look at in the cooler. Eliana looked up at her own sky over her sister’s wedding, and didn’t look at the laptop again.

At the very back, in his plain dark coat, Detective Song Wei Long stood with his carved face still and his eyes bright. He wasn’t pretending he wasn’t crying. He wasn’t pretending he was there officially either.

Yu Chen was beside her. He didn’t take her hand. That was the rule, and the room was full. But down by the cooler, where nobody could see, he hooked one finger through one of hers. And held it.

She let him.

✦ ✦ ✦

They slipped out the back, into the lane, when the party was loud enough that two people wouldn’t be missed.

It was dark and narrow back there. It smelled of flower water and bins. Gold light came out of the shop’s back window and lay across the wet ground in a strip. The party came with it, muffled. Across the lane stood the old tea merchant’s building. Four floors. Dark. A ladder up the back. She looked at it once, out of habit, because she looked at everything. Nothing there. She looked away.

He pulled her into the dark bit, out of the strip of light, between the shop wall and a stack of empty buckets.

“You hung a whole sky. For a time you weren’t going to tell anyone.”

“I told everyone. Spreadsheet.”

His hands were at her waist. Her back was against the cool wall.

“You told everyone spreadsheet.”

“It IS a spreadsheet.”

“You put a whole ceiling of lights on a minute out of a book you weren’t supposed to read. So your sister would get her real wedding at the time of her real one. And you won’t take any credit. And you fell asleep under a ladder.”

“You put your jacket on me and went home. Before anyone saw.”

“Your rules.”

She looked up at him. The gold caught the edge of his face.

“One day,” he said, “I’m going to hang lights for us. In our own lane. At a time out of a book. And I won’t tell anyone why either. And you’ll fall asleep under the ladder, and I’ll put my jacket over you.” He paused. “And I won’t leave. Because by then I’ll be allowed to stay.”

She waited for the fear. It always came, with sentences like that. Sentences that started with a day that hadn’t happened yet and pointed straight at something you could lose. It came. Of course it came. But smaller. It came and sat in her chest, and she looked at it. It didn’t send her down a tree. It didn’t send her up two flights of stairs. She just stood there in the dark with his hands at her waist and the fear the size it should be. And she let it sit there. And let the other thing be bigger.

“One day,” she said.

It came out as hardly anything. But she said it. She never said it. She usually just didn’t answer. He heard. She felt him hear it. His fingers went tight on her waist.

Then he put his hand along her jaw and kissed her. Against the cool wall, in the dark part of the lane, with her own lights gold in the window and her sister married under them. She put her arms round his neck. The laptop was squashed between them. She kissed him back.

His hand slid from her jaw into her hair and pulled the pencil out. It fell somewhere in the buckets. She didn’t care. She got the laptop out from between them and put it down on an upturned bucket without looking. She had never once in her life done that to a laptop. She got both hands inside his jacket. He leaned the whole length of himself against her and kissed her neck, slowly, all the way down to the edge of her hoodie. She bit her lip to keep quiet. It didn’t work.

“Someone’ll come out—”

“The party’s loud.”

“Evangeline’s at the back. She watches the DOOR. She’ll—”

“Then we’ll go.”

He stayed exactly where he was. So did she. A long minute, in the dark between the buckets.

“My pencil’s in a BUCKET…”

“I’ll buy you a pencil.”

“You’ll buy me forty pencils.”

“Probably.”

Then they slipped away up the lane, and didn’t go back in.

Behind them, much later, long after they’d gone, the back door of the shop opened. A woman in pale blue came out with two slices of cake on a paper plate. She looked up at the dark building across the way, and started to climb.

chapters.title: The Photograph
chapters.desc: At nineteen minutes past three in the morning, the fence catches the one thing it was built to catch. By ten she’s home and hollowed out, and the boy next door is on the kerb with his bicycle, because he always is.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to be scared on your own. That part’s mine. You can give me that part.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
The fence woke her at nineteen minutes past three.

A short double buzz from the phone by her pillow. The one she’d built to cut through anything. She was across the room and at the screens before she was properly awake. That was the whole point of the fence. Speed. She was never going to be slow again.

She read what it had caught. Then she went to the bathroom on the landing and was sick.

She knelt on the cold tiles with her forehead on the edge of the bath. Was it real? Was she still asleep? She went back and read it again. It was real. A page on a black site, in three languages. In the middle, a photograph. Taken with a flash, in the dark. Her sister’s face in the white of it. Looking straight down the lens. Not scared. Not anything. And four lines of grey text underneath that she was never going to be able to un-read.

She took it down. Then the copies, every one she could find. Her hands were steady. Her hands were always steady, even when nothing else was.

Then she rang Elowen.

“Yu-er? What—it’s three in the—”

“I found it!”

“Found what?”

“Her. A picture. Of Ev… I found it, Jie. I found it and I took it down and—”

“Stop. Breathe. Where are you?”

“My room.”

“Stay there. I’m coming.”

At four, sitting on the floor in her hood waiting for headlights, her thumb sent one more message. She didn’t remember deciding to.

Eliana: home at ten?

✦ ✦ ✦

He read it at four and one minute. He’d been asleep. Then he wasn’t.

Three words. No full stop. No it’s nothing. She always put it’s nothing. He got up and looked across the garden. Her light was on. A car came down the lane with its headlights off.
