The red door opened and shut. The car went away. Elowen’s car. He knew the sound of it. He didn’t text back. What would he say? Yes was the only answer. She knew it already.

At seven he rang the ward and told the registrar he was ill. The registrar said, “You? You’re never ill,” and Yu Chen said, “I know,” and that was that.

At nine he was on the kerb.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember the morning in order. Only in bits.

Elowen’s car. The textile building by the harbour, six floors up. A long room full of light. And a man in it so big that she stopped in the doorway.

“You’re huge.”

It just came out. She’d been awake since three and her mouth had come loose.

“I know. Everyone says. It’s a lot of work. Come in. Sit down. There’s tea, there’s congee—”

She knew who he was without being told. Evangeline’s man. The one nobody would name. The one who’d found her sister in one night when Eliana couldn’t in three days. She’d stopped looking for him a year ago, because Evangeline asked her to. And here he was. Enormous. Talking. Holding out congee she couldn’t eat.

There was a silver ring on Evangeline’s left hand. Eliana saw it. She knew how to find out everything about a ring. She didn’t. That one wasn’t hers. She’d promised.

She remembered putting the laptop on the long table and turning it round. Watching Evangeline look. Watching her sister’s face not move at all. Wanting to put her own body between her sister and the screen.

She remembered the name that came up with it. Saying it out loud.

“Hwang.”

She remembered the big man breathing in, long and slow, and saying, “I know him.”

And she remembered crying. No noise. In her hood, with both hands over her mouth. Elowen’s hand on the back of her neck. The harbour grey outside the window. And one thought going round and round.

I built the fence so this would never happen. The fence worked perfectly. It still happened. It happened a year ago. I only caught the picture.

At the door, going, she turned round and looked up at him.

“I took it down. Every copy. And if he puts it up again, it’ll go wrong. For him. VERY wrong.”

“Good. Thank you. That’s very good.”

She hugged him. She hadn’t planned to. Her arms didn’t go anywhere near round. Then she ran down the stairs before anybody could look at her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was on the kerb at ten.

Elowen’s car came down the lane and stopped. He was there by his bicycle in his grey jumper, with the flask. Of course he was. She’d sent him three words at four in the morning. He’d read them and come and sat on the kerb. He didn’t know what for. He never asked. He’d waited anyway.

Elowen looked at him through the windscreen. Then at Eliana.

“That’s the boy next door.”

It wasn’t quite a question.

“He holds ladders.”

It was the stupidest thing she could possibly have said. Elowen let it go. She reached over and squeezed Eliana’s hand, hard.

“Go in. Sleep. I’ll deal with Baba. Ring me tonight.”

“Jie—”

“Go.”

Eliana got out. He stood up off the kerb. He looked at her face. Grey and wrecked, crying all over it. He didn’t ask a single thing. Not what happened. Not are you okay. Not who was that. He just put the flask in her hands, because her hands were cold.

Her laces were undone. Both of them, trailing on the step. He knelt down on the pavement and tied them. Double knots. Right there in the lane, in front of Elowen’s car.

“Chen. People can SEE.”

“You’ll trip.”

He stood up. He walked up the three steps beside her. Close. Not touching. He waited while she fought the bolt that stuck. Then he went in after her and shut the red door on the lane.

Behind them, Elowen’s car didn’t move for a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t let her near the stairs.

“Not up there. Not today. Come and sit.”

“I need to check the—”

“It’ll wake you. You built it to wake you. Sit.”

So they sat in the front room nobody used. The cold, stiff one with the good chairs. On the floor, backs against the sofa, because the floor was where she sat when things were bad. He’d learned that. He made tea and brought it. She drank it. She kept quiet, and he let her. The house was empty round them. Baba at the office. Evangeline gone. Ah Sim at the market. The clock in the hall going.

In the afternoon she told him a little of it. Not the whole shape. She couldn’t, and he didn’t ask, and it was theirs. The thing he didn’t ask about.

“The thing I built. It caught something today. The thing it was for. And it worked, and I still…”

She stopped. He put his arm round her and pulled her against his side. She put her face in his jumper and didn’t finish.

“It worked. You said it worked.”

“It was too LATE. A year too late. It already happened. I just found the picture of it.”

“But you found it. And you took it down.” His hand was in her hair. “If you hadn’t built it, it’d still be up. More people would see it. You know that better than me.”

“That’s not—”

“You didn’t make the bad thing. You’re the reason there’s a bit less of it tonight.”

He said it the way he said chrysanthemum was good for tired eyes. A plain fact. One he believed and couldn’t prove.

She didn’t answer. But she stopped shaking.

He pulled the sleeves of her hoodie down over her hands. She pulled the sleeves of his jumper down over his. He looked at his covered hands. She looked at hers.

“Now we’re both STUPID.”

“Now we’re both warm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ah Sim came back from the market and stopped in the doorway with her bags.

She looked at the two of them on the floor. The youngest Lin, hood up, against the side of the boy next door. In the room nobody used.

Eliana waited for her to say something. What would she say? Get up? Go home? I’m telling your father?

Ah Sim went to the kitchen. She came back with a plate of toast, cut into fingers, and put it on the carpet in front of them. On her way out she took off her own cardigan and dropped it over Eliana’s cold feet. Then she pulled the door to.

“She’s going to tell Baba.”

“She’s not.”

“How do you know?”

“She cut the crusts off.”

He got her to eat the toast in the end. One finger at a time. She ate it against his side. Then she slept for an hour, which she never did, and woke up to his hand still moving in her hair and the light going gold, then grey, in the stiff old room.

He went home over the wall at seven, before Baba got back. Because of the rules. Because she asked him to. Because even today she couldn’t stand her father’s face if he found them.

She watched his light come on across the garden. Then she rang Elowen, because she’d said she would.

“Did you eat?”

“Toast.”

“How much toast?”

“…Some toast. Fingers. Ah Sim cut the crusts off.”

A pause on the line.

“Is he still there? The ladder boy.”

“He went home.”

“Hm.”

“Don’t say hm. You’re not Zhao.”

“I’ve been married to him three and a half years. I’m allowed one hm.” Elowen’s voice went careful. “Yu-er. Is he good to you?”

Eliana looked at his window. At the shape moving in it.

“He tied my shoes.”

“I saw.”

“In the LANE. In front of you.”

“I saw that too.” Another pause. “Go to sleep. I mean it.”

“I will.”

She lay on the camp bed and didn’t sleep. At midnight the screens were dark. The fence was quiet. Watching.

At two she got up, put the blue blanket round her shoulders, and went down.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was already on the step.

How did he know? She came out of the red door at two in the morning in the blanket, and he was there. On the third step, in his coat, with the flask. The exact place he’d been on the first night. The June night two years ago. Exams over, the house too quiet. He’d come out and sat down and never asked why.

She sat down beside him. He took half the blanket out of habit, even with his coat on. Across the gardens the tall house was dark except Baba’s window. Yellow. The only light, like always.

“Can’t sleep.”

“No.”

“Is it still—”

“It’s done. For tonight.” She held the flask without opening it. “I keep seeing her face. In the picture. She wasn’t scared. That’s the thing. They took a picture of her to SELL her, and she looked straight at them, and she wasn’t scared of anything.”

He waited.

“And I’m scared all the time. Of everything. She was in a box and she wasn’t. There’s something wrong with me.”

“There’s nothing wrong with you.”

“There IS—”

“You’re not her. She goes still.” He turned his head. “You get scared, and you build a fence, and you take the thing down at three in the morning with your hands steady because somebody has to. That’s your kind of brave. Scared the whole time. Doing it anyway.”

She looked at the yellow window.

“I’d just rather you did it where I can see you,” he said. “You don’t have to be scared on your own. That part’s mine. You can give me that part.”

And the thing came up out of her that never came up.

It came from somewhere low down. Past the place where her voice always stopped. The place that caught at registration, and at the noodle stall, and in the dark of his bed two years ago, when he’d said it first and she couldn’t say it back.

“I love you.”

Fast. Wrong. Much too quiet.

Then she couldn’t look at him. She stared at Baba’s window instead, with her heart going so hard she was sure he could hear it through the blanket.

It was the worst day to say it. That was why she could. Today had proved what she’d always known. Love was the word people said before the hospital. Before the box. Before the thing got taken. Her mother had been loved, and then she was gone, and here was a photo of her sister on a black site proving it all over again. You loved people and the world came for them.

She knew that. She said it anyway. If she could say it today, with the proof right there on her screens, she could say it any day.

He didn’t make it a big thing.

That was what she’d been most scared of, without knowing it. That his face would light up. That he’d make it a moment, a huge one, after two years. And she’d have to stand inside it on the worst day she’d had in years.

He didn’t. He went still beside her. Then he put his arm round her under the blanket and pulled her in against his side. He put his chin on the top of her head.

“I know,” he said. “I’ve got you.”

That was all. Not finally. Not say it again. Nothing that would cost her anything. He took it the way you’d take something from somebody with shaking hands. Carefully. With both of his. She turned her face up. Because she wanted to.

He kissed her. Soft. On the cold step, with the blanket round them and Baba’s window yellow across the garden. Slow, nothing hurried in it anywhere. She held the front of his coat with one hand and kissed him back. And she didn’t cry, for once.

It was the first thing all day that hadn’t hurt.

“Say it again?” she said, when she could. “I know I said don’t ask me things. I’m asking.”

“You never said don’t ask you that.” He tucked the blanket round her shoulder. “I love you, Yu-er. I’ve got you. Go to sleep. I’ll sit here. That’s allowed.”

“Is it in the rules?”

“I’ll write it in.”

She leaned on his arm. Like the first time. Only this time she wasn’t pretending to be asleep. She shut her eyes. Across the garden, the yellow window went out. Baba, going to bed at last.

“He waited up,” she mumbled.

“Yes.”

“For what?”

“I don’t know.” His chin was still on her head. “Maybe the same as me.”

chapters.title: The Night He Lost One
chapters.desc: On a Friday night in the emergency department, Yu Chen does chest compressions on a nineteen-year-old delivery rider, and nothing works. At two in the morning Eliana finds him on the east stairwell, and she stays until the sun comes up.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to say the right thing. You just don’t leave. I learned that from you.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
The whiteboard by the nurses’ station had the students at the bottom, in green pen, under everyone who mattered. On Friday night his was the last name. WANG (STUDENT).

Three weeks in the emergency department. He knew where the gloves lived. He knew not to sit in the chair by the window, because that was Bernie’s, and Bernie was the charge nurse, and Bernie had once made a registrar cry over a chair. He knew students took histories, did bloods, stood where they were put, and kept their hands to themselves. Dr. Ada Toh ran the floor on Friday nights. Small, quick, grey hair cut short, a cardigan over her scrubs she never took off. She called students by their surnames and never got one wrong. People said she was kind at four in the morning. At eight in the evening she was mostly fast.

“Wang. Bay six. Eighty-one, fall at home, hip. Get the story before she tells it to someone who doesn’t listen.”

“Yes, Dr. Toh.”

“Don’t ‘yes, Dr. Toh’ me. Go.”

He got the story. The old woman held his hand the whole time.

“Have you got a girlfriend?”

He thought about the rules. Rule two. Nobody knows. Then he thought, she’s eighty-one and she’s going to the ward.

“Yes.”

“Is she pretty?”

“She’s very clever.”

“That’s not what I asked!”

He was kind to her. He meant it. When the porter wheeled her off, he’d forgotten her name before the lift doors shut. He noticed. He wasn’t proud of it. He couldn’t change it either. Most of him was already taken. At ten he washed his hands, and in the corner by the sink he got out his phone and opened the food app.

Friday. Beef brisket noodles, extra radish. Lemon tea. Delivered.

She’d eaten. He put it away and went back out feeling lighter than he had any right to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The red phone went late in the evening.

Bernie took it, wrote on the board while she listened, and turned round.

“Nineteen. Motorbike versus car, eastern tunnel. Chest. Not talking. Five minutes.”

“Resus one.” Toh was already pulling on an apron. “Wang, with me. Gloves, apron, head end by the wall. When I say compressions, you do compressions. Kenny, you’re after him.”

Kenny was the other student from his year. He talked to fill gaps. He was talking now.

“Oh God. Oh God, okay, okay—”

“Kenny.”

“Shutting up.”

Yu Chen put his gloves on and stood by the wall where he’d been put.

They came in at a run. Two paramedics. The trolley between them. And the boy on it was wearing the orange jacket. Everybody in the city knew that jacket. It was the delivery app. The one on Yu Chen’s own phone. The one she ordered from at three in the morning. The jacket was torn down one side, and dark, and wet. Then it went fast. Toh’s voice, level, giving jobs. Bernie cutting the jacket off. Two lines going in. Somebody reading numbers that weren’t good, then worse. A phone fell out of the jacket pocket onto the floor. Face up. It lit and buzzed against the lino.

New order nearby. Accept?

Nobody picked it up. A nurse read his card out of his wallet for the notes. Fung Ka-lok. Nineteen. There was a cartoon cat sticker on the back of his phone.

The monitor changed its sound.

“He’s arrested. Compressions. Wang.”

Yu Chen stepped up onto the little stool by the trolley. Heel of one hand on the boy’s chest. Other hand on top. Elbows locked. Push.

He’d done it on plastic a hundred times. This was warm. It gave wrong. On the third push something went under his hands. A soft crack. He kept going. You kept going. He counted under his breath. Toh was doing things he’d only read about, quick and sure. Blood went in from bags squeezed by hand. He pushed. He counted. At two minutes Kenny tapped his shoulder and took over. He stood back with his arms shaking. Two minutes later he stepped up again. On the floor, the phone buzzed. New order nearby. He looked at the boy’s face. He shouldn’t have. It was young. Younger than nineteen. A bit of moustache he’d been trying to grow.

Twenty-five minutes. Then Toh looked at the monitor. At the clock. At everyone round the trolley, one by one.

“Anyone got anything we haven’t done?”

Nobody had.

“Then we’re stopping.”

She said the time out loud. The room went still.

His hands were still on the boy’s chest.

“Wang.” Not unkind. “You can stop now.”

He took his hands away.

Bernie bent and picked up the phone and switched it off with her thumb. She put it in a bag with his wallet and his keys and wrote his name on the bag.

✦ ✦ ✦

The mother came after midnight.

He didn’t see her. He was at the desk writing up his part of the notes. Careful capitals. What he’d done. When. He heard the doors. A woman’s voice asking for her son by name. Toh’s voice, low. The relatives’ room door shutting. A minute later, a sound came through that door with no words in it.

It went on. Kenny stopped talking. Bernie put her pen down and looked at the ceiling.

Yu Chen finished his sentence. Signed it. Put the pen back in his pocket.

Toh came out and walked down to the desk and stopped beside him.

“You did it properly. Depth right. Rate right. You didn’t stop when the ribs went. I watched.” She looked at him over her glasses. “It doesn’t help. I know it doesn’t. Go home anyway.”

“Thank you, Dr. Toh.”

“Wang.”

“Yes?”

“Eat something on the way.”

He took his coat off the hook. He said goodnight to Bernie. He walked out of the department like nothing was wrong. He was good at that. He got as far as the east stairwell. ***

The east stairwell ran between the department and the car park. Concrete. Cold. Lit much too bright. It smelled of the porters’ cigarettes. He meant to go up to the car. He sat down instead. Halfway up the first flight. Elbows on his knees. Coat still over his arm. He looked at his hands.

They looked like his hands. White powder in the creases from the gloves. A red mark on the heel of the right one. He could still feel it. The give. The soft crack on three. His phone buzzed.

Eliana: home?

Then, twenty minutes later:

Eliana: chen

He didn’t answer. He’d never not answered her. Instead, without deciding to, he opened the app.

Friday. Beef brisket noodles, extra radish. Lemon tea. Delivered.

Somebody had carried that. Somebody in an orange jacket had put it on the third step of the tall house and gone on to the next one, with the phone buzzing in his pocket. New order nearby. He’d read her orders every night for two and a half years. He’d never once thought about who carried them. He put the phone face down on the step and put his hands over his face. Then he stopped holding anything together at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t hear the door at the bottom. He heard feet on the stairs, coming up two at a time. She never ran. Then they stopped.

“Your car’s still here.”

He took his hands down. She was on the step below him in her black hoodie, hood up, glasses fogged from the cold outside. A carrier bag from the all-night noodle place at the bottom of the hill. Out of breath.

“Yu-er.” He sat up. Wiped his face with the back of his wrist. Made his voice right. “You shouldn’t be here. It’s two in the morning. How did you get here?”

“Taxi.”

“On your own? At this time? You can’t just—”

“You’re being polite to me.”

He stopped.

“You always answer. Always. In a minute. You didn’t answer. You finished at twelve, and your car was still on the top deck, and this is the only door between the department and the car park.” She came up a step. “And now you’re being POLITE to me. You only get polite when it’s really bad.”

“How do you know when I finish?”

“…I don’t.”

“Yu-er.”

“It’s on both our phones. Your rota. I put it there. In September. Don’t make a thing of it.”

He couldn’t think of one thing to say.

She sat down beside him. Close. Shoulder against his arm. Bag on the step above. No what happened. No are you okay. She pulled her knees up under her hoodie and looked at the wall opposite.

“You don’t have to talk. I’ll just sit here.”

It came out of him as a laugh. It wasn’t a laugh by the end.

She didn’t do anything about it. No arms round him. No it’s okay. She sat there against him with her knees up and let him. A porter came through the door at the top, saw them, and went back out. She didn’t even look round.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later he told her. Not all of it. The jacket. The age. The phone on the floor.

“It kept going off. The whole time. By my feet. New order nearby. Nobody picked it up.” He looked at his hands. “He might have brought yours. Some night. He might have carried your noodles up the lane.”

“He didn’t.”

“You don’t know that.”

“Mine come from a man with a beard. He’s had our lane for a year. He’s about forty. He has a dog in his basket on Sundays.”

He turned his head and stared at her.

“I NOTICE things,” she said. A bit defensive.

“Somebody’s, though. Somebody’s noodles. Every night.”

“Yes.” She didn’t argue. “Somebody’s.”

He held his hands out, palms up, under the bad light.

“I did it right. She said so. Depth and rate. I didn’t stop when his ribs went.” His voice wasn’t steady. “I felt them go, Yu-er. On the third one. I kept going because you keep going. And it didn’t matter. None of it. He was never coming back. Probably. Probably he wasn’t. And I did it RIGHT.”

She took his hands.

Both of them. The way he took hers when they were cold. She turned them over and looked. The powder in the creases. The red mark. Then she bent her head and kissed his knuckles. One. The next. The next. All along the right hand, slowly, and then the left. The hands that had pushed and pushed and not been enough.

He couldn’t breathe properly.

“Eliana…”

She looked up. Then she got up on her knees on the step, put her hands either side of his face, and kissed him.

It was nothing like the knuckles. It was hard, and wet with whatever was on his face, and she didn’t let go of his face once. He made a noise into her mouth and pulled her in. All of her. Off the step and into his lap, her knees either side of him on the cold concrete. He kissed her the way he hadn’t let himself all night. Not carefully at all. Hands in the back of her hoodie. Face in her neck. Her mouth again. Holding on like the stairs were moving. She held his head. She kissed his eyes, the wet on his cheeks, his mouth. Said his name against it. Her hands were cold on his neck. He didn’t want anything else in the world. A door banged above them. Footsteps. A trolley. Voices going away. They stopped, foreheads together, breathing.

“You don’t say the right thing,” she said. “When it’s me. You never say anything. You just don’t leave.” She pushed his hair off his forehead. “So I’m not leaving.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate the noodles on the stairs. Cold, out of the cartons. He wasn’t hungry. He ate because she watched him until he did.

“More.”

“I’m full.”

“You had four noodles. I counted. More.”

“Since when do you count?”

“Since you taught me. Eat.”

Then she talked. She never talked. About nothing. A girl in her year who’d cried in a tutorial over a semicolon. Uncle Mok’s new seat covers, which were tartan, which Baba hadn’t noticed yet. Her voice went on, low and steady, filling the stairwell up. After a while he got it. She was doing it on purpose. The way he sat on her floor when her house was too quiet. She took his hands again and put them both in the front pocket of her hoodie, with hers. Warm in there. She kept them.

When the windows at the top went grey, she stood up and held out her hand.

“Come on. Not home yet. Top deck.”

The top deck was open to the sky. The dark-green Volvo sat on its own in the corner, the one he’d bought in September for nights and drove for nothing else. Cold. Empty. Down below the hill the harbour was black with its chain of lights. Over the far side the sky was starting to go from black to something else. They sat in the car with the engine running for the heater.

“Is it on?”

“It’s on.”

“It’s not DOING anything.”

“It takes a minute.”

“Everything takes a minute with this car.”

“It’s a good car.”

“It’s a fridge with wheels.” She put her socked feet up on the dashboard. He didn’t tell her not to.

He fell asleep. One minute he was looking at the harbour. The next, her shoulder was under his cheek. The sky had gone grey and pink. The first buses were crawling up the hill. She hadn’t moved.

“How long?”

“About an hour. You snore. A bit. It’s fine.”

He sat up. His neck hurt. He looked at his hands. They were only hands.

“I’ll drive us.”

“You’ll drive us SLOWLY.”

He drove them slowly. Down the hill. Empty grey streets. Radio off. Her hand on his leg the whole way. When they turned into the lane the noodle man was putting his shutter up. He lifted his chin at them through the windscreen. She lifted hers back.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t let him go to his room alone.

She made tea in Auntie Dai’s kitchen, in his flask. Too much rock sugar, because she didn’t know how much he used. She made him drink half. She took his coat. She knelt down and took his shoes off, one and then the other. She lined them up by the door.

“I can do my own shoes.”

“You can’t even do your own face right now.”

She pushed him down on his bed and lay down behind him on top of the covers in her hoodie. Arm round him. Face against his back. Holding on.

He was the one who did this. That was how it worked. He sat on floors. He carried the tea. He stayed till it got light. He didn’t know how to be the one on the bed being held. He lay there stiff, not knowing what to do with any of himself.

“Stop it.” Into his shoulder blade. “You’re thinking. I can hear it. Go to sleep. I’ll be here.”

He went to sleep.

When he woke it was past noon, with sun on the wall and Auntie Dai moving about downstairs. Eliana was asleep against his back. Arm still over him. Glasses on, crooked, pressed into her cheek. Her laptop was on the floor by the door, in its bag. Zipped. She’d come out at two in the morning without opening it once.

He lay still. He looked at the light on the wall. He thought about a boy with a cartoon cat on his phone who’d never finish growing the moustache, and he let it hurt. It should. He was due back on Sunday night. He’d be on time. He put his hand over hers on his chest and held it there.

“You awake?” she mumbled, without opening her eyes.

“No.”

“Good. Me neither.”

chapters.title: The Criminal Mind
chapters.desc: Eliana goes to a seminar to understand the men she hunts at night, and comes out with friends: a psychology student who never stops talking, her two sisters, and a cold profiler who looks at her half a second too long. Outside, Yu Chen breaks one of her rules.
chapters.epigraph: “I went to learn about monsters. I came home with a group chat.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
She went for work. Obviously.

The poster had been up on the psychology board in the library for a week. THE CRIMINAL MIND. Open evening seminar. Wednesday, six. Guest speaker Arthur Cheung, criminal profiler. She walked past it four times. On the fifth, she took a photo of it.

Finding men was easy. She’d done it for Qian for three years. What she couldn’t do was tell you what a man would do next. She’d got that wrong twice in September. Both times, somebody else paid for it. She was sick of being wrong. Could a man in a suit fix that in an hour? Probably not. Worth a try.

So before six she was in the back row of the psychology lecture theatre with her hood up and her laptop on her knees. The hall filled up round her. Loud. Her shoulders went up to her ears.

In the front row there was a girl in a pink coat with a LOT of hair. She got her phone out. Put it away. Got it out again. She was perched on the edge of her seat with her hands clasped, like she was waiting for a concert.

The speaker came in on the dot.

Younger than she’d expected. Cold, in a way she knew. Not rude. Just switched off to everything he didn’t need. Dark suit, no tie, no slides. He put a black notebook on the lectern and never opened it. He talked for an hour, very plainly, about how people who hurt people organise their lives. And how the organising gives them away long before the hurting does.

“One man was caught because he put his tins in alphabetical order. Including the ones with no labels.”

Eliana snorted. So did the girl in the pink coat. Nobody else did.

She took notes. She also worked.

Qian had sent a job at five. A man selling photographs of women who didn’t know they’d been taken. By the time the profiler got to the difference between a want and a need, she had him. Eleven minutes.

Eliana: here. he has a daughter, so be careful who sees the photographs

Qian: Thank you. Noted.

She shut it and wrote down what the profiler said about tins.

The boy beside her leaned over.

“Sorry—have you got a pen?”

She went hot to the ears. She found one in her pocket and held it out without looking at him.

“Thanks!”

She said nothing. She didn’t look at him for the rest of the hour. Brilliant. She’d just taken a man’s whole life apart in eleven minutes, and she couldn’t say you’re welcome to a boy who wanted a biro.

Near the end, the profiler’s eyes went along the back row.

The way they’d been going along every row all evening. They stopped on her. On her hands, on the keyboard. Half a second. She felt it. Like someone reading over her shoulder. Then his eyes went on, down, all the way to the front. To the girl in the pink coat. They stayed there a beat longer than anywhere else. Then he shut the notebook he hadn’t opened.

“Thank you.”

The hall clapped.

✦ ✦ ✦

The girl in the pink coat came up the steps two at a time.

“You LAUGHED. At the tins. Nobody else laughed. I’m Si-Jie. Who are you? You’re not psychology. I’d know. I know everyone in psychology.”

Eliana pushed her glasses up.

“…Computer science.”

“Oh my God. Even better! Why are you here? No, don’t tell me, tell me downstairs. You’re meeting my sisters. They’re in the café, they’re always in the café. Bring your laptop.” She already had hold of Eliana’s sleeve. “Name?”

“Eliana.”

“Eliana.” Like she’d been handed a present. “Come on!”

Eliana had said no to every single person who’d ever tried this. Mostly by saying nothing until they went away. She opened her mouth to do it now. Si-Jie looked at her with so much delight, like Eliana was the best thing that had happened all week, that she shut it again. She let herself get towed down the stairs by the sleeve.

The café on the ground floor had two people in it, at a table by the window.

One of them was wearing sunglasses. Inside. At night. Her face was on the side of a bus Eliana had taken that morning. People at the other tables were trying very hard not to stare. The other one was in a cream coat, hair cut sharp at the jaw, a black coffee in front of her. Sitting very straight. Like she’d been waiting forty minutes and could easily do forty more.

“Si-Yuan. Si-Wei. This is Eliana. She laughed at the tins. She’s computer science. I’m keeping her.”

Si-Yuan took her sunglasses off and smiled. The bus smile, but warmer. Si-Wei just looked at Eliana.

Eliana looked back.

Si-Jie was already off about the profiler.

“Did he look at me? He looked at me. Si-Yuan. Tell her he looked at me.”

“He looked at everyone. It’s his job.”

“He looked at me LONGER.”

Si-Wei picked up the teapot on the tray, poured a cup, and pushed it across to Eliana without asking.

“She does this. Collects people.” Low voice. Dry. “You can leave whenever you want. I’ll tell her you were kidnapped.”

Eliana laughed. It just came out.

Si-Wei didn’t exactly smile. But something at the corner of her mouth agreed with something. Then she went back to her coffee. Eliana drank the tea. They sat across that little table for twenty minutes while Si-Jie talked for all four of them, and nobody made anybody else say anything. When had that last happened with strangers? Never. Not once. Not ever.

By seven Si-Jie had her number. By ten past there was a group chat called TRIPLETS + 1, and Eliana’s phone wouldn’t shut up.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came out into the foyer together, the four of them, into the crowd still hanging about by the doors.

“Lin Yu!”

She knew the voice before she turned round. Dominic Ip. Her year. By the noticeboard with three friends, grinning. They’d done the second-year group project together, the bus timetable one. He’d been the only one besides her who’d done any work. She’d almost liked him for it. She’d even given him a login to the test server she’d run it on, so he could work nights. Then she’d forgotten all about it.

“Stalking psychology now?” He came over. Loud. Easy. The way he did everything. His friends drifted after him. “Come for a drink. We’re going down the hill.” Then, like he’d just had the idea and liked it: “Actually, no. Come out with me. Friday. Properly. Like a date.”

His friends made a noise. Somebody whistled. Half the foyer turned to look.

She couldn’t move.

It was every room she’d ever been in where people looked at her and waited. Her face went hot. Then her neck. Si-Jie was vibrating with joy beside her. Si-Wei had gone very still on her other side. Every word Eliana owned was at the bottom of her chest, and none of them would come up.

“No.”

Almost nothing. A breath with a word in it.

“Is that a maybe?”

He laughed. His friends laughed. She turned round and walked out through the glass doors into the dark. It was the only thing her legs would do.

He came after her. He thought it was a game.

“Lin Yu, come ON. One drink. I’m a nice guy! Ask anyone!”

Yu Chen was on the path outside with his bicycle.

He’d been there the whole time. She knew it the second she saw him. He came up after his Wednesday clinic to walk her down. He’d seen all of it through the glass. He let go of the handlebars and stepped forward and took her hand.

In front of everyone. On the lit path outside the psychology building, with Dominic and his friends coming out of the doors behind her and half the seminar looking through the glass. He took her cold hand in his warm one and held it. Then he turned his head and looked at Dominic. He didn’t say anything at first. Just looked. It was the look from her father’s table. The pleasant face gone. Something underneath it that didn’t care at all.

“She said no.”

Dominic stopped walking.

“Who are YOU?”

Yu Chen didn’t answer that. He held her hand for maybe three seconds more. Looking at Dominic the whole time. Dominic looked back. Then he looked at the ground.

“All right. All right. Sorry, mate.” To nobody. He went back inside.

Yu Chen let go of her hand.

Behind them, the glass door banged open again.

“Oh my GOD,” said Si-Jie’s voice. “Who is THAT?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her down the hill with the bicycle between them. And he was polite.

“How was the seminar?”

“Good.”

“Your new friends seem nice.”

“They are.”

“I’m glad you went.”

“Si-Wei gave me tea.”

“Did you eat?”

“It was very strong tea.”

“That’s not food, Yu-er.”

“It was VERY strong.”

All of it pleasant. All of it in the voice he used on the girl with the rings. Her phone kept buzzing in her pocket. Her stomach went tight.

“You held my hand.”

“I did.”

“That’s rule three. No holding hands on the hill.”

“I know.” He didn’t look at her. “Sorry. It won’t happen again.”

That was when she knew how bad it was. He’d never once said sorry for breaking a rule on her side. He’d stood in her father’s pantry and said he’d do it again.

She looked at her phone at the bus stop while he waited.

Si-Jie: WHO IS HE. IS HE YOUR BOYFRIEND. HE LOOKED AT DOMINIC LIKE HE WAS GOING TO EAT HIM. ELIANA. ELIANA ANSWER ME

Si-Jie: ELIANA

Si-Wei: He was outside the whole time. He watched you through the glass and didn’t come in until you came out. That’s a good sign.

She put the phone away.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was washing up when she came over the wall.

Auntie Dai had gone at six. The kitchen was warm, the window over the sink steamed up. He was standing at it in his grey jumper with his sleeves pushed up, doing one plate at a time. Slowly. The way he did when he was thinking about something he didn’t want to think about. He heard the back door. He didn’t turn round.

“There’s soup. If you haven’t eaten. I’ll heat it.”

She walked up behind him, hooked two fingers through the belt loops at the back of his jeans, and pulled. He turned round.

His hands came out of the water. He held them up, dripping, away from her hoodie.

“You’re jealous.”

Anyone else would’ve said no. He looked down at her with his wet hands in the air and the polite face coming apart at the edges. He didn’t lie to her. He never had.

“Yes.”

“Of Dominic Ip?”

“Of all of it.” He let his hands drop. Water ran off his fingers onto the floor. “I watched him through the glass and I wanted to put him through it.”

“Chen—”

“I didn’t. I held your hand instead and broke your rule.” He swallowed. “And before that I watched you go in on your own. And come out with three people. And sit at a table laughing for twenty minutes. While I stood outside with a bicycle.”

“You WANTED me to have friends.”

“I’ve wanted it for three years. More than anything. And I got it.” His ears were going red. “And I stood outside, and I didn’t like it. That’s the whole thing. I’m not proud of it.”

She looked up at him.

“You made a plan. For tonight. Didn’t you? Be nice about it. Heat the soup. Ask about the tins.”

His ears went redder.

“…There may have been a plan.”

“I’m not having the soup.”

She went up on her toes and kissed him.

He made a sound against her mouth. His wet hands came down on her back through the hoodie, cold and then warm. He pulled her in and kissed her back hard enough to bend her against the edge of the sink. She didn’t care. She got her hands in his hair and hung on. She kissed him until the polite thing was gone, every bit of it. Until the jealous thing was right out in the open. Then she kissed that too. It was hers.

“Upstairs,” she said against his mouth.

He didn’t argue.

✦ ✦ ✦

His room was dark except for the lamp with the crooked shade. She pushed him down to sit on the edge of the bed and stood between his knees and took his jumper off. He let her. Arms up. Watching her face.

She liked this more than she’d ever admit. His long body going still under her hands, waiting to see what she’d do. He’d wait all night. He always did. She didn’t want him to wait tonight.

“You can stop being careful.”

“I wasn’t being—”

“You were. Since the bottom of the hill.” She took her glasses off and put them on the bedside table. This time they didn’t fall. “So stop.”

He stopped.

He pulled her down and rolled her under him in one go, so fast she laughed out loud. Then he was kissing her throat. Her jaw. The place under her ear that made her arch. Her hoodie went over her head and stuck on her hair, the way his T-shirt had once stuck on his ears.

“Help—I’m STUCK—”

“Hold still.”

“I AM holding still!”

He got her out of it, laughing into her collarbone. Then he wasn’t laughing. Then it was his mouth and his big warm hands, not careful at all, learning her again. Like three years hadn’t been nearly enough. She held on to his shoulders. She said his name. The one she only used in here.

He was different tonight. She felt it. He held her like someone might try to take her out of his hands. His arm hard under her back. His mouth at her ear, saying things he never said in daylight. Plain things.

“Mine.”

“Yes.”

“I watched you. Through the glass. The whole time.”

“I know.”

“I’d have stood out there all night.”

She should have minded. She didn’t mind at all. She wrapped herself round him and pulled him closer, and told him so. The old bed creaked like a boat. The crooked lamp rocked on the table and didn’t fall. Somewhere in the middle she started laughing again and couldn’t stop. He put his forehead against hers and laughed too, and didn’t stop moving. Then nobody was laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on his chest with the lamp still on and his heart going under her ear. She’d stolen his jumper off the floor. It came down to her knees.

Her phone was buzzing in her hoodie pocket, down on the floor. It had been buzzing for an hour.

“Si-Jie. She wants to know if you’re my boyfriend.”

His hand stopped in her hair.

She reached down over the side of the bed and got the phone. She opened the last message. She typed neighbour. Looked at it. Deleted it. Then she didn’t type anything at all. She put the phone face down on the floor and lay back down on his chest.

“You held my hand for three seconds.”

“I know. I said I won’t—”

“Next time,” she said, into his skin, “hold it longer.”

He went quiet. Then she felt him start to smile, slowly, under her cheek. His arm came round her and tightened.

“How much longer?”

“I’ll tell you when I know.”

“Ten seconds?”

“Don’t push it.”

“Eleven.”

She bit his chest. Not hard. He laughed. The phone buzzed again on the floor, and he reached down without letting go of her and turned it over, so the light wouldn’t wake her.

It buzzed once more, face down.

“That’s Si-Jie,” she mumbled.

“How do you know?”

“Only Si-Jie buzzes like that.”

chapters.title: The Boy Next Door, He Always Waits
chapters.desc: A bank wants Eliana quiet, so her family sends Serafina’s fiancé to drive her to her own talk. Nobody tells Yu Chen anything. He’s on the kerb by half past five anyway, and at two in the morning he stops pretending there’s no name for what they are.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody. The boy next door. He always waits.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
There was a man at the bottom of her steps.

Yu Chen saw him from the kitchen window just before eight, while the kettle was going. He made her tea at that counter every morning. Chrysanthemum, dried pear, two bits of rock sugar. He looked out while it boiled, because the window looked at the lane, and the lane was where she came out.

This morning there was a grey estate car at the foot of the Lin steps. A man beside it in a dark jacket, hands at his sides. Where anyone could see them. Yu Chen put the kettle down. The man didn’t look at the house. He looked at the lane. Both ends of it. The roofs. Then, without really moving his head, at the window Yu Chen was standing in. Then away again.

Yu Chen stepped back from the glass. He hadn’t decided to.

At five to eight the red door opened and she came out. Laptop under her arm. Toast in her mouth. The cat hoodie. She stopped on the top step and looked at the man. They talked. He couldn’t hear any of it. Then she got in the front of the grey car, and it went down the lane, slowly, and turned at the noodle stall.

Gone.

The tea was still in the flask on the counter. He’d been going to take it out to her on the step.

Yu Chen: Who was that?

It took her four minutes to answer. That was a very long time for her.

Eliana: Sera’s fiancé. Elowen sent him. it’s nothing. it’s a lift

Yu Chen: Why does Elowen need to send you a lift?

Eliana: because of the talk. the bank. she’s being Elowen. go to your ward

He read it twice in Auntie Dai’s kitchen.

The bank. He knew about the bank. In January she’d found something wrong with a bank and told them. They’d said thank you. Then they’d sent a letter that said something else. She’d laughed about it at the noodle stall. “A lawyer having a feeling,” she’d called it. She was giving a talk about it today. Eleven o’clock, the big hall on the hill.

He’d known all that. He hadn’t known it needed a man in a dark jacket. He poured the tea back into the pot, because there was nobody to take it to. Then he went to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eight weeks to his written finals. He was spending them on a medical ward at City Hospital, fourth floor, beds looking out over the harbour. Most of the patients were old and short of breath. Year Four was supposed to feel like being a doctor. Mostly it felt like being a doctor who wasn’t allowed to sign anything.

The registrar that month was Dr. Yiu. Tired. Kind in the way tired people are. He liked Yu Chen because he wrote neat notes and never needed telling twice. On the ward round Yu Chen presented the man in bed eleven. Pneumonia. Clearly, in the right order. Dr. Yiu nodded and moved on. The man in bed eleven caught Yu Chen’s sleeve.

“You’re the nice one. The tall one. Will you come back later?”

“Of course!”

He smiled and meant it while he was saying it. He took bloods. He wrote up a discharge. He checked his phone in the sluice. Nothing. He checked it again. Nothing. Why would Elowen send a man like that? A man who stood with his hands where people could see them. There was only one answer he could find. Somebody else had a reason to stand near her too.

He opened the food app. No order since last night.

He shut it.

Kenny found him at the nurses’ station.

“Cardiology questions. Library. Tonight. Three hundred of them. Split them?”

“Can’t tonight. Sorry.”

“You never can. What do you even DO?”

“Things…”

Kenny went away. Yu Chen didn’t think about him again. Just after one, she texted.

Eliana: done. it went fine. a lecturer put his head in his hands. that was the good bit. eating noodles

He breathed out. Then he looked at the word noodles. Then at the app. Still nothing. Somebody else had bought them. The man in the dark jacket had bought her lunch. He didn’t like it. He knew he had no right to not like it. He didn’t like it anyway. Steadily. Through a whole afternoon of a man in bed four who couldn’t remember any of his own medicines.

“The white one. For the heart.”

“There are three white ones.”

“The round one!”

“Two of them are round.”

“Then the one my wife puts in the jam.”

Yu Chen wrote that down too. It was the most useful thing anyone had said all day.

Then he went to find Dr. Yiu.

“I need to go.”

Dr. Yiu looked up from a drug chart. In seven months Yu Chen had never once left a ward before he was told he could.

“Is it family?”

The true answer was, it’s a girl who’d be furious if she knew I’d left early because of her.

“Yes.”

“Go on, then.”

He forgot to take his white coat off. He was on the bike and halfway down the hill before he noticed. Pen still in the pocket. He didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was half past five when he got to the bottom of her steps and sat down on the kerb. She hadn’t told him a time. She hadn’t told him anything, except it’s nothing. He sat with the bike beside him and his elbows on his knees and watched the corner by the noodle stall, where the grey car had gone that morning.

The noodle man looked over at him. Then away. He’d seen Yu Chen sit on that kerb more times than anybody could count. After a while he came over with a bowl and put it on the kerb beside him.

“Eat.”

“I’m waiting.”

“You can wait and eat. People do both.”

“Thank you.”

He went back to his pots and banged his ladle on one. Once. Three was for good things. Nothing good had happened yet. It got dark slowly. The lamp at the end of the lane came on. On the far side, the old man was whistling his birds in. Six o’clock. The grey car came round the corner and stopped at the bottom of the steps.

He stood up.

He could see her through the windscreen. She was looking straight at him. Her face did something. He couldn’t have said what. She said something short to the man beside her. Then she got out. Then she stopped and bent down to the window and talked a bit longer. He stood by his bike and waited. Then she came round the car to the steps, and he went up them beside her.

He didn’t take her hand. The man was still in the car, watching. It was the lane. She had rules. He went up the three steps beside her, very close, not touching. At the top she stopped and turned round and looked back at the grey car. She lifted one hand. Just a little. Then she shoved the red door. The bolt stuck, like always. And they were in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hall was dark. Ah Sim had the radio on at the back, and the whole house smelled of ginger. The door shut on the lane, and the car, and the man in the dark jacket. She turned round to say something.

He didn’t let her.

He took her face in his hand, thumb along her jaw, and kissed her. Right there in the dark hall with her back against the inside of the red door.

He wasn’t careful. He’d been careful since before eight that morning. Careful through a ward round. Careful through a man who couldn’t remember his medicines. Careful through an empty app and the word noodles, and half an hour on a kerb. It all went out of him at once.

Her laptop hit his chest between them. She made a surprised little sound. Then her free hand was in the front of his white coat, holding on, pulling him down. She kissed him back the way she did when she’d been frightened and hadn’t said so. He could feel it in her. She’d been frightened too.

“You left early,” she said into his mouth. “You’re in your COAT.”

“Yes.”

“You never leave early.”

“No.”

He kissed her again. In the kitchen, Ah Sim turned the radio up. That was what Ah Sim did instead of coming out. Her glasses had fogged. He took them off, wiped them on the edge of his coat, and put them back on her nose. Straight.

“Who was he?”

“I told you. Sera’s fiancé.”

“Why did your sister send him?”

She looked at him. Close. In the dark. He watched her decide how much to say. He watched her decide on less than all of it. He let her. He’d learned to let her.

“Later. Baba’s due. Go home.” She pushed him gently at the door. “I’ll tell you later. I PROMISE.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t come over the wall. He waited till midnight. Then till one. At his desk, with the cardiology questions he wasn’t doing, looking across the dark garden at her window. Her light was on. Two o’clock. The red door’s bolt stuck and carried across the lane. Same as on a night in June nearly four years ago. He got up, took the blanket from the end of his bed, and went out.

She was on the third step in her black hoodie with her knees up. He stepped over the low wall by the iron rail and sat down beside her. He put half the blanket round her. She let him. She leaned on his arm. For a while nobody said anything.

“I’ll tell you now.”

She told him. Not the bank. He half knew the bank. The rest of it. Plainly, looking at the dark lane.

“After the letter there were messages. Since January. From nobody. Numbers that didn’t exist the next day.”

“Saying what?”

“Nothing. Mostly. Photographs.” She pulled the blanket tighter. “The university gates. The bus stop at the bottom of the hill. Mine.” A pause. “Once, in February, this step. Empty. Taken from the lane.”

He sat very still.

“I’d have found them. I nearly had. By Wednesday I’d have had the whole firm. That’s what I told him. The fiancé.” She pushed her glasses up. “He said that’s WHY they sent someone today. Because they knew I’d find them. They wanted me frightened first.”

“Sent someone?”

“There was a man at the talk. Grey jacket.”

“Who?”

“Nobody. A man they pay. He was going to follow me to the toilets and take a picture of me. Send it to me tonight with nothing written on it. So I’d know they could.” She was looking at her knees. “Haozhen sat down next to him and said something. And he left. I don’t know what he said. He wouldn’t tell me.”

Yu Chen didn’t say anything for a while. He could feel the cold going down through him from the top. Slowly. It had happened at her father’s table. On the path outside the psychology building with Dominic Ip. It felt like a door shutting somewhere inside him on everything that wasn’t useful. A man in a grey jacket had sat in a hall full of people. And waited for her to need the toilet.

“Since January. A photograph of this step. And you didn’t tell me.”

“Because you’d have done THIS. What you’re doing now. Gone all quiet. You’d have sat on that kerb every day for two months and not slept and not done your questions.” She looked at him sideways. “You’ve got FINALS. And your hands have gone cold. Stop it.”

He breathed out. He didn’t stop it, exactly. He put it somewhere he could find it again.

“He drove you all day. He bought you noodles. He sat next to the man. And I was on the fourth floor taking bloods, and you told me it was a lift.”

“It WAS a lift.”

“Eliana.”

She looked down at the step.

“He asked who you were. When we pulled up. He saw you on the kerb, and he asked.” Very quiet. “I said nobody. I said you were nobody. The boy next door. And that you always wait.”

It went in somewhere under his ribs and stayed there. He didn’t let her see. He was good at that. But she knew him better than anyone alive. She heard it anyway, in how still he’d gone. She turned and put her face against his shoulder.

“I didn’t mean nobody.” Into his coat. “I meant—I panicked. He’s Sera’s fiancé. Everybody tells Sera everything. Then Sera tells Elowen, and Elowen tells Aurelia, and by Sunday Baba…”

“I know. I know what you meant.”

He did know. That was the problem. He’d known for three and a half years exactly what she meant every time she said it’s nothing. And he’d said okay every time, because she needed the secret, and he didn’t need anything but her.

Today he’d sat on a kerb with no information and no right to any. A stranger had sat down next to the man who’d come for her, because the stranger was allowed to. Yu Chen wasn’t. If something happened to her, nobody would ring the boy next door. Nobody would even think of it.

He wasn’t anybody’s to ring.

He looked at the lane. The lamp at the end. The noodle stall, shuttered.

“I’m going to say something. You don’t have to answer it. Not tonight. Not soon, if you’re not ready. But I’m going to say it. I’m done not saying it.”

She went still against his shoulder.

“I want to marry you.”

Plainly. Looking at the lane. The way he’d read out a dose. No ring in his pocket. No plan. He’d written eleven over the years and torn every one of them out. He just said it.

“Not now. Not this year, if you don’t want. But I don’t want to be the boy next door who waits. I want to be the one they ring.”

“Chen—”

“I want there to be a word for it. One other people have to use. I’ve been unofficial for three and a half years, and I’d do ten more if you asked me.” He swallowed. “But I’m not going to pretend there isn’t a name for it any more. There is. I know what it is. I’ve always known.”

She’d stopped breathing. He could feel it. Then she was off his shoulder. Off the step. Standing on the cracked stone with the blanket fallen down round her feet, hands at her sides. Looking at him like he’d said something in a language she’d spent her whole life making sure she’d never have to learn.

“You can’t.”

“I just did.”

“You can’t SAY that. That’s the word. That’s the…” Her voice went thin. “People say that and then they’re in a hospital. People say that and they don’t come home. You KNOW that. You know that’s the one thing—”

“I know.”

“Then why would you—”

She stopped. He watched her look for the rest of it. She didn’t find it. She was shaking, and it wasn’t the cold. She looked at him on the step. At the blanket on the stone. At the red door behind her. He stayed sitting. He kept his hands to himself.

He’d made himself a rule on the kerb that afternoon without knowing it. He knew it now. He wasn’t going to touch her to make this easier. Not this. If she came back to him, it would be because she’d answered it. Not because he’d kissed her out of having to.

“I’m not going anywhere. You don’t have to say anything. I’ll be here tomorrow.”

She turned round and went up the steps. She pushed the red door. The bolt stuck. She fought it open. She went in. She shut it. He heard the bolt go home on the inside.

He sat on the third step until the cold came all the way up through him, with the blanket on the stone where she’d dropped it. Then he folded it and left it on the top step by the door, where she’d find it in the morning. He went back over the low wall. He sat at his desk in the dark with the cardiology questions, and looked across the garden at her window.

Her light stayed on until it was nearly light.
